#6406. No Central Air? No Sweat. These Tested Window Air Conditioners Cool Down Spaces Fast

We got our hands on multiple units and looked for models that are quiet, energy-efficient, and easy to install.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When it’s really hot or humid out, opening a window or turning on a fan only gets you so far, especially when your house feels like it’s holding onto heat long after the sun goes down. If you’ve ever tried to sleep in a hot, airless room, you know how quickly feeling “a little warm” turns into being completely miserable. For homeowners and renters without central air conditioning, the standard solutions are typically ductless air conditioners, freestanding units, or window air conditioners.

Window air conditioning units work by pulling in warm and humid air, cooling and drying it, and sending it back into the room while pushing heat outside. Most units double as fans, and many now include dehumidifier modes, which is something you’ll appreciate on those sticky, midsummer days when the air feels truly soupy. And, unlike central air, a window air conditioner can run on a generator during a blackout. That’s a major plus in extreme climates.

The tricky part is finding a window air conditioner that actually fits your space, is easy to install, and doesn’t drive up your energy bill. We looked at a range of models with various features and specs. Some of these we’ve tested hands-on, and a few are newer standouts with great customer reviews. Continue reading to find the window air conditioners that are worth buying right now.

As someone who lives in an older home without ductwork, I’ve owned quite a few window air conditioners over the years in my never-ending quest to find the perfect unit for my house and family. Beyond this personal experience, I worked with a team of testers here at Popular Mechanics to find units on the market that feature reliable construction, notable energy efficiency, quiet operation, and exceptional functionality.

I also spoke with industry expert Kim Lincoln to make sure our recommendations check every box. She’s a third-generation HVAC expert and sales trainer at Service Experts with 25 years of experience.

For the most recent update, I added three new products. The GE 14,000-BTU Smart Window Air Conditioner is an excellent air conditioner for cooling spA/Ces up to about 700 square feet (like living rooms or some open space floors). Meanwhile, the LG ThinQ Window Air Conditioner includes the best collection of smart features I’ve seen out of a window AC.

The GE Profile ClearView sits on your windowsill, taking up just a few inches of space while preserving most of your view. This type of AC may not work well in older homes with radiators below the windows, but it’s a great option if you have the clearance space.

We love that you can still fully open the window for fresh air, which is a rare win for a window unit. This AC also uses an inverter compressor for efficient, low-noise cooling, which makes it perfect for offices and nurseries. The digital controls are simple and straightforward, and the app makes it easy to adjust settings without needing to walk over to the unit itself. Installation can be a bit of a project due to its shape and length, so plan on having an extra set of hands close by.

Full GE Profile ClearView Window Air Conditioner Review

There’s a reason my family owns several of these air conditioners: it’s a no-frills model that’s inexpensive, reliable, and well-sized for rooms up to 150 square feet (most small- to medium-sized bedrooms). My family was gifted one, and we loved it so much that we purchased more for our kids’ bedrooms because the knobs are easy to use and there are no smart features for them to mess with.

This air conditioner has a simple two-knob control system. The top knob controls the cooling setting, while the bottom knob controls fan speed, and you have the option to run the fan with or without cooling. The appliance’s thermostat cycles the air conditioner on and off to keep the temperature within range based on the temperature you set with the top knob.

The lack of smart tech means it can only be controlled from the knobs. That was a pro for us, but it may be a con for other shoppers. Still, it’s an efficient window unit that won’t hurt your wallet and its washable filter saves you money on having to buy replacements.

Full Frigidaire FFRA051WAE Window Air Conditioner Review

This Windmill AC stands out for combining energy efficiency with reliable performance and quiet operation, all of which make it especially useful in bedrooms up to 350 square feet. Its CEER rating of 15 is one of the strongest in this lineup, and the inverter design helps it maintain temperature without the hard stop-start cycling of many traditional window units.

On lower settings, our testing team found it to run subtly enough for overnight use, and we loved how the display dims automatically for better sleep. The fan alone can handle cooler evenings, while hotter days call for full cooling. The app is intuitive and truly smart, letting you adjust settings remotely and sending helpful alerts when it’s time to clean or replace the filter. Maintenance is a key factor in air conditioner longevity, so that’s a huge plus.

Similar in design to our best overall pick, this Midea window unit uses a true U shape so the window can close deeper into the body of the air conditioner. The end benefit is quieter cooling: Once it’s properly installed, the window acts as a sound barrier between the compressor outside and your room inside. That makes it a strong choice for offices up to 350 square feet, where excess noise can become an unwelcome distraction.

The U shape also means the window does not need to be all the way closed—you can lift the window midway up the body of the unit, and let in air from the outside without uninstalling the entire air conditioner. The biggest issue with this option is that it requires a more skilled hand when installing it, with many customers reporting difficulty doing it themselves.

We’ve been using this beast of an AC to cool the entire first floor of our home with great success for a few summers now. It’s a solid pick for larger rooms up to 700 square feet, per the unit’s specifications, which is about the total square footage of our first-floor foyer, dining room, living room, kitchen, and pantry. Depending on your home’s layout and airflow, it’s hard to guarantee it will successfully and sufficiently cool multiple spaces, but it packs serious power for big rooms, too. That said, it’s noisier than other models, so take that into consideration.

While we didn’t need smart features, it’s nice that it connects to Wi-Fi so you can control settings from your phone (or with the included remote), and the interface is straightforward. The unit is designed with energy efficiency in mind, which helps to keep operating costs reasonable for its size. Installation is fairly standard with the included kit, though the unit is heavy, so you’ll want an extra set of hands. It’s likely you’ll need a support bracket, too.

Overall, this is a dependable option for cooling bigger living spaces without overcomplicating things or having to install a mini-split.

If you need an AC that can bring down the temperature quickly in a medium-sized room, take a look at this model. This smart GE unit impressed our team with speed, cooling a 100-square-foot room from 85 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit in about 15 minutes, and it’s rated for spaces up to 350 square feet. That powerful fan helps move cool air farther into the room, so it’s a good fit if you want quick relief without jumping up to an oversized unit that will drive up energy costs for no reason.

The standout feature here (and the reason for that great performance) is the powerful fan, which kept air moving even when full cooling wasn’t necessary. We love the unit’s eco mode, which cycles the compressor and fan to maintain temperature without overworking the unit. We found the installation to be manageable, but easier with two people. We love that GE includes insulation, though you may need to purchase some additional products to create a perfect seal depending on your window. The main drawback is the app, which was difficult to connect to, despite troubleshooting. Customer service at GE is great, though, and the one-year warranty gives peace of mind.

Read Full GE 8,000 BTU Air Conditioner Review

This LG 6,000 BTU unit is a strong small-space pick that adds genuinely useful smart features without overcomplicating things. It’s designed for rooms up to about 250 square feet, making it a better option for bedrooms and home offices than larger living areas.

It pairs easily with LG’s ThinQ app, so you can adjust temperature, fan speed, and schedules from your phone (or with Alexa or Google Assistant). While it’s easy to find an app-controlled window AC these days, this one stands out from the pack a bit. LG has a deeper smart-home ecosystem than most brands manufacturing window ACs, and this model brings that app control, voice-assistant compatibility, scheduling, energy-saver mode, and filter alerts to rooms up to 250 square feet. Customers find the cooling performance is consistent, and the unit includes practical touches like a filter alert and energy saver mode. It’s not the quietest or most powerful option out there, but it balances size, features, and price well for a smart-enabled window AC.

Air conditioners are rated in British thermal units (BTUs), which indicate how much space they can effectively cool. A unit that’s too small will run constantly and never quite get there, but one that’s too large will cool too quickly without removing enough humidity. This leaves the room feeling clammy and uncomfortable.

That’s why several of our superlatives are organized around room size and use case, rather than just standout features. A 5,000-BTU unit may be a smart pick for a small bedroom, dorm room, or compact home office, while an 8,000-BTU model is better suited to a medium-size room where faster cooling and stronger air movement matter. Larger living rooms, open layouts, or rooms with high ceilings may need 10,000 BTUs or more. As a loose rule of thumb, small bedrooms may need around 5,000 to 8,000 BTUs, while larger living areas can require 10,000 BTUs or more. Lincoln says the most common issue is choosing a unit that is too small.

“A window unit may be able to knock down the temperature right near the unit, but that doesn’t mean it’s doing a good job across the full area,” says Lincoln. “In oversized rooms or open floor plans, I see units run nearly nonstop while still leaving parts of the space warm and damp.” She says that’s when customers note a room feels cool but clammy. “The system may be lowering temperature near the unit, but it isn’t really winning the humidity battle across the space.”

This also explains why a powerful fan, efficient compressor, or smart app only matters if it supports the way you’ll actually use the A/C. A stronger fan is most helpful when it moves cool air across a medium or large room, while an efficient inverter unit is especially useful in bedrooms or offices where the AC may run for long stretches. Smart controls are most valuable when they make daily use easier, whether that means scheduling, remote adjustments, energy tracking, or filter reminders.

Before you buy, measure your window—twice. Window units are designed for specific opening widths and heights, and some, like casement or sliding windows, require specialized models. Even with careful planning, you may strike out at first.

“Not every window unit fits every window well, even when the box says it should,” says Lincoln. “Consumers need to look at more than width. The window style, the sash opening, the weight of the unit, and the need for support all matter.” A window unit should be level side-to-side and pitched slightly outward so condensed water drains out of the house—not into your room.

It’s important to consider the unit’s weight, too. Larger units may require a bracket or homemade support to avoid strain and damage to the window and air conditioner.

CEER stands for Combined Energy Efficiency Ratio, and it tells you how efficiently a unit uses electricity over time, not just when it’s actively cooling. Older ratings like EER measure efficiency only while the compressor is running. CEER goes a step further by also factoring in energy used when the unit is idle, like when it’s on standby or cycling on and off throughout the day.

Efficient units use less electricity to deliver the same cooling power, which matters if you’re running the A/C daily through peak summer. Features like programmable timers, eco modes, and inverter technology can further reduce energy use.

When it comes to energy efficiency, Lincoln says it’s just as much about the rating as it is about how you install the unit—specifically how well-sealed the gaps are.

“The best sealing materials are simple, cheap, and worth the effort,” says Lincoln. Foam weatherstripping, rope caulk, and other similar materials can go a long way. “I’ve seen homeowners blame the A/C when the real issue was a half-inch gap letting hot, wet air pour in all afternoon. Sealing is not just about stopping heat. It’s about stopping humidity. And in summer comfort, that distinction matters.”

If you’re used to old-school window units, you’re familiar with the buzz and crackle as they cool. Thankfully, advancements in technology have resolved that issue a bit. Not all A/Cs are created equal when it comes to sound, though. “Traditional window units tend to be louder because they cycle on and off more abruptly,” shares Lincoln. She says inverter models are often better for bedrooms and offices. An inverter unit works more like a dimmer switch than an on/off switch. Instead of turning the AC off, it slows down once it reaches your desired temperature and maintains it by running at a lower, steady speed. “The difference between a hard compressor kick and a steadier low hum is noticeable when you live with it every night.” We’ve noted this feature on the units we reviewed when applicable.

Check the decibel (dB) rating, too. Units in the low 40s are considered quiet, while anything pushing 60 dB or higher can be disruptive, especially at night.

Modern air conditioners do more than just cool. Remote controls, WiFi connectivity, and app integration let you adjust settings from anywhere. Some units include dehumidifier modes, sleep settings, or directional airflow controls that improve comfort without cranking the temperature.

Lincoln says that the “extras” worth paying for don’t often top the specs list, though. “The features worth paying for aren’t always the flashy ones. A lot of people get distracted by phone apps and forget the basics,” she says of most consumers. “The extra features I’d actually pay attention to are variable-speed operation, a true dry mode if you live in a humid climate, auto-restart after a power outage, and a thermostat or sensor that’s actually useful for where people sit or sleep.”

“Window units can be efficient, but only if the install is right,” says our expert Kim Lincoln. “A poorly sealed window AC is basically paying to cool the air around the leak.”

With the right setup, though, window air conditioners can be surprisingly efficient — especially compared to cooling an entire home with central air. Window units give you the option of cooling only the rooms you need at that time.

The key is choosing the right size and looking for models with strong CEER ratings or Energy Star certification. Features like eco mode, programmable timers, and inverter compressors can further reduce energy use by preventing the unit from constantly running at full power.

BTUs measure cooling power, and getting this right is critical. As a baseline, you’ll need about 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. For example, a 150-square-foot room typically calls for a 5,000–6,000 BTU unit. You should also factor in real-world conditions: increase capacity for sunny rooms, kitchens, or higher ceilings, and scale down slightly for shaded spaces.

“When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close.” Be careful about over-purchasing power, though. That doesn’t mean your room will be cooler. Oversizing can lead to quick cooling without proper dehumidification, while undersizing can leave the unit running constantly.

“This is the least glamorous advice and still one of the most important,” says Lincoln. “Clean filters are still one of the biggest performance factors. For window units, the filter should be checked regularly and cleaned about once a month during heavy cooling season, sometimes more often if the home has pets, dust, smoke, renovation debris, or high traffic.”

Most manufacturer specs recommend cleaning the filter every two to four weeks during periods of heavy use, as well. A clogged filter restricts airflow, which can reduce efficiency and force the unit to work harder. The good news is that most window AC filters are washable—just remove, rinse, let dry, and reinstall. Keeping the filter clean helps maintain strong airflow, improves cooling performance, and can extend the lifespan of the unit. If your AC does not have a washable filter, Lincoln recommends keeping a spare on hand. If your AC does not have smart features or a filter reminder, it’s clutch to add this task to your personal calendar so it is not neglected.

#6405. A Lost World of Hippos and Ancient Humans Emerges From the Arabian Desert

Scientists from around the world have joined forces to uncover a remarkably detailed picture of how people lived in Arabia 125,000 years ago.

Around 125,000 years ago, the desert landscape of southern Saudi Arabia looked very different. A vast freshwater lake surrounded by vegetation and open grasslands provided an environment where early humans could live, hunt, and gather resources. Archaeologists have now uncovered an unusually detailed record of life along its shores, offering a glimpse into a period known as Green Arabia.

The discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in Mundafan, within Saudi Arabia’s Empty Quarter. Published in Science, the study was jointly led by the Saudi Heritage Commission, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), and Griffith University, with contributions from several other international institutions. Specialists in geology, archaeology, botany, and micropaleontology combined their expertise to reconstruct the environment and human activities during the last Interglacial period, a warm, humid phase around 125,000 years ago.

Using satellite terrain modeling, researchers mapped an ancient lake covering approximately 340 square kilometers (131 square miles), with a maximum depth of 29 meters (95 feet). Sediments, landforms, and aquatic remains indicated that it was a relatively stable freshwater body surrounded by vegetation and grasslands.

Systematic surveys across more than 130 locations documented over 500 fossil specimens of plants and animals, including invertebrates. Animal remains included hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, and ostriches, revealing the variety of wildlife that inhabited the region when water was far more abundant.

Dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen, a participating researcher from the Heritage Commission and professor of Paleolithic archaeology, described the discovery in the sands of Lake Mundafan as an important archaeological find that sheds light on the relationship between humans, animals, and the ancient environment of southern Saudi Arabia.

Researchers also collected 5,511 stone tools larger than 2 centimeters (0.8 inches) from the main study area. More than 98% were made of flint, and their manufacture showed evidence of Levallois techniques, in which stone is carefully shaped to produce flakes of a desired form. The team used two dating methods on sand and fossil teeth, along with 3D-refitting techniques to investigate how the tools were produced.

Microscopic and chemical analyses of the tools revealed traces of numerous plants, including tubers, bushes, and palm leaves. These residues suggest that people processed plant resources for food and everyday activities. Traces of resin and woody tissue also indicate that some stone points may have been attached to handles or shafts to create hunting weapons.

More intriguingly, some tools contained residues from toxic plants, raising the possibility that early hunters used poisonous compounds in their equipment. Although their precise purpose remains uncertain, the findings represent some of the earliest potential evidence of this practice in Saudi Arabia. The discoveries also include some of the region’s earliest evidence of palm-related vegetation.

The combination of freshwater, animals, plants, and raw materials along the lakeshore supported a range of activities, from stone tool production and hunting equipment preparation to processing food and working with fibers. Because these different traces were preserved together at a single dated site, researchers could examine their relationships in unusual detail.

“This site gives us a rare and richly detailed view of how people lived in a landscape that looks nothing like Arabia today,” said Professor Chris Clarkson, co-lead scientist and Professor of Archaeology at Griffith University’s Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution. “The combination of animal remains, stone tools and plant material in a single, dated context is what makes this discovery so significant.”

Reconstructing that ancient landscape required the combined efforts of researchers across several scientific disciplines and institutions. Their work demonstrates how geological evidence, fossils, archaeological discoveries, and microscopic traces can contribute to a more complete understanding of early human life.

“It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behavior and the environment in the distant past,” said Professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST Professor of Geology and co-lead scientist.

The findings add to growing evidence of Saudi Arabia’s deep human and environmental history, with implications for understanding early human movement and technological development across the Arabian Peninsula. They also highlight the importance of international research partnerships and expanding heritage science expertise within the Kingdom.

“Saudi Arabia has an exceptional archaeological heritage. Building Heritage Science capabilities in the Kingdom will enable us to turn the smallest traces into the biggest stories,” said Professor Laurence Hapiot, co-author and Head of Heritage Research at KAUST.

Reference: “Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore” by Chris Clarkson, Gilbert J. Price, Amir Kalifi, Giacomo Losi, Carney Matheson, Faisal Al-Jibreen, Abdullah M. Alsharekh, Simon J. Armitage, Ikram Blilou, Nicole Boivin, Paul S. Sobbe, Mathew Stewart, Michael D. Petraglia and Frans van Buchem, 12 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aef9342

#6404. This Rare Binary Star Emits Radio Pulses Every Few Minutes. Will It Eventually Explode?

Unusual electromagnetic signals permeate the cosmos, and they range from powerful and deadly gamma-rays down to generally harmless radio waves. The sources of many of these signals are well-understood, and in some cases, special spacecraft have been launched to monitor them. But some remain unexplained.

Radio waves are widespread throughout the cosmos because they come from objects with a wide variety of temperatures. Radio astronomy has been around for decades, so many of these are well-understood. But not all of them. Some of them have only been discovered more recently and are awaiting an explanation.

One of these phenomenon are called long-period radio transients (LPTs), and their periodic radio pulses range from a few minutes to several hours. That's important because it differentiates them from pulsars and their extremely short radio periods. Astronomers have only detected about 15 LPTs in total, and they've had difficulty explaining exactly what they are and how they generate their radio pulses.

There are different hypotheses invoked to explain them. They could be magnetars, which are neutron stars with extremely powerful magnetic fields that rotate very slowly. Or they could be something exotic and speculative, like strange dwarf pulsars.

But at least some of them have been confirmed to be White Dwarf-Main Sequence (WDMS) binaries, a binary star containing a white dwarf (WD) and another main sequence star. Astronomers have only been able to confirm the white dwarf's companion in a handful of cases, and in those, the companion is a red dwarf.

Now astronomers have identified for the first time a LPT that consists of a white dwarf with a Sun-like, G-type star as its companion. Their results are published in Nature Astronomy in a paper titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion." The lead author is Dr. Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR.

At the time of this research, there were only 12 detected LPTs, and the ones with identified components favoured WD and red dwarf pairs. "An optical follow-up confirmed that at least 4 (ouf of 12) long-period transients are binary systems comprising a white dwarf and an M dwarf," the authors write. But this newly-detected LPT, named GPM J071507â114153, bucks that trend. "It is a binary system comprising a low-mass white dwarf and a G-type star identified via optical spectroscopy."

âWe detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,â said co-author Natasha Hurley-Walker, Associate Professor at the Curtin Institute of Radio Astronomy.

The MWA detected 214 separate pulses, and the MeerKAT pinpointed its location based on 33 detected pulses. 26 of MeerKAT's pulses were co-detected by the MWA.

The new LPT has a period of only 7.9âminutes, which is almost certainly from its rotation. The properties of its radio pulses, like its polarization, are modulated by a longer period of about 1.3âdays, which the researchers say is the binary system's orbital period.

Follow-up optical observations and spectrometry came from the Keck Telescopes. "The optical counterpart of J0715-1141 was observed with the low-resolution imaging spectrometer on the Keck 1 telescope on Mauna Kea, Hawaii," the authors write. Those observations were a pair of 1,200 second exposures. They let the researchers determine the nature of the WD's partner star.

This figure from the research shows the optical spectrum of the new LPT, J0715-1141, compared to model spectra from F-type, G-type, and K-type stars. The spectrum most closely matches that of a G-type, Sun-like star. "As a comparison, hotter F-type and cooler K-type stars show distinct spectral features not present in the data," the authors write. The three panels on the right highlight this in three different elements. Image Credit: McSweeney, S.J., Hurley-Walker, N., Bahramian, A. et al. A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion. Nat Astron (2026).

In this case, the WD's binary partner is a star like our Sun, which is far more massive and luminous than the M dwarfs (red dwarfs) found in other LPTs. So this rules out the idea that only WD-red dwarf pairs can generate LPTs.

Astronomers and astrophysicists want to know exactly how these radio pulses are generated. Can any of their observations help researchers determine the exact source of the radio pulses? Not exactly, but the clarity of the pulses helps narrow it down.

âThis is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,â said lead author McSweeney.

"We conclude that in long-period transients powered by white dwarf binaries, the coherent radio pulsed emission crucially depends on its interaction with the companion star, which we show can be G-type stars in day-long orbits," the researchers write.

There's another suprise in these findings. The pulses from the WD let the researchers detect stellar flares from the Sun-like star as it passed in front of the WD.

âAs a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a âstellar prominenceâ, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a starâs surface,â Hurley-Walker said. âItâs amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.â

This image shows a solar prominence from the Sun in 2010, with Earth shown for scale. The researchers were able to detect one of these coming from the main sequence star in the pair, as the white dwarf moved behind it. That's pretty impressive for a star that's 5,000 light years away. Image Credit: NASA/SDO

One questions astronomers ask is how these types of binaries form, and the researchers have a hypothesis for that. They say the system could've formed through binary evolution. "One possibility is that the present configuration of the system arises through post-common-envelope (CE) binary evolution," they write. The progenitor of the system most likely had an intermediate-mass primary with a lower-mass companion on a wider orbit. "As the primary evolved off the main sequence and expanded into a giant, unstable mass transfer initiated a CE phase, during which orbital energy and angular momentum were transferred to the envelope, leading to its ejection and substantial orbital shrinkage."

The primary star was left as an exposed stellar core, and evolved to become a WD, creating the situation the astronomers see today: a WD star with a G-type partner, that are still in a binary relationship, but detached from the common envelope they once shared.

As for the system's future, it could hold a cataclysmic explosion.

Binaries like this that have left their common envelopes, and that consist of a WD and a massive main-sequence star, are potential breeding grounds for eventual Type Ia supernovae. This can happen as their orbit decays and the WD accretes material from its companion. Once enough material builds up on the accreting WD, it explodes and destroys the WD. Or they could created a double degenerate WD-WD merger, if the main sequence companion collapses before the binary orbit decays.

Could the radio signals from LPTs be used to find the progenitors of these supernovae explosions?

"Radio detections of LPTs may offer a route to finding cooler WDs around hotter stars at greater distances than traditional ultraviolet and optical surveys," the authors write.

The upcoming Square Kilometre Array could be the key to this.

"In an era of larger and more sensitive radio surveys, such as those to be conducted by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, this may form a new pathway for investigating the progenitors of type Ia supernovae," the authors write.

#6403. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.

#6402. 12 Years of Research Reveal Something Alarming Happening to Wild Elephants

A 12-year study in Sri Lanka links declining numbers of wild female Asian elephants to abrupt social fractures that may be difficult to repair.

Asian elephants rely on one another to find food, acquire information, and care for young. Keeping that support network intact requires opportunities to build new relationships as old connections are lost.

In Sri Lanka’s Udawalawe National Park, a shrinking population appears to be straining that social system. An analysis of more than 440 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years found that large, densely connected communities had given way to smaller, more isolated groups. The remaining females were changing their relationships with one another as their numbers fell.

“We see individual elephants leaving and possibly dying at accelerating rates, but new individuals are not coming into the population,” said Anastasia Madsen, the postdoctoral researcher who led the study. “With fewer individuals in the population, those who are left will naturally have fewer relationships. However, the remaining elephants are also changing their relationships with each other.”

Published November 12 in Science, the research comes from the University of California San Diego’s School of Biological Sciences. Madsen works in Associate Professor Shermin de Silva’s laboratory in the Department of Ecology, Behavior and Evolution.

The analysis points to a combination of likely deaths, elephants leaving permanently, and fewer incoming individuals as explanations for the population decline. Poaching and conflicts with humans already cause deaths in many elephant populations. Disrupted connections between habitats and reduced food availability may also contribute as ecological conditions change across the 119-square-mile park and its surroundings, though these remain possible pressures rather than established causes of the social changes observed here.

The researchers interpret the shift in community structure as evidence that the population may have crossed a critical threshold, or social tipping point.

“We found that gradual accumulation of losses from turnover preceded sudden change in the social networks among females in a wild population of Asian elephants,” the researchers explained in the study.

That sequence raises the possibility that losses can build for years before the organization of an animal society changes abruptly. The resulting fragmentation could be difficult to repair.

“In general, we need to be more aware of these types of tipping points where we see sudden shifts after changes have been slowly building up,” said Madsen. “Once we move past the tipping point, it’s much harder to go back to previous states.”

The findings add to discussions about conserving elephant populations as people expand into areas where the animals historically thrived. For social species, opportunities to share space and develop relationships are part of what sustains a community.

“We can probably all relate to the feeling of social isolation brought about, paradoxically, with the advent of digital communications that seem to remove the physical constraints of needing to be in the same place at the same time,” said de Silva, who also serves as president and founder of the conservation nonprofit Trunks & Leaves Inc.. “But for many social species, which includes ourselves as much as elephants, we have to remember that social connectivity is very much a matter of sharing space and building relationships throughout our lives. Crucially, in order to have resilient communities, we need to be able to replace the relationships that are lost over time.”

Future studies can use the findings to investigate how animal societies change, how to detect those shifts, and which factors make communities vulnerable.

“We are gaining more evidence that studying social patterns is an important tool for us to see when things are going wrong in natural populations and, hopefully, to be able to do something about it,” said Madsen.

Reference: “Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants” by Anastasia E. Madsen, T. V. Pushpakumara, U. Sameera Weerathunga, Devaka K. Weerakoon and Shermin de Silva, 12 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aef6714

#6400. This Supernova is 50 Million Light Years Away, But That's Close Enough For Astronomers

A new supernova has been spotted in NGC 1433, a spiral galaxy about 50 million light years away. That's pretty close for supernova observations, and it's an opportunity for detailed follow-up study. It's not a core-collapse supernova, where a massive star has burned through its fuel and collapses and explodes. It's a Type Ia supernova. That means it's happening in a binary star, where the exploding star is a white dwarf.

In type Ia supernova, a white dwarf, called the accretor star, draws material away from another star called the donor star. Material builds up on the surface of the white dwarf until it breaches the Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.44 solar masses. Then the white dwarf explodes and is obliterated. A type Ia supernova can also occur in a double white dwarf binary, where the two stars merge and explode.

This supernova is named SN 2026ahvu, where the suffix ahvu is a chronological identifier. It signifies that the supernova is the 41,855th transient discovered in 2026. But even though thousands of transients and supernovae have been found this year, this one is still particularly noteworthy for its relative proximity to Earth, and because it was detected early.

SN 2026ahvu was discovered on November 2nd by ATLAS, the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System. ATLAS is designed and optimized to detect incoming near-Earth Objects shortly before they reach Earth, but it can also detect other transients.

New transients are recorded on the Transient Name Server (TNS), a transient registry sanctioned by the International Astronomical Union (IAU). The TNS also hosts AstroNotes, where short notes are posted describing new transients when they're discovered.

The AstroNotes for SN 2026ahvu reads: "ATLAS operates with 4 x 0.5m telescopes in Hawaii (Haleakala and Mauna Loa), Chile (El Sauce) and South Africa (Sutherland), and a fifth unit in Tenerife, Canary Islands. We are robotically surveying the whole sky with a cadence of 1 day between -50 and +50 and 2 days in the polar regions, weather permitting. While carrying out the primary mission for Near-Earth Objects, we search for and publicly report stationary transients to the IAU Transient Name Server."

"We report a new transient source, most likely a supernova in the galaxy NGC 1433. We are submitting AstroNotes for transients that are either within 100 Mpc, or have some other interesting feature to bring to the community's attention, such as bright nuclear transients, slowly rising or rapidly fading objects."

In this case, the SN's brightness is rising, and that's important for observations. It gives astrophysicists an opportunity to observe the supernova from an earlier point in its evolution. When it was first discovered, its apparent magnitude was 17. A few days later, it was at 13.5. (Lower apparent magnitude means the object is brighter.)

The Dark Energy Camera on the VÃ­ctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope captured these images of NGC 1433 before and after SN 2026ahvu exploded. The before images are from the Dark Energy Survey, DECam's primary job. The after image was taken after ATLAS detected the supernova and alerted other astronomers. The orange star below and to the right is a foreground Milky Way star. Image Credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Acknowledgment: PIs: G. Narayan & T. Murphey (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign) Image processing: M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

When supernovae are detected, astronomers are alerted and other telescopes watch closely. In this case, there are new images of SN 2026ahvu from the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and the Gemini South telescope.

Type Ia supernovae are typically brightest for about 6 months, but their brightness inevitably drops over time. Their peak brightness lasts several days and is powered by the decay of an unstable nickel isotope, Nickel-56 (56Ni.) Then the decay of âµâ¶Co â âµâ¶Fe creates a weaker tail of light.

This simple schematic shows the typical light curve for a Type Ia supernova, relative to the Sun. The peak is primarily due to the decay of nickel-56 (56Ni), while the later stage is powered by 56-Cobalt to 56-Iron, which is stable. Image Credit: By Xenoforme~commonswiki (attribution as on the source page); SVG reconstruction: PJ Geest. - This file was derived from: SNIacurva.png, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/201323073

About 2 or 3 months after the initial explosion, the ejecta will have thinned out and expanded enough to form a nebula. At that point, when astronomers look at the spectra, they're seeing the composition of the entire exploded star, not just its core. It's a fairly well-understood progression, but there's always room for more observations and more refinement.

Type Ia supernovae are important because they serve as standard candles in the cosmic distance ladder. It's the system astronomers use to find distances to celestial objects that are way too distant for more direct measurements like parallax. So the more opportunities they have to study Type Ia supernovae, the more accurate the cosmic distance ladder is.

Beyond their scientific importance, supernova remnants are among the most visually stunning objects that exist.

This is the Crab Nebula, probably the most well-known supernova remnant. The Hubble captured this image of the nebula, showing it less than 1,000 years after its progenitor exploded. So it's possible that our descendants will see something similar when they observe SN 2026ahvu reads a millennium from now. Image Credit: By NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (Arizona State University) - A Giant Hubble Mosaic of the Crab Nebula, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/516106

More images and observations, included detailed study of how the explosion's light changes over time, will follow. The supernova is also within reach of astrophotographers, so there could be some fantastic images arriving soon.

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#6398. A Deadly Blood Cancer May Begin More Than 50 Years Before Symptoms Appear

Many older adults carry blood mutations linked to acute myeloid leukemia, yet most never develop it. The difference may lie in how those cells grow.

Acute myeloid leukemia can begin developing decades before diagnosis. In two-thirds of women who eventually developed the aggressive blood cancer, researchers traced the first cancer-driving mutation to before age 20. In some cases, more than 50 years passed before the disease was diagnosed.

The discovery reveals how slowly leukemia can take shape, with mutated blood cells gradually accumulating genetic changes before their growth accelerates. It also points to a possible opportunity to identify people at risk long before they become ill.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) affects around 2,700 people in the UK each year. Only about one in six survive five years after diagnosis. Predicting who will develop it has been difficult because many healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations also found in leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, rarely progresses to cancer, and scientists have not fully understood what separates those who eventually develop AML from those who do not.

To investigate, researchers from the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL) turned to years of stored blood samples. Their study, published November 11, 2026, in Nature, examined 47 women who later developed AML and 46 matched women who remained free of blood cancer.

The samples came from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS), which collected annual blood samples from around 50,000 women for up to 11 years. Some provided a record reaching 15 years before diagnosis. The women who developed AML were diagnosed between ages 53 and 83, at an average age of 72. None of the samples were collected at diagnosis.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led UKCTOCS, explained how the ovarian cancer screening trial created an unexpected resource for studying other diseases.

“While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement.”

Using ultra-sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical modeling, the researchers reconstructed when mutations appeared and how quickly the affected blood cells multiplied.

The earliest mutations often gave these cells a decades-long head start. At first, their numbers increased very slowly, taking years to double. Each additional cancer-driving mutation accelerated their growth by roughly two- to threefold. By the time cells carried four cancer-driving mutations, their populations could double in just weeks.

These expanding populations of genetically related cells are called clones. Once established, they tended to grow at a predictable rate, slowing only when they ran out of room or a faster-growing clone overtook them.

That consistency could make it possible to estimate a person’s future risk from a relatively small number of blood samples. Professor Jamie Blundell of the University of Cambridge’s Early Cancer Institute, who led the study, said:

“Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood’s evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now.”

The researchers also identified a particularly concerning pattern. In at least one-third of the women who developed AML, a mutated cell population had already become dominant in the blood years before diagnosis. This is known as a somatic sweep. None of the women who remained free of blood cancer showed the same phenomenon.

The team found further evidence linking these sweeps to AML risk using UK Biobank data. People with this pattern had a greatly increased risk of developing the disease. However, standard genetic analysis can overlook the warning sign by mistaking these acquired mutations for inherited genetic variants.

There was also an important difference in how early the changes became detectable. In around one in five cases, expanding populations of mutated cells did not appear until just one to two years before diagnosis. This means that the opportunity to identify and monitor high-risk individuals may vary considerably.

Dr. Caroline Watson, a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute and first author of the study, said the findings help explain why AML can seem to emerge so suddenly.

“As a hematologist, I’ve seen how suddenly AML can change someone’s life. This study shows that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways.”

Watson is also an Honorary Consultant Hematologist at Addenbrooke’s Hospital, where she sees patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic, Europe’s first clinic focused on leukemia prevention. The clinic already monitors people with blood-cell mutations associated with an increased risk of leukemia.

“At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today’s findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible.”

The researchers now want to find out whether slowing the growth of high-risk clones could prevent them from developing into leukemia. Their mathematical models suggest that even a modest reduction in growth over the decade or more between the second mutation and diagnosis could substantially lower the chance of progression.

Professor Blundell said: “Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia.”

Testing whether this approach can safely and effectively slow mutated cell populations in people at high risk is the team’s next step.

Reference: “Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia” by Caroline J. Watson, Gladys Y. P. Poon, Hamish A. J. MacGregor, Adriana V. A. Fonseca, Sophia Apostolidou, Aristi Damaskou, Christopher Boniface, Samuel Hackett, Aleksandra Gentry-Maharaj, Usha Menon and Jamie R. Blundell, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x

If you don’t mind skipping the bells and whistles, these affordable appliances—all priced under $1,000—get the job done.

Many of today’s high-end washers have price tags in the thousands, but if you’re shopping on a budget, the good news is that you can find cheap washing machines that cost much less and work just as well.

Whether you want a full-size washing machine to handle your family’s oversized loads or a more compact model that can be tucked in a closet, there are a number of highly rated appliances well under $1,000. Some even have high-end features that are generally reserved for more expensive machines, such as a built-in water faucet or sanitization cycle, which helps make laundry day quicker and easier than ever.

For more of the best washing machines available today, check out our top picks for front-loading washers, top-loading washers, and all-in-one washer-dryers.

All the products have a rating of three stars or higher, and we prioritized washing machines from well-regarded brands with good customer service and warranties.

For our most recent update, we reviewed current pricing and availability across major retailers, replaced outdated models, and added new picks based on what offers the best features for different situations. We also consulted with Amy Chernoff at AJ Madison to make sure our buying advice reflects how today’s budget washers compare to their pricier counterparts.

A full-size, high-efficiency washing machine for under $700 isn’t easy to find, but this model from Whirlpool checks all the boxes. The top-loading machine has a 3.5-cubic-foot capacity, and it uses a dual-action spiral agitator to deeply clean your clothing.

This popular washing machine comes with a wide selection of cycles and settings to customize each load. It has options for quick washes, delicates, and bulky items, as well as an auto-sensing feature that uses just the right amount of water for each load.

If all you want is a dependable full-size washer for the least money, this Amana is where I’d start. The high-efficiency agitator and wash system dig into everyday dirt and stains, and I like that the stainless steel wash basket won’t chip or rust over the years the way porcelain-tubs can. When you need to fully soak a bulky load like towels or a comforter, the Deep Water Wash option fills the tub to the max instead of leaving you stuck with an auto-sensed water level.

There’s also an automatic fabric softener dispenser that releases at the right point in the cycle, plus a Quick Wash for small, lightly soiled loads. And thanks to the Late Lid Lock, you get extra time to toss in a stray sock or forgotten shirt before the spin cycle kicks in.

The trade-off is no Wi-Fi, no app, and no sanitize cycle. For a no-frills workhorse that just gets laundry clean, though, those are easy features to give up.

This Samsung washing machine packs an impressive number of features, including a quick wash cycle that completes a full load in under 30 minutes. It has an extra-large 5.2-cubic-foot drum that can easily handle king-size comforters and bulky loads, and a built-in faucet at the back of the tub for pretreating stains before starting a cycle.

Unlike most washers in this price range, Samsung includes Wi-Fi connectivity and smart home integration, so you can remotely start, stop, and schedule loads and get end-of-cycle alerts on your phone. It also works with Alexa and Google Assistant.

Other features include a soft-close lid, a manual water-level override for filling the tub higher than the automatic sensor would, and Energy Star certification, which many budget washers lack. The only notable omission is a steam cycle, but that’s a minor trade-off at this price.

At 4.5 cubic feet, this GE model has a drum that’s big enough to wash a comforter or a week’s worth of clothes for a small family. Similar to the Amana, this GE washer uses a dual-action agitator, where the top half moves independently from the bottom to guide clothes through the water while the lower section agitates along the bottom of the basket. That two-piece design circulates clothes more evenly than a single-piece agitator, which tends to push everything in one direction.

Stainless steel lines the tub instead of porcelain-coated plastic, so chipping and rust spots aren’t a concern down the road. You can also manually control the water level up to 26 gallons—something other high-efficiency washers don’t let you do.

A sanitize cycle hits temperatures high enough to kill 99 percent of bacteria, which is useful for towels, bedding, and sweaty gym clothes. There is no app support, so you can’t start a load remotely or get a notification when a cycle finishes. Instead, you’ll have to listen for the buzzer or set your own timer.

The agitator in this Whirlpool can pop out, setting it apart from other machines on this list. You can remove it when you need to fit something bulky, like a comforter or sleeping bag, then snap it back in for everyday loads. The capacity shifts from 4.2 to 4.3 cubic feet with the agitator removed, and bulky items sit flatter without bunching up around a center post.

In addition to its removable agitator, there are twelve wash cycles that give you several options for different loads. A presoak option lets you loosen stains and wash in a single run instead of soaking separately in a sink or bucket. The sanitize cycle uses higher water temperatures to kill bacteria, which is useful for bedding and gym clothes. A soft-close lid keeps it from slamming every time you load clothes.

While other models on this list let you manually override the water level to fully submerge a bulky comforter or sleeping bag, this Whirlpool relies on auto-sensing only, so you’re stuck with whatever the sensor decides is enough.

Samsung’s front-load washer can easily stack with a matching dryer to cut your laundry footprint roughly in half. It has a depth at just over 31 inches with the door closed, so it can tuck into tighter spaces than a standard front-loader. The drum itself is also 4.5 cubic feet with a stainless steel interior, matching the capacity of the full-size top-loaders on this list.

Samsung’s vibration reduction system dampens noise and movement during spin cycles, which matters if the washer sits on an upper floor or shares a wall with a living space. You can pause a cycle and add a forgotten item through the door—something some front-loaders won’t let you do.

Ten wash cycles cover the basics, plus there’s a prewash and a soak option. However, there’s no sanitizing cycle, so you may have a harder time hitting the higher temperature needed to kill bacteria in towels or bedding.

Other washers push hair around and hope it goes down the drain, which can clog pipes over time. This Maytag model features a built-in filter that catches pet hair during the wash cycle, collecting it so you can clean it out later. The Pet Pro option adds extra water and a deep rinse specifically to work with that filter, so hair actually lifts off fabric instead of reattaching during the spin.

The drum is 4.7 cubic feet with a stainless steel basket and agitator. An Extra Power option adds a pre-wash and extra agitation to any cycle, which helps get rid of stains, rather than pretreating by hand. There’s also a built-in water faucet on the machine itself for spot-treating stains before you start a load.

There are 11 wash cycles, plus an option to add more water when auto-sensing isn’t enough. It’s a good option to have when washing heavy blankets or dog beds that need to be fully submerged. Note, though, that there isn’t a delay start feature, so you can’t load it and schedule it to run so it finishes right when you get home from work.

This GE model features app support, allowing you to start, stop, and monitor cycles from your phone. It can also send you notifications when a load finishes and download extra wash cycles that weren’t on the machine when you bought it. It works with Alexa and Google Assistant too, so you can check on a load with just your voice.

The drum is a spacious 5.0 cubic feet with an impeller instead of an agitator, so there’s more room for bulky items. Antimicrobial protection is built into the tub cover, dispenser drawer, and drain hose to help keep mildew and odor from building up between washes. There’s a sanitize cycle too, while the dispenser has separate slots for liquid detergent, detergent pods, fabric softener, and bleach.

There is no steam option and the agitator isn’t as tough on stains, but the GE is a great option if you’re looking for smart features.

When shopping for a cheap washing machine, you’ll need to decide whether you want a full-size, portable, or manual model. Most of the full-size options you’ll find under $1,000 are top-loading washers, and they offer a large capacity as well as more settings and cycles. However, there are a few select front-loading models in this price range, as well.

For those with limited space, portable washing machines have a more compact footprint and can easily be stored in a closet. However, these machines typically require a faucet connection for operation and don’t always wring out your clothes, making them trickier to dry.

Finally, manual washing machines are the most affordable, but they require a bit of elbow grease for operation. You usually have to crank or agitate the machine by hand, but these models don’t require electricity, making them ideal for camping or off-the-grid living.

The capacity of washing machines is generally measured in cubic feet. Most standard-size appliances have a capacity of 3.5 to 5 cubic feet and are suitable for average households. For reference, a washer with a capacity of 4.5 cubic feet can wash a king-size comforter. If you have a small household, you’ll likely be fine with a smaller-capacity washing machine. A compact machine with 2.3 cubic feet can wash about 6 towels.

Cheap washing machines often have fewer wash cycles than more expensive models. In general, you’ll find most affordable washers have between eight and 12 wash cycles, including standard ones like quick or light wash, delicates, and heavy-duty. There are also several temperature settings on most washers, and some allow you to select the water level and soil level as well. These basics are generally sufficient for most loads of laundry, but if you want more advanced settings—such as sanitization or fabric-specific cycles—you may need to spend a little extra.

To help save money on operation costs, you may want to look for a high-efficiency washing machine, frequently abbreviated as HE. These models use 20 to 66 percent less water, saving around 6,000 gallons of water per year for an average family. You may also want to look for an Energy Star-certified appliance, which uses 25 percent less energy than standard models.

Amy Chernoff, VP of Marketing and Appliance Expert at AJ Madison, says that budget washing machines will still get the job done. The differences are in everything else—build quality, noise, fabric care, and how long the machine holds up under heavy use.

The trade-offs at lower price points are less about cleaning power and more about small details. “You are usually giving up fabric care refinement and overall build quality rather than basic cleaning performance,” Chernoff says.

That means simpler drum movement, fewer specialty cycles, and suspension systems that don’t dampen vibration as well. Over the years, a pricier washer tends to be gentler on your clothes, but for most people washing everyday loads, a more affordable model gets the job done.

A cheap washer doesn’t automatically mean higher utility bills. “Many affordable modern models are still quite efficient, especially if they carry an Energy Star certification,” Chernoff says. Some of the machines on this list are Energy Star certified, so they should be just as efficient as more expensive models.

A single person or couple can usually get by with 3.5 to 4.5 cubic feet. Families should look at 4.5 cubic feet or larger, which offers enough room for bedding, towels, and several days of clothes in one load.

“Choosing a slightly larger machine than you think you need can reduce the number of loads per week and make laundry more convenient over time,” Chernoff says. Every washer on this list falls between 4.2 and 5.0 cubic feet, so even the smallest option here handles a full week of laundry for two people without cramming everything in.

#6396. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Z. Yu et al. High fiber diet mitigates exposure risk of nanoplastics in male mice. Nature Communications. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78675-7
