Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. But it has already improved, by a lot. In the latest tests, this brain-to-voice process produces words that are understandable – reaching about 95 percent accuracy for listeners. Here’s Casey speaking test sentences. It comes from a preprint manuscript posted on the website bioRxiv.

[Audio] The day is not over yet. Please come in with me.

Sanders: Scientists have another thing on their to-do list. And this one goes beyond the words themselves. Here’s Gilja, from Paradromics.

Gilja: Let’s say I identify whether a sentence is a statement or a question. Well, now you can pass that information on to speech synthesis, so that you get these two different versions.

Sanders: The same words could be a statement or a question. You see what he means. You see what he means? And that information can be pulled out from a person’s brain activity.

Gilja: If I’m decoding prosodic information, if I’m decoding speed, when a word is meant to appear, that can also be passed on to modern speech synthesis systems, so that you’re more accurately capturing the prosody that somebody intends. Same thing with loudness, right? So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Now, today’s voice clones can add these emotional layers onto words already. Here’s what Jules told me when I asked him about whether his voice clone can do it.

Jules: Oh, there are plenty of things it does that are all the above. But one thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: So there’s loudness, emphasis, pitch — all of these things contribute to what words means. But imagine if a brain implant can pick up these cues directly — no typing required. Here’s Hochberg.

Hochberg: There’s a lot that can be conveyed through the emphasis, through the tone, through even the humor that can sometimes be conveyed by the way that somebody who’s able-bodied may speak a particular sentence. All of those, I think, really can be captured by these implantable brain-computer interfaces by harnessing the rich neural activity that’s available from the brain. We should be able to restore a lot of that.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky is one of the UC Davis researchers working with Casey and Hochberg. He and his colleagues are working on some of these ideas.

Stavisky: And even now we’re continuing to improve that and actually adding additional layers. So we have one forward-looking project where we can maybe decode the kind of emotional valence of how he’s trying to say it. Is he trying to say something in an angry way or in a surprised way or in a happy-sounding way, to kind of further make it more expressive.

Sanders: They’re even trying  to decode singing. Well, OK, it’s really more of a hum at this point, he says. But those sorts of tone shifts could, in theory, be deciphered.

Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6357. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

#6356. The 6 Best Air Hockey Tables for Your Home Arcade

Ice out your opponents with these editor-approved picks.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Whether it’s competitive head-to-head matches or family game night, air hockey tables are an endlessly replayable way to bring the fun of the arcade and the ice rink into your home. Just like pool tables and ping-pong tables, air hockey tables come in several sizes and styles to suit your space and aesthetic.

A basic tabletop air hockey table runs under $100, though for an upgraded model with a frame and legs, expect to pay $300 to $500. For the most premium air hockey tables, you’re looking at what’s essentially a significant piece of furniture that typically costs $750 and up. High-quality tables often have wood or metal frames, LED lighting, and powerful fan motors for smoother gameplay.

While air hockey tables miniaturize the sport, buying one isn’t a small decision. Before you drop some change on a table, check out our list of the best air hockey tables we recommend, plus all the key features to look out for as you shop.

Looking for more games to play at home? Check out our stories on the best PS5 games, the best Xbox games, and the best Nintendo Switch games.

This 7.5-foot-long air hockey table is a perfect size for teens and adults. With a near-regulation 82-inch rink and a 120-volt motor, the air hockey table is both big enough and powerful enough to provide high-level gameplay for even the most competitive players.

The table is bordered by multi-colored LED lights that illuminate the rink as well as the two goals. The purchase also includes two rechargeable LED light-up pushers and a hockey puck for in-the-dark action.

The air hockey table has a built-in scoreboard that automatically registers and counts goals as they happen in real time. This sensor is also synced up to speakers that play upbeat music throughout the game and sound effects whenever you score.

For powerful action without the size and cost of a regulation table, this option from Triumph Sports is well worth considering. The 54-inch-long air hockey table is affordably priced yet still offers many of the features of more expensive choices.

It features a dual-motor blower, LED corner lights that light up when you score, and a digital scorekeeper that automatically racks up goals as they happen. The air hockey table also has a built-in abacus for manually counting your goals.

Similar to other tables on this list, it comes with light-up LED pushers and a light-up LED puck that make it easy to play in dark rooms.

Forget the legs and focus on the gameplay. This space-saving 40-inch-long tabletop air hockey table is a win for your wallet and your game. The tabletop design still offers a high-powered, 100V fan motor that propels air to replicate arcade-quality machines, with quiet, even airflow and a smooth, frictionless surface.

The air hockey table also has two manual sliding abacus scorers on each end, so you can keep track of your own goals as you play. Because it has no legs, the table can be easily stored in a closet or under the couch whenever it isn’t in use, saving valuable space in your game room.

Don’t limit yourself to just one game. This air hockey table also has an attachable top table designed for ping pong. The ping pong table has a mesh net in the center and comes with two paddles and two balls. In order to use it, simply place it on top of your air hockey table and slide it into place.

Underneath that table tennis top is one of the higher quality air hockey tables on this list. It sits at 80 inches long for near-regulation size and comes with NHL logos on the table legs and in the center of the rink.

The air hockey table also has an LED scoreboard built directly into the rail and speakers that play sound effects while you play. An underrated but well-appreciated feature of this table are the leg levelers. This helps maintain a level and fair playing field for both table tennis and air hockey.

For a serious gameroom upgrade, you might want to go with an all-in-one machine, especially if you’re limited on space. This one offers virtually every tabletop game imaginable, including chess, cards, checkers, bowling, and backgammon. In other words, you can host poker night and wind down the night with an intense game of air hockey, with little work involved. It features over 50 accessories to keep game night exciting, and the space-saving design makes it compact and portable for easy storage. This is a two-birds-with-one-stone situation here.

Some people consider air hockey tables an “eyesore.” Or at least my mom did when I was a kid. The Brookdale Air Hockey Table from Wayfair, though, features an elevated, rustic design and blends in well with modern decor. It offers just as much function as form, though, with a strong 110-volt airflow, in-game sound effects, and a built-in control panel for quick, easy play. Sort of the best of both worlds.

Air hockey table sizes range from full regulation length (84 inches), which you see at an arcade, to miniature tabletop options that are not much bigger than a board game. Between the two of them are a large number of mid-sized choices that fit comfortably into game rooms without monopolizing the entire space. If you plan on building a room around your air hockey table, we recommend regulation size. Otherwise, measure out the space you want to place the table in and buy one with dimensions that fit it.

There’s a big difference in the price and quality of the tables we selected below depending on their use case. For casual fun, you can get away with choosing a smaller, less expensive table. Tabletop options that can be set up and stored when not in use are also a great option for the less competitive air hockey fan.

More serious players should stick with larger options, which have powerful motors and well-placed fans that create a consistent feel across the entire playing surface. They should also look for a table with wide, sturdy legs that keep it in place even as you move and dive for the puck.

Many air hockey tables come with more than just a rink and pucks. Several options have LED lights to up the atmosphere or come with a digital scoreboard that automatically keeps track of goals and time. Some air hockey tables even have speakers that blast music and sound effects tied to the game. Several options on our list also provide a set of light-up pushers and pucks so you can even play in the dark.

We kept a range of ages, abilities, and prices in mind when making our air hockey table selections. The goal was to find high-quality products that would suit different space and design needs without absolutely breaking the bank. We researched hundreds of products ourselves, consulted expert assessments, and of course read through thousands of consumer reviews before making our final choices. Our final choices on this list reflect what we believe to be the best air hockey tables depending on your personal needs and budget.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6353. The 7 Best Noise-Canceling Headphones Clear Out the World So You Can Listen to What You Love

These cans and earbuds knock out background noise so you can focus or relax.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Noise-canceling headphones were once a niche category, dominated by high-priced over-ear cans. Throughout most of the 2010s, those seeking to drown out ambient noise distractions at work or during travel had to spend upward of $300 to get a pair up to the task. These days, that's no longer the case. The market is jam-packed with quality noise-canceling headphones, including reliable models that start below $100. Having so many options to choose from can rightfully be overwhelming even for tech-savvy shoppers. To help you find the best noise-canceling headphones worth investing in, I spent months testing highly rated options from leading brands and created this buying guide to share my recommendations.

Read more related reviews in our best wireless headphones and best wireless earbuds buying guides.

I’ve been testing consumer tech products, including audio gear, since 2011. Before I began testing, I spent a day sifting through product specs and features to handpick up-to-date products from reputable makers across the price spectrum—from budget to premium.

My testing routine included spending at least a week with each headset on this list. I used it at work, during my daily commutes, and, of course, while traveling domestically and internationally. These scenarios allowed me to properly evaluate the products’ design and ergonomics.

To evaluate the audio performance of the headphones, I streamed a carefully curated Apple Music playlist with tracks in various genres, including live albums. The eclectic music selection helped me experience the ability of the headphones to produce bass, treble, and midrange. I also used the cans to stream podcasts, watch video content, and play video games.

Traveling by plane and working in a large open office gave me perfect scenarios to test the noise-canceling capabilities of all headphones. I paid close attention to how each set performed in this critical area, keeping in mind its form factor and price tag.

Ambient mode for being aware of your surroundings is just as essential and a key component of my testing routine. I also made sure that the headphones performed well during telephone, FaceTime, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom calls.

Regarding battery life, I meticulously observed how frequently I had to charge each headset. Spending days without battery anxiety was a benchmark for excellence in this department.

Lastly, where available, I tinkered with the companion app of every pair of headphones. I looked for tools to customize sound and additional features that help enhance the overall experience.

With all of the above tips in mind, enjoy a more peaceful daily and travel routine by switching to one of the products I vouch for below.

Bose QuietComfort headphones (and earbuds) have been synonymous with best-in-class noise cancellation for years. It stands to reason, then, that the Ultra cans top this product category.

The Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 headphones, which launched in late 2025, offer up to 30 hours of battery life and superior wired playback. The headphones’ ability to tune out ambient noise distractions by generating almost complete silence is commendable and alone worth splurging on. What’s more, their companion app lets you customize its intensity and save the setting for easy access in a specific scenario. Such a level of modularity sets the product apart from its rivals, just as the core feature’s performance does.

On the audio front, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones deliver a balanced sound that’s customizable via an app. Dubbed Bose Immersive Audio, the cans’ ability to deliver multidimensional spatial sound with optional head tracking is superb and, crucially, easy to access. I like that the feature works with any audio content rather than requiring Dolby Atmos-enhanced audio. I successfully used it to make live music albums and videos more lifelike during my testing.

The 24-hour battery life of the QuietComfort Ultra headphones leaves a little to be desired, as competitors, including those in lower price tiers, can last longer between charges.

With an under-$100 sticker before additional and frequent discounts, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 noise-canceling headphones by 1More are a legit impulse buy for such a product without skimping on design, ergonomics, performance, and battery life. The cans are surprisingly sleek and comfy, capable of delivering a high-quality audio experience across the board, as well as long battery life.

The sound quality of the headphones thoroughly exceeded my expectations when I put them through their paces. Tuned by a master audio engineer, the cans treated me to a balanced sound that made me feel like I was using a much pricier set. The tools for customizing the sound via their companion app are just as impressive.

When it comes to noise cancellation, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 is among the best for the money. The headphones did a solid job in tuning out distractions, but couldn’t match the serenity of costlier cans. That’s totally fine considering their agreeable price.

With up to a staggering 65 hours of battery life with noise cancellation, the SonoFlow Pro HQ51 leaves rivals that cost several times more in the dust. I could easily spend a week using them without battery anxiety. And believe it or not, you can get up to 100 hours of wireless playback from the 1More headphones by disabling the core functionality.

The Beats Studio Pro headphones are a must-have for owners of multiple Apple devices. Just like AirPods (and other Beats products), the cans will instantly connect to Apple devices that are linked to the same iCloud account. Once I paired them with my iPhone, I could instantly use the cans with an iPad, a MacBook, and a Mac mini, as well as keep tabs on their whereabouts in the Apple Find My app.

In addition to the seamless hardware compatibility mentioned above, the Beats Studio Pro headphones deserve the attention of Apple users for their ability to deliver a superb spatial audio experience. Accessing the functionality on an iPhone or an iPad is as easy as long-pressing the volume control button in the command center.

The Studio Pro headphones’ audio quality and noise cancellation are among the best in their price category. Their sound is balanced, melodic, and versatile, making it suitable for a wide range of music styles. There is no option to customize it via an app, but I didn’t feel like I had to make any changes while using the cans.

Unlike many competitors, the Beats Studio Pro headphones can deliver lossless audio over a direct USB-C link to phone, tablet, or computer. Listening in higher fidelity doesn’t include noise cancellation. Thankfully, I could access the latter via the standard audio jack when I needed to use the entertainment system during a flight.

The Beats headphones integrate well with Android and Chrome OS hardware, too, but I prefer the Apple experience for its superior spatial audio and because I don't need to install a companion app. Consider the recently released AirPods Max 2 over the Beats Studio Pro if you have a bigger budget for Apple-ready headphones. Their audio performance, craftsmanship, and controls are on a much higher level. However, you’ll have to settle for a heavier headset with shorter battery life and spend extra on a suitable protective case and a cable with a standard audio connector.

On-ear headphones have largely taken a back seat to larger over-ear ANC headphones, which offer more passive noise cancellation, and earbuds for their pocketable form factor. Marshall’s Milton ANC headphones offer a now-rare premium on-ear design that gives you the best version of a middle ground between the two, with a lightweight design, great sound quality, and a less ostentatious on-ear fit. With a foldable design and scratch-resistant ear cup covers, the Milton wears really well over the course of a long day on the go.

On the audio front, the Marshall Milton ANC impressed me with crisp, energetic sound that's customizable via a companion app. Its noise cancellation is also stellar, though does not generate the same auditory void as my top over-ear picks.

The headphones’ knob and customizable button controls are a benchmark for excellence and miles ahead of their competitors. The same goes for its 50-hour battery life. (Or 80 hours if you turn the ANC off.)

On-ear headphones are especially niche if ANC is your top priority, but it’s a great everyday carry headphone if your earbuds just aren’t cutting it. If you dig Marshall’s look, but would prefer an over-ear solution, the Monitor III ANC has a similar design and controls, but with a heavier, more deeply isolating form factor.

Reviewed: Marshall Milton ANC Wireless Headphones

The Bowers & Wilkins PX8 S2 wireless headphones are, hands down, my favorite wireless ANC headphones for discerning audiophiles looking for something more detailed than the standard options from Sony, Bose, and Apple.

Like the legendary British audio maker’s (very) expensive floor speakers, these over-ear cans produce pristine, infinitely customizable stereo sound that faithfully generates every detail of whatever you’re listening to.

At a time when wireless headphones generally try to earn attention with digital enhancements like spatial audio, the PX8 S2 impressed me with Their old-school approach to audio fidelity. (Note: B&W has added spatial audio since my review via a firmware update.) Experiencing the headphones’ sound with noise cancellation enabled is like listening to Bowers & Wilkins speakers in your own private space.

For $800, you know every aspect of these headphones has to work incredibly well, and they do. Its craftsmanship and tactility, headlined by genuine leather and metal accents in several colors, are a marvel for folks with extremely discerning taste... And plenty of disposable income.

The Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones are all about delivering incredibly powerful bass that’s available and adjustable via a dedicated button on the left cup. The sensory experience is truly remarkable and unlike anything rivals can offer, even though it predictably impacts the overall audio fidelity. The headphones’ noise cancellation is solid, if not on par with pricier sets from leading makers.

I didn’t reach for the Crusher ANC 2 when I felt like streaming classical jazz, but I grinned every time I played my favorite downtempo tracks on the product. Using the cans for playing action-packed games with the bass cranked up was also a ton of fun.

Disabling the thunderous low-end brought me a more “grown-up” sound, customizable via an app. That’s not what I’d recommend the product for, however. This Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 is all about celebrating bass.

The Crusher ANC 2 is also comfy to wear and equipped with convenient button controls. I also like the headphones’ integrated Tile tracker, as well as their sleek design with a contrasting, brightly colored button for activating the Crusher experience. There are tons of color options.

Skullcandy’s Icon ANC wireless headphones are handily the best for exercising on this list. The surprisingly affordable cans have a compact on-ear design, a secure fit, and an IPX4 rating for sweat- and water resistance. These qualities, together with convenient button controls, make the Icon ANC equally suitable for indoor and outdoor workouts.

The default sound of the headphones has an enhanced bass, which helped me stay motivated during my workouts. The Skullcandy app has several presets for customizing the sound, as well as a graphic equalizer to create your own. The noise cancellation worked, but it didn’t stop me in my tracks with its efficiency. That’s hardly a surprise considering the product’s price category.

I found the Skullcandy Icon ANC’s multidirectional control knob to be incredibly convenient during my testing. Their 50-hour battery life with noise cancellation exceeded my expectations, too. I didn’t expect this longevity from a compact pair of wireless headphones.

Skullcandy offers the Icon ANC in several colors. Every set comes bundled with a soft carrying pouch.

Noise cancellation relies on built-in microphones that continuously monitor your surroundings. A dedicated chip processes the sound captured by the microphones before sending its exact aural opposite to your ears via the headphones' audio drivers. This sophisticated technology naturally contributes to the cost of noise-canceling headphones. Translation? The more you spend, the better you'll isolate yourself from your surroundings. Prepare to drop north of $300 if you are looking to achieve (almost) complete silence from your purchase.

High-quality sound is also a must for a great pair of noise-canceling headphones. Support for immersive spatial audio is particularly important for top-shelf headphones. It makes live albums and video content more immersive and the listening experience more lifelike, especially if dynamic head tracking is available. Spatial audio is available on most top-shelf noise-canceling headphones. High-end sets without this functionality make up for it by producing pristine stereo sound, which makes them worth investing in. Speaking of stereo sound, today's best headphones in this space, including budget-friendly models, support lossless audio over wireless and wired connections. If you are using a streaming service that offers lossless audio, keep an eye out for this feature. It will serve you well.

Your next set of headphones should get you at least 20 to 30 hours of wireless playback between power-ups with noise cancellation. That’s the bare minimum for these products, with class-leading sets by Apple, Bose, and Sony delivering battery endurance in this ballpark. That’s enough to get you through a long flight or hectic workday in silence.Remarkably, cheaper cans now have much longer battery life. Some will give you double the endurance of the class-leading options with noise cancellation and a three-digit number of hours without it. Those numbers are remarkable, but trust me, stronger noise cancellation and higher-quality sound are worth the more frequent charging sessions.

A companion app for customizing the sound and the noise cancellation, among other things, is essential for any set of wireless headphones or earbuds today, so look for it while shopping. Apple AirPods and Beats products don’t have an iPhone app. Their settings are easily accessible directly in iOS, iPadOS, and macOS.

Stefan is an award-winning consumer technology editor with over a decade of experience in reviewing gadgets, particularly smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, desktop and laptop computers across multiple form factors and platforms, as well as accessories for them. He also covers televisions and audio equipment, including headphones, earbuds, wireless speakers, and soundbars. Since joining Hearst in 2015, Stefan has contributed to BestProducts, Popular Mechanics, and numerous other publications. Prior to his current role, he served as the US Editor for GSMArena.com.

#6352. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Tina Hesman Saey is the senior staff writer and reports on molecular biology. She has a Ph.D. in molecular genetics from Washington University in St. Louis and a master’s degree in science journalism from Boston University.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

#6347. Paying down debt can leave a country more exposed when the next hurricane hits

After Hurricane Melissa, Jamaica borrowed about 18% of its economy to recover, and researchers say lenders reward debt cuts but not seawalls.

Paying down debt is supposed to make a country safer. Lenders reward it with better credit ratings and lower borrowing costs. Jamaica spent more than a decade doing exactly that, but one hurricane undid much of the progress in a matter of weeks.

The reason, four researchers argue, is that the rules rewarding a country for paying off loans offer nothing comparable for building seawalls and drains.

Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica as a Category 5 storm in October 2025. It caused an estimated $12.2 billion in damage, losses, and costs.

This represents about 57 percent of the country’s entire economic output for 2024. Insurance covered about 2 percent of that, and Jamaica borrowed roughly $3.6 billion to recover.

Aayushi Mishra, a doctoral candidate at Northeastern University, traced what happened next. Her co-authors are Advait Arun of the Center for Public Enterprise and Northeastern’s Evan Kodra and Auroop Ganguly.

The paper is a policy analysis built on Jamaica’s public finance and disaster-loss figures, not a new data study. It argues for changes at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the development banks, and the rating agencies.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mishra said the people running those institutions are not the villains of the story. “No one here is acting in bad faith: every institution is doing exactly what its own rules ask of it,” she said.

“The problem is that those rules, once taken together, leave resilience underfunded.”

In 2013, Jamaica owed about 144 percent of its yearly economic output in debt. By 2023 it had cut that to about 72 percent, and it was on track for 60 percent by the 2027 to 2028 budget year.

The country did this through years of tight budgets and strict spending rules that it adopted on its own, not as a condition set by the IMF.

Lenders noticed. In September 2025, the rating agency S&P Global upgraded Jamaica’s credit rating. A few weeks later, Melissa made landfall.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Mishra pointed to the speed of the reversal. “Honestly, how little time it took for Jamaica’s hard-won progress to get diluted by just one storm, albeit a massive one,” she said.

The team projects Jamaica’s debt will now peak at about 68.5 percent of its economy, roughly 8.5 points above the path it was on. New borrowing makes up most of that increase, and the storm’s damage to output accounts for the rest, shrinking the economy against which analysts measure the debt.

Jamaica had done the things disaster experts recommend. It held a catastrophe bond through the World Bank, which pays investors’ money to the country if a storm crosses set thresholds for wind speed, track, and pressure.

It also bought insurance from a regional pool, the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF), that pays on the same measurements rather than on assessed damage.

Both paid quickly. The bond paid its full $150 million, and with the insurance and other aid the total reached about $242 million, within 3 to 14 days of landfall. Jamaica waited about three months for its IMF money to be approved.

But $242 million against $12.2 billion in losses is 2 percent. Speed was never the problem; scale was.

The year before, Hurricane Beryl had caused about $1 billion in damage, and the bond paid nothing because the storm’s measured strength fell short of its trigger. The insurance pool covered $26.6 million of Beryl’s damage, under 3 percent.

The instruments worked exactly as specified, the team wrote. Insurers have a name for the gap between what a storm measures and what it costs: basis risk. For a whole country, that gap was about 98 cents of every dollar lost.

The country is paying for the rest of the recovery with roughly $3.6 billion in new loans, about 18 percent of Jamaica’s pre-storm output in a single year. That is above the level the IMF treats as a warning sign for emerging economies.

The loans come from the IMF, the World Bank, and three regional development banks, mostly on terms that have not been made public.

So the team modeled a range, from low-cost development lending to near-market rates. The team put total repayments, including interest, at $4.9 billion to $5.7 billion.

What matters to Jamaica’s budget is the yearly cash payment. At peak repayment, the team estimates, servicing the new debt alone would approach or exceed Jamaica’s entire annual budget for public investment.

Jamaica’s investment budget was already small. In the 2024 to 2025 budget year, Jamaica spent about $3.15 billion servicing debt and about $510 million on public capital projects.

That second budget is the one that pays for coastal defenses and drainage. “So for every $1 the country spent on things like public infrastructure, it paid $6 in debt service,” Mishra told Earth.com.

How much would it have taken to avoid the borrowing? Using cost-benefit ratios from disaster research, the team estimates that spending $360 million to $900 million a year on protection before the storm could have offset the new debt entirely.

The IMF’s own 2025 review of Jamaica’s economy found the country could afford only $40 million to $80 million a year on climate adaptation without straining its debt path. That is 4 to 22 times less than the estimated need.

The gap narrows if private investors cover most of the cost, as the researchers assume they would.

The government’s share would then be about $120 million to $300 million a year, still 1.5 to 7.5 times what the IMF considered sustainable.

The team wrote that these figures can’t say which investments would have worked best, or how long they would have taken to build.

Researchers have modeled this pattern before and call it a climate-debt doom loop.

A disaster hits an underprepared country, and the country borrows to recover. The repayments then crowd out spending on protection, so the country is just as exposed when the next disaster arrives.

The authors wrote that no one had documented the loop unfolding in real time inside a single country before.

Rating agencies grade countries on budget surpluses, how fast debt falls, and how strictly budget rules are followed. Some have begun adding climate risk to side reports, but the authors wrote that it stays peripheral to the core decision. Nothing in that system changes when a country builds a seawall.

The IMF’s health check on a country’s debt added climate risk guidance for some programs in 2024. The authors wrote that it is still not part of the core method.

Jamaica’s 2025 review asked how much adaptation the country could afford without hurting its debt path. It didn’t ask the reverse: what happens to the debt when adaptation falls short and a catastrophe follows.

The paper’s four proposals aim at the lenders, not at Jamaica. Resilience spending should count in the IMF’s debt analysis as something that lowers the odds of a catastrophic loss.

An IMF trust fund created in 2022 for low-cost, long-term climate lending should be scaled up for the most indebted small island states.

Storm insurance triggers should use rainfall and surge as well as wind, and development banks should back the pools so they can pay more.

The fourth is a clause in loan contracts. Mishra said countries can add these now, while their finances are strong, as Barbados has.

“Simply put, these clauses let debt payments pause for up to two years after a disaster, so the country doesn’t have to take on new debt to cover them,” she said. Seventy-three countries and the major development banks have committed to them.

Ganguly, Mishra’s doctoral advisor, said much of the underlying data in this field is kept behind institutional walls or never disclosed.

“We would like to see funders and multilateral institutions to treat disclosure of these terms as standard practice (and not a courtesy), since the public and researchers alike are left to trust conclusions that they can’t necessarily check independently,” he said.

Nearly a year after Melissa, many of the terms of Jamaica’s recovery loans have still not been disclosed, Mishra said. Until they are, the cost of one storm to Jamaica is a range, not a number.

The next test is whether pause clauses get written into loans before the next hurricane arrives, rather than after.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.
