#6345. The 7 Best Smokeless Fire Pits We Tested (and Yes, They Produced Hardly Any Smoke)

From set-it-and-forget-it backyard centerpieces to grab-and-go options for weekend camping trips, we tried well-regarded options from Solo Stove, Breeo, Blue Sky, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire. They achieve this through two points of combustion: The first happens at the bottom, where airflow feeds burning wood; the second occurs at the top, where the fire’s smoke and gas output are burned off. And while no smokeless fire pit is 100 percent smokeless, if you use best practices (like burning dry wood) they come pretty darn close.

We tested smokeless fire pits in our New York and Pennsylvania backyards, building fires rather than judging them on specs alone. Along with smoke output, we considered size, which affects wood capacity and where the heat actually lands, as well as how easy each pit was to empty of ash and store once done, among other factors. We also used them repeatedly over time to see how their finishes held up, because a brand-new pit can look very different after several fires.

Solo Stove is the brand most people associate with smokeless fire pits (though Breeo was the first game in town). The latest joiner in Solo Stove’s lineup is the Summit, an upgraded take on the ever-popular Bonfire. Its 23-pound weight makes it just as easy to lift and store off-season, and there’s even less setup required. All-in-all, it’s the best smokeless fire pit for most people who want to enjoy a backyard fire pit that can be stored off-season.

Because the Summit is four to five inches shorter than the Bonfire, it does a better job of keeping your feet warm, one of the major gripes our Test Editor Brad Ford had of the earlier model. He says that while it holds less firewood, it undoubtedly produces a higher flame that extends well above the rim.

Another improvement he points out is the Summit’s integrated stand, which he says is sturdier and allows for better airflow than that of the Bonfire’s detached stand. There’s also a deeper ash pan, which is particularly helpful because the Summit burns through wood fast and needs frequent reloading. In terms of price, the 19.5-inch Summit is $100 more than a Bonfire of the same size, an extra cost that’s well worth the investment.

Full Solo Stove Summit Smokeless Fire Pit Review

After trying out the Breeo X Series 24 for several months, test editor Brad Ford loved it. According to Ford, “One of the coolest details of the X Series 24 is its Corten finish. (It is also available in a stainless-steel finish.) Corten is a structural steel alloy you often see used for bridges or power line towers. It’s designed to oxidize, or rust, creating a natural finish that protects the steel rather than continuing to degrade it. This eliminates the frustration I’ve had with some stainless-steel fire pits that discolor after a couple uses.”

Beyond this, Ford also liked, “that Breeo intended for their smokeless fire pits to be used for cooking from the get-go, which means they’ve got accessories for the X 24 that work very well. And most of their cooking accessories are compatible with all their fire pits. Top this all off with the fact that the X 24 is made right in Lancaster PA, USA, unlike most other popular brands.”

The Breeo X 24 weighs more than twice as much as the other models we’ve tested, so it’s not exactly portable—but it is long-lasting.

As the largest pick of the lot, the X Series was easy to load with wood and start a fire. We fit 18- to 20-inch logs into it, laying them across the raised X in the bottom of the pit. This patented design keeps the logs high, allowing air to flow in and feed the fire from the bottom.

Cleanup required scooping ash out, as the unit is too heavy to dump out easily—Breeo sells a shovel designed to ease this process. The brand also offers several accessories for cooking over the fire, which make the X Series as much a grill as it is a fire pit.

This hefty, all-black fire pit is a great-value addition to an outdoor setup. Its wide diameter gives you plenty of room to build a substantial fire, and the shape and airflow make for a good, largely smokeless burn. It takes both wood and pellets right out of the box, no adapter or switch-up required. And the lift-out ash catch has two handles, making it one of the easiest models to empty. (You still have to reach into the drum to lift it out, though, so wear gloves.)

The black coating is practical, too: Unlike stainless steel, it doesn’t show every fire mark. Once in place, it blends nicely with patio furniture, particularly setups with black metal legs. While it does scratch more easily than others we tested, you can touch it up with high-heat spray paint, just like you would a grill.

Some things to bear in mind: At 35 pounds, it’s heavier than many of the models we tested, so you’re unlikely to move it around much once it’s situated. The price doesn’t include a cover, which you’ll definitely want if it’s going to live outside for the season.

Because the ash catch sits inside the main body, with no separate base beneath it, we’d also place this one on a fireproof mat to be extra safe. And this may be petty, but the branding is the most prominent of any pit we tested: you’ll be looking at the words “Blue Sky” on the base every time you sit down.

If you want to bring the campfire with you wherever you go, the Packfire portable fire pit is an ideal choice. It packs down into a backpack, so you can carry it on your shoulders and set it up wherever your adventures take you. In fact, its innovative design won it a spot in our 2026 Home Awards.

The fire pit is composed of three sections: the base, which serves as a stand and ash pan; the body, which, when fully set up, surrounds the base; and the ring, which holds the body in place. Cleanup is easy: Simply lift the ring and body off the base, pour the ashes out, and break everything back down for travel.

It’s worth noting that even though it’s built for travel, the fire pit is still a bit cumbersome to carry around. While our Director of Product Content, Will Egensteiner was testing the Packfire, he said its 27.5 weight was a factor. “As I heaved it onto my back to put it away, I almost tipped over. And I’m not a small guy.”

The substance of this fire pit starts with the box: One of the largest and heaviest we had to maneuver into location for testing (only the Breeo was heavier), moving it really requires two people or a dolly. Some of that initial box weight comes from the generous bag of wood pellets packed inside, but the pit itself, at 45 pounds with nothing in it, is hardly lightweight.

Assembly is a little less impressive. Attaching the legs required a drill, as, while an Allen key and screws were included, some of the holes weren’t perfectly aligned, making the process more fiddly than it should have been. It does, however, come with spare screws.

Once assembled, though, this thing is a very good-looking workhorse. The large bag of wood pellets kept going for about 35 minutes before burning down to embers; produced virtually no smoke; and the heat output was surprisingly high.

Simply by flipping the inside container, you can also fire up 14-inch logs inside. The exterior frame stayed remarkably cool and, given it’s black, didn’t discolor the way the stainless steel ones did. While the inside picked up some black streaks from the flames, they looked more like evidence of a real fire than damage, which we actually liked.

The ash disposal is a true highlight. You don’t have to lift, twist, or tip the pit to empty it: An ash pan slides out from the side, shovel-style, so you can dump the refuse without moving the fire pit at all. It also comes with a perfectly fitted cover, which is particularly useful given how difficult this one would be to haul away when not in use.

This seriously smart, compact fire pit is made for small spaces and taking on the road. It’s lightweight, straightforward to assemble, and comes with six pieces: a pit and ash can that sit on top of one another; two pieces that twist together to form a fire poker (a little tight to sync up, but ultimately quite a useful piece); and a spark screen with a screw-in knob to lift it (also a very nice extra).

Truly, the whole kit is quite remarkable, given the price. The ash catch is also cleverly designed to fit inside the fire pit for storage, so there’s nothing extra to haul around when not in use. The black finish looks sharp and has the added benefit of hiding burn marks better than lighter finishes. (The downside is, it scratches easily.)

The whole thing packs into a carrying bag with a shoulder strap and drawstring closure. It’s also lighter than any other model we tested, making it an excellent choice for beach parties, camping trips, or anywhere you need to carry your fire pit more than a few feet.

There is one important caveat: Because the pit is so compact, you’ll mostly be limited to twigs, which burn quickly. Use wood pellets instead, for a longer, more consistent fire. The carrying bag also feels flimsy, like it could break down quickly with repeat use, but, for the price, that may not matter.

This one looks like a saucer and comes with just three pieces: a main body that locks securely into the ash holder base and a wind guard that twists onto the rim. It’s also one of the roomier pits we tested, with a wider, more-open design that accommodates both more and larger pieces of wood than many others. The manufacturer says it handles logs up to one pound. We’d have preferred a measurement in inches, but went with 16 inches, which it handled better than the Tiki. You can also add a griddle attachment to turn it into a cooker.

This one really does produce a roaring fire that can warm four people comfortably. The wide, funnel-like shape seems to encourage a bigger, more expansive flame; sitting around it felt more like a bonfire than simply burning wood in a container. After 25 minutes, we still had a substantial fire going. Its lower stature kept our feet warm too.

The biggest downside is ash removal. The pan in the base is relatively shallow, and the wide fire pit is awkward to twist and lift off for cleaning. You’ll want long arms—or a second person—to do it comfortably. The stainless-steel finish also turned a light bronze after just one use. A cover costs extra.

Before lighting a single fire, we evaluated the things that can make or break a smokeless fire pit before you ever use them. We assessed the packaging and how well each pit was protected in transit, weighed every model, and evaluated assembly. We read the instructions, noting whether they were clear, complete, and actually useful.

We considered whether it could be disassembled for storage, and what came in the box versus what required an additional purchase. While We had plenty of outdoor space to work with, safety always came first: we set every pit on heavy-duty pavers and kept a fire extinguisher close at hand.

Then we lit them up. We used comparable loads of seasoned firewood to assess how easily each pit started, how much smoke it produced, how evenly it burned, and how much heat it put out. We paid attention to flame height and consistency, too, and whether the fire actually warmed people sitting around it—not just looked good from a distance. We measured logs to see exactly what each pit could accommodate and tested wood pellets where models supported them.

Finally, we evaluated the less glamorous but equally important details: how easy each pit was to tend, how much ash accumulated, how easily that ash could be removed, and what it took to clean and put each model away. And because a fire pit can be beautiful at 7 p.m. and a pain in the ass at 10 p.m., we tested for both.

Whether you want a smokeless fire pit to heat your outdoor space or be more of an ambient seasonal moment is an important consideration. For long nights by the fire with family and friends, you’ll likely want to invest in a larger model that measures 24 inches in diameter. In testing, models that size and up exuded warmth for several feet, and could easily warm four to six people.

They could also handle 14- to 16-inch-long logs. The trade-off: Models this size are a lot heavier and harder to move. If you’re looking for more of a warming accent, narrower fire pits work wonders. You can also maximize some models’ output by adding a heat deflector that sits above the flames and pushes heat out laterally, instead of letting it escape upward.

Ideally, the smokeless fire pit should work right out of the box, with limited-to-no setup, besides setting the pit on a base. It should also break down easily. If you’ll be storing it between fires or seasons, a model that’s easy to disassemble, carry, and put away is key.

The shallower and wider the smokeless fire pit, the easier it is to make a fire from scratch. You simply have more base room to work with to set up your paper, kindling, and wood, and less depth to maneuver to light your fire once ready. No matter your choice, you’ll definitely want a lighter with a long metal wand and a safety catch. None of the models we tested included one.

Burning pellets instead of wood was the closest we got to a truly smokeless fire during our testing. Made of compressed wood waste like sawdust, chips, and shavings, pellets are easy to light, always bone dry, and produce a hotter, more consistent flame than logs. There are trade-offs, though: They lack the classic crackle and pop of a wood-burning fire and that wonderful smell.

Bags of the stuff also typically cost more than a handful of logs at the hardware store, yet burn about the same length of time. But, if you’re allergic to smoke, don’t want your sweaters to smell of it, have wet wood drying out, or want a reliable and even fire every single time, pellets are an excellent way to go. Some fire pits work with them right out of the box; others need an adapter.

Every smokeless pit burns wood. Many smokeless fire pits can also use wood pellets right out of the box. Some, like Solo Stove, need an adapter, so the tiny pellets don’t drop right through the pit’s air holes into the ashcan below. Some portable options may only be wide or deep enough to handle twigs (pellets may be a better option for those).

Pro tip: Wet or green wood will always be slow to burn and emit a lot of smoke; use a moisture meter to suss out whether your logs are dry enough to light up before putting a match to them.

If you plan to use your fire pit regularly, easy ash removal should be a deciding factor. The last thing you want to have to do is pick up and tip a heavy steel drum over a trashcan in order to empty it of ash. Instead, look for a removable ash pan or tray that allows you to lift the ash out cleanly once the pit has fully cooled (usually 12 to 24 hours after a fire has ended). Otherwise, you’ll need a shovel to scoop out the ash.

If you don’t have space to leave your fire pit outside all year, think about who will move it and how often. Even a small pit designed for camping trips can weigh as much as 20 pounds. Fortunately, these options usually come with a carrying bag, so you can sling them over your shoulder. Meanwhile, larger models can top 45 pounds (the 24-inch Breeo weighs just over 60 pounds), which matters when you have to move it under cover or into the garage at the end of the season. Units that come apart make this easier; having a dolly or hand truck on hand helps, too.

Material affects how long your new pit will look the way it does on arrival. While stainless steel looks shiny and modern from the start, heat from the flames will discolor it, and potentially quite quickly, as some testing showed. (You can restore its original shine with a stainless-steel cleaner such as Bar Keepers Friend, but that’s extra work.) Corten-steel usually costs more but forms a protective rust-colored patina that looks attractively weathered over time. Painted or powder-coated steel usually costs less, but can scratch and chip with repeat use.

Whatever finish you choose, keeping your smokeless fire pit empty of ash and covered when it’s not in use will help extend its life. Rainwater sitting in a fire pit full of ash can create a corrosive, alkaline slurry that accelerates rust and can damage the metal. Some models come with a cover as part of their bundle; others charge extra for it. Our reviews note whether a cover is included in every pick.

Smokeless fire pits can be a lot more than a place to warm your hands on chilly nights. In some cases, you can turn them into an outdoor kitchen. Brands like Breeo, Solo Stove, and Cuisinart have grill grates, griddles, pizza ovens, or roasting sticks that let you cook over an open fire. Other add-ons also make a difference, like a cover, if you plan to leave it outside when not in use; a spark screen, particularly if you have toddlers and pets around (though, warning: they can also get hot to the touch); and fire pokers or ashtray lifters, so you don’t get your hands dirty. Definitely check the accessory lineup before you buy your pit; they’re often model-specific. A pair of fire-resistant gloves is always a good investment.

While product photos often depict smokeless fire pits sitting on wood decks or backyards, it’s worth noting that their bases can get hot enough to scorch or discolor lawns, wood decks, composite, and asphalt. Ideally, yours should sit on brick, concrete, stone, or sand. But in the absence of that, a dedicated base (sometimes included, other times sold separately) helps raise the unit off the ground. For an even safer setup, consider adding a fireproof mat underneath. You should also keep a bucket of water or a fire extinguisher nearby and check for local burn bans before lighting. For more on fire pit safety, check out our story.

Arabella Bowen is a seasoned product tester who specializes in travel, design, tech, home improvement, and outdoor essentials. #6344. One of the dodo’s closest relatives was seen in Samoa for the first time in five years, but no one got a photo

Five sightings of Samoa's critically endangered manumea, a rare relative of the dodo, offer hope for a bird threatened by hunting and habitat loss.

The manumea, or tooth-billed pigeon, is Samoa’s national bird and one of only three surviving relatives of the extinct dodo. Its scientific name is Didunculus strigirostris, and the genus name means “little dodo” in Latin.

During a survey from October 17 to November 13, 2025, the Samoa Conservation Society recorded five manumea sightings in Upolu’s Uafato rainforest.

No photograph was taken, the society said. The bird’s call is also easily confused with that of the more common Pacific imperial pigeon.

Like the dodo, the manumea is a pigeon. It is stout and short-toed, about 12 inches (31 centimeters) long.

Its head and neck are a glossy blackish green, and its back and wing coverts are chestnut brown.

The bird is named for several notches along the cutting edge of its lower bill. Its bill is adapted to saw through the tough seeds of Dysoxylum trees, relatives of mahogany, according to the EDGE of Existence program.

It flies clumsily and slowly along a low path, which helps set it apart from other Samoan pigeons. The only nest ever recorded sat about 82 feet (25 meters) up in a banyan tree.

The bird prefers the large, hard-coated fruits of Dysoxylum. Hunters interviewed for the conservation effort said it also feeds on several other fruiting trees, and it may forage on the ground.

The species has been listed as Critically Endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) since 2014. It had been listed as Endangered from 2000 to 2014.

Samoa’s Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Conservation Society published a recovery plan for the species in March 2020. At that time, the last definite, confirmed sighting dated from August 4, 2017, in the Uafato forest.

A juvenile photographed on Savai’i in December 2013 was the first certain record of the species this century. It also showed that the manumea was still breeding.

The species is known from ten localities on Savai’i, and remote areas of forest on that island have never been surveyed.

Earlier fieldwork suggested that one definite sighting was possible every three to five years, even with medium to intensive search effort.

The 2025 observers saw only adult birds, and the society has said it is unclear whether the sightings involved one bird or several.

The manumea’s advertising call is nearly identical to one of the calls of the Pacific imperial pigeon, or lupe. Even local hunters and experts struggle to tell the two apart.

A 2020 study in Pacific Conservation Biology tested whether hunters’ traditional knowledge could help. Recordings at nine forest sites on Upolu and Savai’i yielded 104 clear call sequences.

Two top hunters each identified the species behind 80 sequences. They agreed on 54 of them, or 67 percent.

Sound analysis found that the manumea’s coo calls are lower in pitch and more regularly spaced than those of the lupe. The regular rhythm may help observers recognize the bird in the field.

The study also described the manumea as actively hiding in the dense canopy when it hears people moving through the forest.

Surveys in the late 1980s put the population at 4,800 to 7,200 birds across Samoa.

A later estimate of about 500 birds, from 2005 and 2006, is now considered far too high. It relied on calls that are easily confused with the lupe’s.

Surveys in 2012 and 2013 estimated fewer than 50 birds on each of Samoa’s two main islands, Upolu and Savai’i.

The recovery plan names three main threats: habitat loss and degradation, hunting and invasive predators. In recent decades, it appears that manumea have been killed mainly by mistake or as bycatch during lupe hunts.

Black rats and feral cats may also harm the species, though there is no direct evidence of it yet. Cyclones Ofa in 1990 and Val in 1991 reduced forest canopy cover by an estimated 27 percent, and the population appears never to have recovered.

Samoa has banned hunting all endemic pigeons, doves and fruit bats since at least 2004, but the rule has never been enforced nationally.

The ten-year plan sets out eight objectives and 26 activities, with an estimated budget of about $1.8 million. Its goal is to improve the species’ status from Critically Endangered to Endangered by 2029.

Early priorities included a conservation working group, a two-year fundraising campaign and a dedicated manumea coordinator.

A 2019 to 2020 national campaign strategy called the manumea “highly threatened and at risk of extinction in our lifetimes.”

Surveys of remote forest areas are still needed to find any undiscovered groups of the bird.

The information was obtained from the Samoa Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Conservation Society.

#6343. Malaria mosquito bites aren’t one quick jab but five separate moves under the skin

Under the skin, a malaria mosquito bite runs in five steps, and the researchers who filmed it say the first two are the ones to stop.

A mosquito bite feels like a single stab. Beneath the surface, however, it’s a sequence. A malaria mosquito pierces the skin in a fraction of a second.

Then she spends about 20 seconds pushing a flexible needle in and out, searching for a blood vessel. Only then does she start to drink.

Researchers who filmed and recorded that process on a living human arm counted five separate steps, and the mosquito’s legs and mouthparts move in time with each one.

The experiments were done in Christopher Potter’s lab in the Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine.

Joanna Konopka, who is at the Johns Hopkins Malaria Research Institute, and Danny Poinapen, who also works at Western University’s Robarts Research Institute in Canada, led the work.

Every bite happened on the right forearm of one volunteer, and the mosquitoes were lab-raised Anopheles coluzzii, a malaria carrier from sub-Saharan Africa.

In an interview with Earth.com, Konopka was asked whether any of the five steps could be interrupted to stop a bite or an infection. Her answer named the first two.

“The first two stages of the bite (skin piercing and blood vessel searching) are most important for disease transmission, because this is when the pathogen is most likely to be introduced via mosquito saliva,” she said.

The volunteer wore a small, clear acrylic box strapped to her forearm with sports wristbands. It left a window of skin about an inch (2.5 centimeters) square.

One female mosquito at a time was released onto that patch while a high-speed camera recorded at up to 250 frames per second. A tracking program followed the legs, the mouthparts, and the two feelers beside them, which are called palps.

What happens below the surface can’t be filmed, so the team recorded it electrically instead. Each mosquito was glued at the back to a gold wire finer than a human hair while the volunteer held an electrode.

The moment the needle broke the skin, the circuit closed, and every movement underneath showed up as a change in voltage.

“We were fascinated by the coordinated and synchronized movements that female mosquitoes exhibit above and below our skin when they are biting us,” Poinapen told Earth.com.

“And some of these movements occur as fast as an eye blink yet they are finely coordinated!”

Five stages stood out in the voltage traces: piercing the skin, searching for a vessel, drinking blood, pulling the mouthparts back, and withdrawing them.

A full bite took about 160 seconds on average. Roughly 128 of those seconds went to drinking and about 21 to the search for a vessel.

Above the skin, the body kept pace. As the mosquito pushes the needle deeper, her front legs bend and lift off the skin.

When she pulls back, the legs straighten and press down, and the bend begins a fraction of a second before the mouthpart moves.

A mosquito repeated that push and pull about three times before settling into a steadier search. Her palps changed with each stage too. During the hunt for a vessel they swung side to side above the skin, 10 to 25 times a second.

The moment blood began to flow, the palps stopped swinging and started a faint up-and-down vibration. The team suspects that vibration matches the pumps in the mosquito’s head that draw blood in.

The team ran the same recordings on Aedes aegypti, the mosquito that spreads yellow fever and dengue.

The two groups split about 150 million years ago, and the traces showed it. The malaria mosquito stabbed its needle in abruptly, while Aedes worked it in gradually, with a steady rhythm.

Once inside, Anopheles found a vessel about 17 seconds sooner, with shorter and more targeted probing. Even so, both finished a meal in about the same time, roughly 160 seconds for Anopheles and 165 for Aedes.

The volunteer reported that every Anopheles bite was noticeable whereas the Aedes bites were painless. Whether that holds for anyone else is still an open question, and Earth.com asked the researchers whether the abrupt stab is why malaria mosquito bites seem to hurt more.

“This is not an established phenomenon – different people can have different experiences and reactions to the bites of these two mosquitoes,” Konopka and Poinapen said.

They added that the different piercing patterns might relate to when each mosquito is active. Malaria mosquitoes bite mainly at dusk and at night, while yellow fever mosquitoes bite mostly in the daytime.

Mosquitoes taste and smell with their legs and mouthparts as well as their antennae. To test how much the bite depends on that, the team bred Anopheles that lacked one of two genes.

Whole families of taste and smell receptors need those genes in order to work.

One gene, called IR76b, is active in nerve cells of the legs, the mouth tip, and the needle itself, the three parts that touch the skin. The other, orco, is active in the mouth tip but not in the legs or the needle.

Mosquitoes missing both copies of IR76b mostly didn’t bite at all. More than half made no attempt in 20 minutes on the volunteer’s arm. Of the 14 tested, six probed and only four managed a partial meal.

Mosquitoes missing orco still bit, some of them a little later than normal, and 98 percent of their probes ended in a blood meal.

Mutants that did bite kept the same timing through all five steps. The one difference was in the drinking itself, which ran in a more regular, repetitive pattern than in normal mosquitoes.

“We found that some malaria mosquitoes with impaired sense of taste and smell had difficulty initiating and completing bites,” the two researchers wrote.

“This indicates that mosquitoes heavily rely on their ability to flavor us during the biting process.”

All of this rests on one volunteer’s arm and on lab strains of each species. So the team can’t yet say how much a bite changes on a different person’s skin, or with wild mosquitoes.

The mosquitoes with no working IR76b never fed while wired up, so there are no recordings of their bites. A third family of taste receptors couldn’t be switched off at all, because no shared gene controls it.

The biggest gap is under the skin. One possibility the researchers raise is that the needle itself senses chemical cues on the way to a blood vessel, and that mosquitoes without IR76b can no longer aim it.

Following the needle’s movements inside the skin, and finding those cues, is the work the team says is needed next. The same setup, they wrote, could also test how repellents, skin microbes, and different hosts change a bite.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6342. Standing desks may change how people work, even while sitting

Workers with sit-stand desks logged more active computer time, but researchers could not determine whether standing explained the difference.

Sit-stand desks are meant to get office workers out of their chairs. A large study has now linked the desks to roughly 43 extra minutes of active computer use each day.

The comparison was with coworkers who used fixed-height desks.

More than 10,000 employees of one company were included in the analysis. The company never recorded whether any of them actually stood up.

The analysis was led by Tricia Salzar, a regional ergonomist with the U.S. Army Public Health Command. Mark Benden, a professor at the Texas A&M University School of Public Health, co-led the work.

Benden also directs the school’s Center for Worker Health.

The records were drawn from a workplace wellness program. They cover workers who joined that program between 2012 and 2014.

Desks were not assigned by the researchers. The study can therefore show that the desks and the extra computer time went together.

The company is a California energy firm that employs about 24,000 people. Under its wellness program, keypresses and mouse clicks were logged by software on each worker’s computer.

A worker was counted as active only while the keyboard or mouse was in use. If 30 seconds passed without a keypress or a click, the clock stopped.

Workers were also asked in a survey whether they used a height-adjustable desk. That is another name for a sit-stand desk.

Salzar’s team identified 3,404 workers who answered yes on two surveys taken a year apart. They were compared with 6,741 workers who answered no both times. Anyone who switched desks during the year was left out.

Over the year, workers at fixed desks averaged 2.95 hours of active computer use a day. An average of 3.66 hours was recorded for workers with sit-stand desks.

The difference between the two groups did not take a year to appear. A gap of about 40 minutes a day in active computer time was already present in the first month.

Across a work year, the authors calculated, the daily difference comes to about 171 hours. That is more than four full-time weeks.

The sit-stand group also typed more. They averaged about 860 more keypresses a day than the fixed-desk group. They also typed roughly 80 more words.

Sit-stand users also made slightly more typos. This remained true after the team adjusted for the number of words typed. The authors wrote that this difference in typos may be too small to matter.

Long hours of uninterrupted sitting have been linked to health risks and to muscle and joint pain.

The survey therefore also asked how often workers felt physical discomfort at work. Soreness, tired muscles and eye strain were given as examples.

More discomfort was reported by sit-stand users, not less. In the first month, 30.1% of them said they never felt discomfort. The figure for workers at fixed desks was 35.7%.

The two groups then moved closer together. By the end of the year, 32.5% of sit-stand users said they never felt discomfort. Among fixed-desk workers, the share was 34.3%.

The change was described by the authors as negligible. In a group this large, they wrote, a difference can pass a statistical test. It can still be too small to matter in practice.

Why would workers with sit-stand desks report more discomfort in the first place? Some may have requested the desks because they were already in pain, the authors wrote.

The records do not show why any worker had one.

Salzar’s team converted the extra time into money. The federal Office of Personnel Management standard for a work year was used. The average wage was set at $52.04 an hour.

The authors put the value of the added computer time at about $8,900 per worker per year. A fully adjustable sit-stand desk costs about $2,200 delivered and set up, they estimated. It could therefore pay for itself in under three months.

The estimate assumes that computer activity can stand in for productivity. It also assumes that giving a worker the desk would produce the extra minutes.

Benden said the findings suggest that the desks “can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity.”

The paper he co-wrote is more cautious. The authors wrote that “the only thing that we can truly determine” is an association. Workers who had the desks also used their computers more.

Benden has worked on standing desks as an inventor as well as a researcher. He founded Stand2Learn, a company that made standing desks for classrooms. It was acquired by the desk maker Varidesk in 2018.

He is also the named inventor on patents for adjustable-height desk accessories. Those patents are held by the Texas A&M University System. No outside funding and no conflicts of interest are listed in the paper.

The two groups were not matched. Sit-stand users were younger, with an average age of about 43.

The average for the fixed-desk group was 49. A larger share of the sit-stand users were women.

Salzar’s team also had no record of any worker’s job.

An administrative worker might spend more time typing, the authors wrote. An engineer might instead spend time at the computer reading reports and specifications.

Reading without typing or clicking does not register as active time.

Suppose sit-stand desks went mostly to workers in keyboard-heavy jobs. The job, not the desk, could then account for the gap.

The company’s records are also more than a decade old, and they come from its offices. They cannot show what the desks do for people working from home.

How often a desk was raised was not recorded in the survey. Neither was how long a worker stood or how many times a day the worker changed posture.

Standing may not explain the 43 minutes. The authors cited an earlier study from Benden’s group on this point. They wrote that fewer than 10% of people with these desks choose to stand.

People who do stand may spend only 10% to 20% of the day on their feet.

The authors offered another explanation. A standard desk is fixed at a height of 29 to 30 inches (74 to 76 cm). A sit-stand desk can be set to fit the person sitting at it. The benefit may come from that fit.

Benden said his group is also interested in how AI tools could change the physical workspace.

Future studies should record how often workers raise their desks and how long they stand, the authors wrote. Until one does, the extra 43 minutes cannot be credited to standing.

The full study was published in the journal Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6339. Childhood health problems may share hidden environmental links

A study following children into adolescence links early environmental exposures to overlapping patterns in physical and mental health.

The environment children grow up in can shape their health in more ways than we might realize.

From the air they breathe to the food they eat, everyday exposures may be connected to several health problems that continue into adolescence.

In a study of 586 European children, some exposures were linked to several problems at once.

A mother’s smoking during pregnancy was tied to a higher body mass index in her child and to more aggressive, impulsive behavior. Both links were still there in the teen years.

The findings suggest that a single early exposure may be tied to several parts of a child’s health.

Studying several health outcomes together can help reveal these overlapping links.

Augusto Anguita-Ruiz of the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal) and the University of Barcelona led the work with colleagues at Inserm, France’s national institute for health and medical research.

From pregnancy into the teen years, the researchers observed families and changed nothing about how they lived.

Xavier Basagaña, an ISGlobal researcher, is a senior co-author of the study.

“The study does not establish that these exposures cause the observed health outcomes,” said Basagaña.

All of the children came from six long-running birth studies in the United Kingdom, France, Spain, Lithuania, Norway and Greece. The six studies belong to a European project called HELIX.

For each mother and child, the team had 69 measures from pregnancy and 129 from childhood. Scientists have a name for that full mix of what a person eats, breathes and lives around: the exposome.

Blood and urine samples provided measures of tobacco exposure, metals, pesticides and other chemical pollutants.

Other exposure measures came from home and school addresses, which the team used to estimate outdoor air pollution, traffic and nearby natural spaces.

Questionnaires covered diet, sleep, physical activity and pets.

The team compared those measures with 11 health outcomes in four areas: weight and blood pressure, mental health, breathing, and allergies. Each child was examined twice, at an average age of about 8 and again at about 15.

Researchers behind a recent US atlas compared 619 exposures with 305 health traits, but their survey data captured each person at a single point in time.

Six pregnancy exposures and 42 childhood exposures were linked to more than one health outcome. The researchers call these four health areas domains.

Valérie Siroux is an Inserm researcher and senior co-author.

“Although no exposure was associated with all four domains, around one in three of the selected exposures was linked to more than one, suggesting that certain exposures can have broad and multisystemic effects on health,” said Siroux.

Smoking during pregnancy was one of those exposures. It was also tied to more ADHD symptoms in the teen years.

Among childhood exposures, fine particles in indoor air, known as PM2.5, were linked to worse results for weight and blood pressure and for mental health.

Higher copper levels in a child’s blood were linked to worse results in the same two areas.

Secondhand smoke and benzene in indoor air were each linked to higher BMI or blood pressure at both exams.

Why would one exposure be tied to such different problems? The authors suggested that the four health areas share biological pathways, most notably inflammation throughout the body. The team didn’t measure inflammation here.

Of those 42 childhood exposures, 16 were linked to outcomes across more than one health area, and 12 of those involved diet.

Diet also appeared when the team analyzed weight and blood pressure alone. There, following a diet closer to the Mediterranean pattern and eating more fruit were each linked to lower BMI and blood pressure.

In the team’s models, childhood exposures explained up to about 15% of the variation in mental health and in weight and blood pressure.

Pregnancy exposures explained up to about 7% of the variation in mental health and about 1.5% in weight and blood pressure.

So the measured exposures left most of the differences among children unexplained. Allergy outcomes were scarcely related to the exposures.

Some results were the reverse of what the team expected.

Higher blood levels of certain long-lasting chemicals, including PCBs and the PFAS chemical PFOA, were linked to lower BMI and blood pressure in children.

The authors didn’t read that as protection. These chemicals are stored in body fat, so a child’s body fat and growth are expected to affect how much of each chemical appears in blood.

Body size may be shaping the blood reading rather than the chemical shaping body size, the authors wrote, and they urged caution with those results.

The team also repeated every analysis six times, each time leaving out the children from one of the six birth studies.

Most links appeared again, in the same direction, in more than four of the six runs.

A few links didn’t meet that standard. One tied how much meat a mother ate during pregnancy to asthma and wheezing in her child. Another tied fast food in childhood to worse mental health.

Such links may reflect conditions in one region or one group of families rather than a general pattern, the authors wrote.

Among the 1,301 mother-child pairs in HELIX, the 586 in this study were those with data from every stage. About 87% of the children were white, and 53% of their mothers held a university degree.

The authors described the group as highly selective, so the links may not apply to other populations. The group was also too small to analyze boys and girls separately.

Some chemicals with highly variable levels were measured in only one or a few urine samples, which could make a link look stronger or weaker than it is.

The bacteria, viruses and fungi a child encounters weren’t measured. The authors suggested that could be why breathing and allergy problems were less clearly tied to the exposures.

Every association is posted in a free interactive online atlas that anyone can search or download.

“Further studies in larger and more diverse populations will be needed to better understand these relationships and determine whether modifying some of these exposures can alter health trajectories during childhood and adolescence,” Basagaña said.

Future research could also add outcomes this study lacked, such as thinking skills and metabolic health, and examine children at other ages.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6338. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

#6337. I’m a Neurosurgeon. My Near-Death Experience Showed Me ‘Universal Consciousness’ for the First Time.

By comparison, it makes our material world feel “murky.”

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When I earned my medical degree at Duke University, I was taught that consciousness is created out of chemical reactions occurring within the brain, a foundational assumption of scientific materialism, or physicalism—the notion that only the physical exists. After eleven years of rigorous training, I practiced as a neurosurgeon for more than two decades, including 15 years teaching and operating at Harvard Medical School.

I performed surgical procedures that took patients from extreme discomfort to full relief by releasing a nerve blockage or removing a tumor. I could stimulate the brain in conscious patients and affect their mental experience, which initially seemed to support my physicalist worldview. At the same time, patients deeply comatose from brain maladies would sometimes become fully alert right before dying. I couldn’t explain these phenomena, and so I dismissed them. That is, until November 2008, when a severe case of bacterial meningitis caused me to spend seven days in deep coma—and later reshaped my view of the universe.

Over three hours, I went from back pain and headache to epileptic fits and coma, as E. coli bacteria devoured my neocortex, or the outer surface of the brain, the part that is most responsible for human mentation. Healthcare professionals use the Glasgow Coma Scale to measure decreases in consciousness, with scores less than 9 indicating deep coma. A corpse would score a 3, the lowest grade on the scale, and my scores were 6 to 7 during most of that week—the doctor was out! Lumbar puncture revealed my cerebrospinal fluid to be filled with pus under pressure, and the glucose level in that fluid was only 1 mg/dl (normally 80-90, with severe bacterial meningitis occasionally as low as 20). CT and MRI scans revealed my entire neocortex was involved, meaning there was no physical functioning brain left to produce a dream or hallucination.

By the tenets of modern neuroscience, my awareness should have been zero. Without a functioning neocortex, my brain was incapable of producing a simple thought or image—and yet, I lived through a vivid, richly-detailed, hyper-real event, by comparison making this material world appear murky and dreamlike. I was unbound by space and time, immersed in universal consciousness, and wrapped in unconditional love. I had visions revealing structure to the non-physical realm that fully relates to and intertwines with our lives here on earth.

Back in the hospital, my prospects for survival were down to 2 percent when, on day seven, I startled everyone as I began to awaken. My doctors were even more surprised when I fully recovered over about two months. As my medical knowledge returned, I reviewed my records and scans, and discussed them with my doctors, trying to make sense of it all. I searched for a physicalist explanation, yet the case was unyielding—no conventional explanation could suffice. I was forced to acknowledge that an expansive model of reality was required to explain my experience.

In 2018, when my case records were peer-reviewed before publication in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, the editors asked the authors to explain my unprecedented recovery. They replied that my miraculous recovery occurred because of my spiritual journey, knowing of similar extraordinary recoveries in the near-death literature. Due to techniques of cardiac resuscitation developed in the 1960s, millions of others have escaped the shackles of the physical brain and body, and reported similar near-death experiences (NDEs) of connection with a non-physical realm. Those descriptions have been categorized and evaluated using Greyson’s NDE Scale (developed by UVA psychiatrist Bruce Greyson), which quantifies the cognitive, affective, paranormal, and transcendental aspects of the experiences.

The vast evidence from these unusual experiences has convinced many former physicalists that their model is outdated. A more sufficient explanation is that the brain serves as a transceiver or antenna for tuning in to a larger, collective consciousness. Renowned Harvard psychologist William James, French philosopher Henri Bergson, and English writer Aldous Huxley, all postulated this “reducing valve” role for the brain in the early 20th century, noting that a shift in the primary physicalist assumption was required to explain these phenomena.

With a growing abundance of data, it is clearer that consciousness is fundamental and influences physical matter from the top down, rather than the bottom-up model of physicalism, where consciousness arises from the brain. Spontaneous remissions and the placebo effect confirm the power of the mind over matter and validate the observer effect seen in quantum mechanics experiments.

The “hard problem of consciousness” remains unsolved because its underlying premise is false.

I believe merging first-person subjective inquiry with rigorous empirical science will take us farther in knowing the true nature of our consensus reality.

To that point, humanity will thrive when science finally acknowledges that we are interconnected through love and part of one larger consciousness, with free will to become the best version of ourselves, both as individuals and collectively. The golden rule is woven directly into the fabric of the universe, providing a moral compass that shows that, ultimately, what matters most is how we treat each other.

#6336. Diabetes and Alzheimer’s share a link that scientists are still trying to explain

A review of 40 studies examines the link between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s, offering new estimates of risk and unanswered questions.

How many people with type 2 diabetes go on to develop Alzheimer’s each year? Five in every 1,000, according to a new estimate.

The estimate comes from a review of 40 studies. In it, people with type 2 diabetes were about 53% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s than people without it.

Diabetes has been tied to dementia for years. Trouble is, most earlier reviews threw several kinds of diabetes or dementia into one pot.

This one was limited to type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease, and a link between the two was still found. Yearly case counts, rarely reported before, were worked out as well.

Emmanuel Adewuyi is a researcher at the Curtin School of Population Health at Curtin University in Australia.

Adewuyi worked on the review with lead author Thi Thu Huong Nguyen and colleagues in Australia, the UK, and Nigeria.

The 53% figure describes the relative increase in risk. The rate of new cases over time is called incidence.

“Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer’s disease among people living with type 2 diabetes,” Adewuyi said.

Every study in the review was observational. People’s health was recorded, and no treatment was assigned.

Research like that can show that two conditions go together. It can’t show that one causes the other.

Dementia affects more than 57 million people worldwide. Alzheimer’s disease accounts for about 60% to 70% of those cases.

Type 2 is by far the most common form of diabetes, accounting for more than 90% of cases.

Both conditions become more common with age. Many of the same heart and metabolic risk factors are shared by the two.

Type 2 diabetes has a stronger link to vascular dementia than to Alzheimer’s. Vascular dementia follows damage to blood vessels in the brain.

Mixing the two, the authors wrote, blurs how much of the risk belongs to Alzheimer’s. Adewuyi’s team therefore kept only studies in which both type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s were clearly identified.

Studies that mixed type 2 with type 1 or pregnancy-related diabetes were dropped. Studies that could not separate Alzheimer’s from other dementias were dropped as well.

The researchers searched four medical databases for studies published through April 2026. They found 9,431 articles, but only 40 met their criteria.

Those 40 studies were published between 1997 and 2026 and covered 12 countries. South Korea contributed 10 studies, the United States eight, and the United Kingdom seven.

In 38 studies, researchers followed participants over time, with average follow-up periods ranging from two to 15 years. In most studies, the average participant age was between 55 and 75.

The combined study samples totaled more than 27 million people, though some people may have appeared in more than one study. For example, all seven UK studies used data from the same source, the UK Biobank.

In 26 of the studies, people with type 2 diabetes were compared with people without it. New Alzheimer’s cases were counted in each group.

The results had already been adjusted for other factors, most often age and sex, the authors wrote.

When the 26 were pooled, Alzheimer’s risk was 53% higher for people with type 2 diabetes. With any single study taken out, the increase stayed between 50% and 57%, the authors wrote.

Across subgroups such as region, age, and study date, the increase ranged from 40% to 66%.

Separate results for men and women were given in only a handful of studies. Similar increases were seen there: 76% for men and 73% for women.

The authors wrote that the sex-specific figures should be treated with caution.

The International Diabetes Federation’s Diabetes Atlas has its own, lower estimate. In the atlas, the increase for Alzheimer’s was put at 34%.

The authors wrote that the two estimates are compatible with each other. Different sets of studies in the two reviews may explain the gap, they wrote.

Across 23 of the 40 studies, covering about 9 million people, the pooled rate among people with type 2 diabetes was about 4.7 new Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 people a year.

From study to study, it swung from under 1 case per 1,000 people a year to almost 14. Much depended on how a study went looking for Alzheimer’s.

Where hospital or national health records were combed, about 4 cases per 1,000 people a year were found.

Where participants were diagnosed using clinical criteria or memory tests, the figure was about 10. Health records probably miss milder cases, the authors wrote.

The yearly rate per 1,000 people varied by region. It was about 7.5 in North America and 5.8 in East Asia and the Pacific. In Europe and Central Asia, it was 1.2.

Health, access to care, and diagnosis may all differ by region, the authors wrote. Those explanations still need to be tested.

Only a few studies split their results by sex. In that small set, the yearly rate was 3.6 per 1,000 women and 2.8 per 1,000 men.

The authors used a standard scale to assess the evidence behind both main estimates. They rated its certainty as very low.

None of the 40 studies tested a treatment, and their results varied widely.

The team rated 38 studies as having a low risk of bias and two as having a moderate risk. But those ratings did not account for how often participants visited a doctor.

People with type 2 diabetes may have more medical appointments. That could give doctors more chances to notice and diagnose Alzheimer’s.

Earlier research by Adewuyi and colleagues found that the two diseases share some genetic influences. However, it found limited evidence that genes linked to type 2 diabetes directly increase Alzheimer’s risk.

Insulin resistance, high blood sugar, and inflammation could also help explain the connection, the authors said. But the 53% higher risk shows a pattern across groups of people, not proof that diabetes directly causes Alzheimer’s.

In 11 of the 40 studies, researchers relied on participants to report whether they had diabetes. Most studies also took place in high-income countries.

The review could not determine whether better diabetes management changes a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s.

Studies inconsistently reported how long participants had lived with diabetes, how well their blood sugar was controlled, and which medications they used.

Metformin, pioglitazone, and acarbose have each been tied to lower dementia risk in earlier research. So have other diabetes drugs, GLP-1 drugs among them, in people with type 2 diabetes. Cause is as hard to pin down there as here.

Adewuyi’s team described the new figures as a benchmark for future studies testing whether diabetes treatment changes Alzheimer’s risk.

In the meantime, the team sees a case for watching memory and thinking as part of long-term diabetes care.

The authors said that future studies would be better if researchers combined individual patient data from multiple studies instead of relying on published summaries.

This would help them account for other risk factors more accurately.

The full study was published in the journal Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.

From an award-winning expert on DNA, discover the myth-busting book that opens a dazzling window into the world of modern genetics.

Fascinating, compassionate, and entirely captivating, The Secrets of Our DNA is the essential book that explains how genetics has changed and transformed the world around us.

Turi King is renowned for presenting complex findings on DNA and genetic science in an accessible and compelling way and she has won awards for her public engagement in science. Turi is the director of the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath. She is an honorary fellow of the British Science Association, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London, a member of the Chartered Society of Forensic Sciences, and a member of the International Society of Forensic Geneticists. She is well known for her academic work leading the identification of Richard III; advising on the case of Mary Jane Kelly (the last victim of Jack the Ripper); leading the project on sequencing Hitler’s genome; as well as her media work co-presenting BBC’s DNA Family Secrets.
