#6334. Tropical cyclones may follow a hidden winter pattern months before they form

A February weather pattern may offer clues to East Asia’s summer typhoon activity, providing information beyond El Niño.

Predicting how many tropical cyclones will reach East Asia months ahead is difficult. But a weather pattern that develops in late winter may offer an early clue.

New research suggests that this pattern could help researchers anticipate summer tropical cyclone activity beyond what El Niño alone can explain.

The study was led by Zeming Wu from Zhejiang University and examined more than 40 years of observations.

This year, many blamed the strong El Niño for the storms.

El Niño is a periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific that can influence where tropical cyclones form and how they travel.

But the researchers argue it may not be entirely El Niño’s fault this time.

The team focused on the Pacific–North American pattern, or PNA, a large-scale pattern of atmospheric pressure variations over the North Pacific and North America.

It operates in phases. Its “positive phase” brings warmer temperatures across the western United States and Canada and cooler temperatures across the central and southeastern United States. The negative phase is the reverse.

The researchers found that the February PNA pattern was linked to tropical cyclone activity over East Asia the following summer.

The relationship remained after accounting for the influence of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a recurring climate pattern that includes El Niño and La Niña.

“Our findings suggest that late-winter atmospheric variability may provide valuable information about East Asian summer tropical cyclone activity beyond the influence of ENSO,” Wu said.

“This highlights the potential importance of atmospheric circulation outside the tropics as an additional source of seasonal predictability.”

The positive phase of PNA in late winter is linked to fewer tropical cyclones forming over the western North Pacific and fewer storms reaching East Asia several months later.

But how does a February pattern stay connected to summer storms?

The original atmospheric anomalies may have weakened or vanished. Ocean temperatures kept the events linked.

“Through interactions between the atmosphere and ocean, sea surface temperature anomalies can preserve and transmit climate signals across seasons,” said co-author Chundi Hu from the same university.

The team found two complementary pathways, both mediated by the ocean and linking late-winter PNA variability to summer tropical cyclone activity.

“The ocean appears to act as a bridge between winter atmospheric variability and summer tropical cyclone activity,” Wu said.

“More importantly, our results suggest that this connection involves not only the familiar ENSO-related pathway but also another pathway associated with atmospheric variability beyond preceding-winter ENSO.”

The first pathway involves ENSO. A positive PNA pattern in late winter is associated with warming in the tropical North Atlantic and a relatively rapid weakening of El Niño in the tropical Pacific.

According to the researchers, these temperature changes match shifts in large-scale atmospheric circulation.

Those shifts favored the development and persistence of an anomalous anticyclone over the western North Pacific into summer.

The second pathway works beyond the linear influence of preceding-winter ENSO. Hu pointed to a mechanism called seasonal footprinting.

This pattern lets anomalies in atmospheric circulation leave a lasting and developing imprint on ocean temperatures.

In this case, the anomalies were wind changes over the subtropical North Pacific and were associated with cooling in the central tropical Pacific.

“Despite their different origins, both pathways converge on a similar atmospheric response: an anomalous anticyclone, or unusual system of high pressure, over the western North Pacific,” Wu said.

“This circulation pattern suppresses conditions favorable for tropical cyclone formation and modifies the winds that steer storms, reducing the number of tropical cyclones reaching East Asia during summer.”

Next, the researchers plan targeted climate model experiments to investigate these pathways further.

“Ultimately, our goal is to better understand the sources of tropical cyclone predictability and contribute to more reliable seasonal risk assessments for East Asian coastal communities,” Hu said.

Seasonal forecasts give coastal communities time to plan for storm risks. The findings suggest that February’s PNA pattern could provide useful information alongside ENSO.

Further testing will help establish whether this winter signal improves forecasts of summer tropical cyclone activity.

The PNA pattern is large scale. It distributes air and heat across the North Pacific and North America. Its late-winter phase may offer a clue months before the storms arrive.

For coastal communities in East Asia, better forecasts could mean better preparation and more reliable seasonal risk assessments. That could help people get ready before the storms hit.

The study is published in the journal Ocean-Land-Atmosphere Research.

#6333. Humans Have Used the Same Comb Design Since the Stone Age. This One Might Finally Beat Baldness.

Named after Disney’s Tangled, this comb zaps hair-growth molecules straight into shrinking follicles.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The oldest-known comb, fashioned from animal bone, dates back nearly 8,000 years to mesolithic Syria. But in those intervening 10,000 years, the comb hasn’t seen much innovation. Sure, plastics have long since replaced bone as the material of choice for this particular piece of grooming gear (though animal bone combs are still a thing). But the comb’s overall shape and function—individual tines and all—has remained remarkably unchanged.

“The basic design evolved from the fingers of the human hand,” the Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford writes on its website. “From Bronze-Age man to Cleopatra, to Napoleon's wife, Josephine, all would recognize these items as such.”

But just because something’s remained largely unchanged for millennia doesn’t mean there isn’t room for innovation. Take, for instance, the “Detangle,” an experimental comb developed by Beihang University in China as a tool for tackling androgenetic alopecia (AGA), or just simply baldness. At first glance, the comb looks much like any other hand-inspired comb—there’s a long handle and the recognizable tines. However, that’s where the similarities end, because this comb has teeth packed with embedded electrodes as well as small compartments for delivering molecules designed to stimulate hair growth. Researchers published a study detailing the efficacy of this experimental comb in the journal Nature Communications.

“Androgenetic alopecia affects over 1.5 billion individuals, causing progressive hair loss with psychological and quality-of-life burdens,” the authors write. “This system features electronic teeth embedded with height-differentiated electrodes and integrated drug-loading modules, which generate an enhanced electric field penetrating up to ~9 times deeper into hair follicle regions than conventional external application.”

This “Detangle” device, whose name the authors admit was inspired by the Disney animated film Tangled, isn’t a new hair-loss treatment so much as a revolutionary way to deliver one. One of its most high-tech features is a control circuit that creates pulsed electric fields across two types of electronic teeth. These teeth have different heights that generate a stronger electric field than if the teeth were aligned. That generates a positive environment for the transmembrane delivery of a therapeutic molecule into the impacted follicular cells, increasing uptake by more than three times, the authors report.

The authors tested the comb on mouse models and found hair growth recovered near 100 percent within a month, a steep increase from the approximate 70 percent recovery rate of typical minoxidil treatments—one of the go-to FDA-approved treatments for hair loss. To achieve this impressive recovery rate, the authors relied on the SRD5A2 siRNA molecule and a VEGFA plasmid. The first molecule inhibits dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a hormone that causes hair follicles to shrink, while the latter boosts blood vessel growth around the impacted follicles.

“By co‑delivering VEGFA plasmid and SRD5A2 siRNA, the Detangle system promotes hair follicle regeneration via a dual mechanism that synergizes electrostimulation with molecular regulation,” the authors write. “Given the multifaceted signaling abnormalities in AGA, the Detangle system presents a versatile platform for co‑delivering therapeutic agents beyond metabolic modulation.”

After 10,000 years, the comb finally gets a serious glow up.

#6332. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

#6331. Instagram posts may reveal subtle clues about loneliness

Instagram habits may reveal loneliness in college students but cannot reliably show their support networks, according to a new study.

Instagram users carefully choose what they share, but their posts may still reveal signs of loneliness.

A new study of U.S. college students found that posting habits, captions, and photos offered clues about how lonely students felt.

Those same accounts revealed far less about how many friends or relatives students could turn to for support.

The work was led by Sherry (Yueyi) Jiang with psychology professor Piotr Winkielman at the University of California San Diego. Jiang completed a doctorate in experimental psychology there in 2025.

All of the students attended that one university, and most of them were women. The results describe patterns across a group. They are not presented by the authors as a way to screen any single person.

Loneliness is difficult for other people to see. The authors also described it as a serious risk factor for early death. The effects are comparable in size to those of smoking and obesity, they wrote.

Each student completed questionnaires, then downloaded a full archive of their Instagram account and uploaded it to a secure server.

In total, 541 students took part, and 415 of them were kept in the analysis. A total of 93 students were excluded by the team because posts, likes, or comments were missing from their archives.

A further 33 students were removed since their questionnaires had been left unfinished.

Only part of an account can be seen on a public profile. About 62% of the students had private accounts.

Posts, likes, and comments that remain invisible to strangers on the app could therefore be studied by the researchers.

The archives contained 9,353 captions and 353,407 comments, together with the photos and the time of every post.

Faces in the photos were detected by one program, and the expression and head tilt of each face were estimated.

The tone of captions and comments was scored by other programs. Words were also sorted by these programs into themes, such as family or the past.

The share of each student’s posts made late at night, defined as 11 p.m. to 5 a.m., was also calculated.

Computer models were subsequently trained by the team to identify the lonelier students from those Instagram measures alone.

Data from 80% of the students were used to build the models, which were tested on the remaining 20%.

From the questionnaires, five scores were obtained for every student, and four of these reflected how lonely the student felt.

The fifth score addressed a separate matter. It reflected how many relatives and friends a student contacted regularly and could ask for help.

The main loneliness questionnaire included 20 statements, among them “I feel isolated from others.”

Model performance was judged on a scale where 0.5 equals a coin flip and 1 is perfect. A value of 0.77 was reached by the best model for this main questionnaire.

For each of two more specific loneliness scores, the models achieved 0.74, while a single-question score was predicted at 0.68. The first three results were described by the authors as moderate, and the last one as modest.

Weaker performance was recorded for the fifth score, which concerned support.

The best model reached 0.61, with an uncertainty range of 0.42 to 0.79. Because that range included 0.5, the result did not clearly establish performance better than chance.

Two kinds of loneliness have been separated by researchers since the 1970s.

Emotional loneliness is the distress of having no one close. Social loneliness is dissatisfaction with a person’s wider social circle.

On Instagram, students with higher social loneliness scores tended to be less active with other people.

These students liked fewer posts. They also commented less often and posted less on weekends.

A different pattern was seen in students with higher emotional loneliness scores. More of their posts went up late at night.

Their captions were more negative in tone, and sad or angry facial expressions were more common in their photos.

The emotionally lonely students also posted more often, not less. Frequent posting, the authors suggested, might be an effort to find emotional connection when close ties are missing.

Word choice was examined as well. Students who wrote “we” more often tended to score lower on emotional loneliness. Those who wrote “I” more often tended to score higher on social loneliness.

“Loneliness isn’t a one-size-fits-all experience, and neither are the solutions,” Winkielman said.

Two ideas were proposed by the authors for future testing. Social loneliness might be eased by more chances to engage with others.

For emotional loneliness, help with low mood and disrupted daily routines was suggested instead.

Lonely people are often depressed or anxious as well, and the same was true of these students.

The team therefore checked each Instagram sign again. This time, each student’s depression and anxiety scores were taken into account.

Only one sign was still linked to loneliness: fewer faces per post. Students whose photos contained fewer faces were more likely to score high on two of the loneliness measures.

According to the authors, fewer moments shared with other people may be reflected in photos that contain fewer faces. The same link between loneliness and the number of faces had been reported in an earlier study of Instagram users.

Past-focused words in captions were tied to two of the loneliness measures. Profile photos with the head tilted upward were tied to three.

That tilt is probably no accident, Jiang’s team wrote, given how carefully people pick their photo angles. But once depression and anxiety scores entered the analysis, neither sign was still tied to loneliness.

Nobody in the study was followed over time. Each of the 415 students filled out the questionnaires once and handed over an archive.

So the order is unknown: the Instagram habits may have come first, or the loneliness, or both.

The group itself was narrow. About 85% of the students were 21 or younger and about 79% were women.

Asian students (43.9%) and White students (38.8%) made up the two largest groups.

Age and culture change how loneliness is felt, the authors wrote, and they change posting habits on social media too.

Patterns found among San Diego undergraduates need to be tested in other populations.

There is also the question of misuse, which the authors raised themselves.

Flag the wrong person, and the result may be stigma or outreach that was never wanted. Miss the right person, and support does not arrive.

For that reason, the team limited its suggestion to consent-based research and to support services that people opt into.

Covert screening built only on these signs was advised against.

Two kinds of follow-up were proposed. One would measure the same people’s loneliness repeatedly while their Instagram activity is collected.

The other would briefly change how lonely people feel in an experiment, then record what they do online afterward. Cause is easier to isolate that way, according to the authors.

The full study was published in the journal npj Mental Health Research.

#6330. Ancient Egyptians Revered Cats as Sacred. Then 131 Skulls Revealed What Really Happened to Them.

Fractured skulls, healed wounds, and signs of strangling suggest sacred cats lived—and died—brutally.

Not every Egyptian necropolis was meant for humans. Across Egypt, the cemeteries of Bubastis in the eastern Nile Delta, the Bubasteion in northern Saqqara, and Speos Artemidos near Beni Hassan, along with others in Giza and the Dakhla Oasis, were meant for animals, especially cats. Cats were seen as the earthly embodiment of the feline goddess Bastet. Yet although they were often mummified as votive offerings, their treatment did not always match their status.

Early archaeologists usually ignored animal mummies in favor of human mummies, which were often showcased at theatrical unwrapping parties. Some animal mummies were used as ship ballast for the journey home after an expedition, while others were powdered for questionable medicine, burned for fuel, or ground into fertilizer. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, however, some animal mummies were unwrapped (without a party) so that their skeletal remains could inform studies of Egyptian fauna. Many of these skulls remain in museum collections in Egypt and abroad. Zooarchaeologist Wim Van Neer of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences and his research team studied one such collection: 131 exceptionally well-preserved skulls of small cats from Beni Hassan, now housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna. Their goal was to find out how the cats lived before they died.

“Attention was also paid to the presence of pathologies and marks on the skulls, which could provide information about the conditions in which the cats were kept and their cause of death,” Van Neer and his colleagues wrote in their study, recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science. In addition to carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis to determine diet, “characteristics such as dental abnormalities, infectious or metabolic disorders and trauma were recorded.”

Most of the skulls turned out to be from domestic cats (Felis catus), with several jungle cats (Felis chaus) among them. Many of the animals apparently suffered from conditions such as gum disease and infections, and some skulls had puncture marks and fractures that could indicate fights between cats. How the cats met their end, however, was more disturbing. Evidence suggests that cats were deliberately killed so they could be turned into offerings to Bastet. Fourteen of the skulls show traumatic injuries, including blunt-force and sharp-force trauma. Sharp-force trauma is thought to have possibly killed the humans who were sacrificed to join First Dynasty pharaohs in the afterlife. Beyond fight wounds, some injuries were inflicted long enough before death to show signs of healing, which suggests that the animals may have endured physical violence from humans while still alive.

When Van Neer and his team took a closer look at one skull, they found marks consistent with blows from a sharp metal weapon. Wounds on some of the other skulls were thought to have been made by strikes from a heavy wooden implement. The cats’ treatment before death also seems to have been deplorable. Although no ancient records describe how the cats were kept, the researchers inferred that they were probably held in crowded enclosures. This could explain the fights, as well as the attacks on domestic cats by jungle cats, which were caught in marshlands or along the banks of the Nile when Egypt was lusher than it is today. Isotope analysis showed that the jungle cats’ diet clearly differed from that of the domestic cats, further suggesting that this species was unlikely to have been bred in captivity.

Even among the wild-caught jungle cats, six of the seven skulls came from animals with conditions similar to those of their domestic relatives. This was probably a sign that all of the cats, the overwhelming majority of which were adults, were kept in conditions that caused illness and injury before death. Radiocarbon dating revealed when they died.

Cats are generally thought to have first been domesticated in the Fertile Crescent of the Near East roughly 10,000 years ago, although some recent genetic studies suggest it happened later, in Egypt or elsewhere in North Africa. In Egypt, the earliest clear evidence of domestic cats dates to the Middle Kingdom (c. 2000–1700 B.C.E.). However, demand for mummified cat offerings was greatest much later, in the Late and Ptolemaic Periods. Older feline mummies do exist, and one of the nine dated skulls goes back to the Third Intermediate Period. The other eight, however, date to between 380 and 40 B.C.E., from the end of the Late Period into the Ptolemaic era.

As for how the cats were killed, blunt- or sharp-force trauma appears to have been the main cause of death. Some cats were strangled, but a blow to the head was apparently the more common method. “Skull fractures were the most common cause of death, whereas evidence of strangulation occurred less frequently,” the researchers said. “Our observations of traumatic lesions on the skulls provide evidence of fatal injuries, as well as cases of animals that survived violent interactions with humans.”

She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6329. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 14: Venus and Mercury in Virgo

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M.Sunset: 4:44 P.M.Moonrise: 11:33 A.M.Moonset: 8:56 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time on the 15th, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6328. Breast cancer leaves signs in blood that may hint at its return

A new blood test showed promise for spotting breast cancer and predicting relapse, but larger studies remain essential.

Mammograms can sometimes miss breast cancer in women with dense breasts. A new blood test called EPINUC showed promise in detecting breast cancer regardless of breast density.

The test also found signs linked to cancer returning within five years.

Larger studies are needed to confirm whether it can help detect cancer early and predict its return.

The test was developed in the lab of Efrat Shema at the Weizmann Institute of Science.

For the new study, her team worked with Guy Ron, a physicist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Ron’s group belongs to the university’s Racah Institute of Physics.

The cancer status of every woman was already known when her blood sample was analyzed. The test has not yet been applied to women undergoing routine screening.

Inside a cell, DNA is wound around protein spools. Each spool, with its loop of DNA, is called a nucleosome.

Small chemical tags are added to the spool proteins. These tags help set which genes the cell uses, and biologists call them epigenetic tags.

Dying cells, whether healthy or cancerous, release nucleosomes into the bloodstream. The tags stay on.

Tumor DNA is the target of several blood tests for cancer. In Shema’s method, the tagged spools are instead examined individually under a microscope.

Each type of tag is marked with a fluorescent label of a different color. Tags that occur together on a single spool can therefore be identified.

The test needs less than 1 milliliter of plasma, the liquid part of blood – about one-fifth of a teaspoon.

Colorectal cancer was detected by an earlier version of the test.

Two further tags and three proteins related to breast tissue were added for the present study. A total of 29 measurements is now obtained from each sample.

The relevant tags were first sought in tumor tissue. Twelve women who had not yet received any treatment provided the samples.

The operations were performed at Kaplan Medical Center in Israel. Noa Furth, a researcher in Shema’s lab, is one of the study’s lead authors.

“Once a tumor is removed, there’s only a short window of opportunity before its epigenetic tags begin to deteriorate,” said Furth.

“So as each surgery began, the doctors would alert me. I would rush the tissue sample from the hospital to our lab on ice, and we’d start analyzing it that very day.”

The team measured the tags in more than 1.1 million individual cells.

Eleven of the 12 tumors were luminal. Hormone receptors are present on the cells of luminal tumors, which generally respond well to hormone-blocking drugs.

Each luminal tumor also contained a minor population of unusual cells. These cells resembled a different form of breast cancer, known as basal-like. A worse outlook is associated with that form.

Hormone signaling was reduced in the basal-like cells.

The same pattern of tags was observed in these cells across patients. In laboratory cultures of breast cancer cells, greater movement was recorded for cells of this kind.

The researchers then investigated whether genetic differences could explain the aggressive cells.

New colonies were established in the laboratory, each from a single cell.

“The differences appear to be mainly epigenetic,” Shema said.

“When we grew breast cancer models in the lab starting with nonaggressive cells, an aggressive population always emerged eventually.”

The test was then applied to stored blood from 77 women with luminal breast cancer. All had been treated at Mayo Clinic in Florida. Blood from 30 healthy women was also tested.

A computer model was trained to distinguish cancer samples from healthy samples. Its performance score was 0.95, where 0.5 indicates chance-level performance and 1 indicates perfect separation.

An identical score was obtained for the 42 patients with tumors in the smallest size class. Such tumors measure about 0.8 inches (2 centimeters) or less.

No change in performance was seen across density scores, which are assigned by radiologists from mammograms. This was also true of women with extremely dense breasts.

Samples from two Israeli hospitals and a second Mayo batch were subsequently included. The combined set comprised 137 patients and 51 healthy women.

Three-quarters of these samples were used to train a new model, and the remainder served as a test.

In the test group, 92% of the 13 healthy women were correctly identified as cancer-free.

Cancer was detected in 85% of the 34 patients and missed in 15%.

The test did about as well in 22 women with triple-negative breast cancer, which lacks hormone receptors.

Luminal breast cancer usually responds to treatment, but in many women it comes back. Differences among the cells within a tumor are suspected to be one reason tumors return.

All 77 Mayo patients gave blood before surgery. The women were then followed for at least five years. Cancer returned in 33 of them within five years, while 44 remained disease-free.

Two tags characteristic of the basal-like cells were elevated in the blood of women who later relapsed.

A model built on the blood measurements separated the two groups. It scored 0.81 on the same scale. Models based on age, tumor stage, grade, and other standard measures scored lower.

A score of 0.92 was recorded in a second, smaller set of 30 patients.

These differences in blood markers were also present in women with early-stage or low-grade tumors. Such tumors are rated as lower risk by standard measures.

The team also looked at Oncotype DX scores. Oncotype DX is a gene test performed on tumor tissue to estimate the risk of relapse.

Its scores did not differ between 40 women who stayed disease-free and nine who relapsed.

All samples had been collected earlier and were analyzed once the outcomes were known. The group to which each sample belonged was not concealed from the analysts.

The groups were small as well. Cancer returned in only 10 of the 30 patients in the second set.

Blood from healthy women was collected at the Weizmann Institute. Blood from patients was supplied by hospitals in the United States and Israel.

Nearly all of the tumors examined were luminal. Triple-negative tumors are usually treated with drugs before surgery, and few untreated ones were available.

The authors wrote that the tumor findings may not extend to other types of breast cancer.

Signals from tumor cells, damaged healthy tissue, and the immune system are combined in blood. A tag found in blood therefore cannot be attributed to the basal-like cells alone.

Both tumor tissue and blood were available from ten women. For most tags, higher levels in the tumor were accompanied by higher levels in the blood.

The blood-test method is covered by a patent application on which Shema is a named inventor. The exclusive license is held by a company called Epivision Genetics. Four of the study’s authors are affiliated with that company.

Larger studies of the blood test are still required, the authors wrote. In such studies, blood would be collected first and each woman’s outcome learned afterward.

A separate question concerns the basal-like cells. It remains to be tested whether tumor cells can be kept from switching states by epigenetic drugs.

“We’re now looking for treatments that could deprive cancer cells of their epigenetic flexibility – and perhaps even coax cells that have already turned aggressive into adopting less aggressive traits,” Shema said.

No such treatment was tested in this study.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.

We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

Are cows really the top contender for animal farts?

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"

If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.

But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

#6326. The rise of oxygen on Earth may have unfolded differently than we thought

Ancient rocks suggest major rises in Earth’s atmospheric oxygen occurred earlier than thought, while the deep ocean took longer to catch up.

For most of Earth’s history, the planet lacked enough atmospheric oxygen to sustain wildfires.

Charcoal preserved in rocks indicates that oxygen had reached levels capable of supporting wildfire by about 420 million years ago – roughly three-quarters of today’s atmospheric level.

Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at Chengdu University of Technology, reviewed evidence suggesting that major increases in atmospheric oxygen preceded corresponding changes in the ocean.

Their review suggests that two major atmospheric oxygen increases occurred earlier than traditionally thought.

Many widely used clues to ancient oxygen levels come from marine rocks, including their minerals, isotopes, and trace metals.

These records primarily reflect ocean chemistry, providing indirect evidence of atmospheric conditions.

Ocean chemistry is highly complicated. It answers to nutrient supply, biological productivity, how water circulates, even the shape of the basin.

Sulfate offers a more direct connection to the atmosphere. Atmospheric oxygen carries a distinctive isotopic signature that can pass into sulfate when sulfide minerals oxidize.

Preserved in sedimentary rocks, that signature helps researchers reconstruct ancient atmospheric conditions.

The Great Oxidation Event, 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago, still holds. Cyanobacteria had been quietly making oxygen in shallow coastal waters for ages before that.

Oxygen concentrations in these shallow waters may have reached levels sufficient to support oxygen-using microbes. Reactions with minerals and gases consumed much of that oxygen before it could accumulate in the atmosphere.

Then production finally outran consumption and the atmosphere flipped.

Steps two and three are where the textbooks take the hit. Wang and Li date them to 1.3–1.0 billion and 0.44–0.41 billion years ago.

Those dates precede the conventional timings of the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event, around 800–500 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event, around 420–360 million years ago.

But according to the sulfate record, those weren’t the atmosphere oxygenating.

They were the ocean catching up to atmospheric changes that had already happened – about 200 million years late in the first case, and 30 million years late in the second.

Between about a billion and 410 million years ago, the carbon isotope record is peppered with sharp excursions that generations of scientists read as oxygen rising.

The sulfate evidence suggests that some ocean oxygenation events temporarily lowered atmospheric oxygen. As oxygen entered the ocean, reactions with stored organic carbon and sulfur compounds consumed it.

The “boring billion” suddenly looks less boring. Modeling pegged to the sulfate data puts mid-Proterozoic atmospheric oxygen at 0.1–1% of today’s atmospheric oxygen level.

At those low atmospheric levels, local photosynthesis likely supplied much of the oxygen in shallow waters, while the deep ocean remained largely oxygen-free.

Two oxygen modes coexisted through most of this history. The first was local: cyanobacterial mats producing oxygen in shallow, sunlit patches.

The second was global: oxygen dissolving from the atmosphere into surface water and being shoved deep by circulation.

The local mode is older than three billion years. The global mode becomes more influential as atmospheric oxygen levels rise.

Widespread oxygenation of the deep ocean developed around 410 million years ago.

Oxygen-poor zones persisted, however, and episodes of widespread ocean oxygen loss occurred later.

Strangely, the ancient local mode still runs today. Redox-stratified lakes in Antarctica and Venezuela sustain oxygenated pockets above anoxic bottoms.

There, they are powered by the same benthic microbial photosynthesis that kept tiny patches of Earth’s ocean alive for two billion years.

Low oxygen availability initially restricted the habitats available to oxygen-dependent life.

During the Proterozoic, fluctuating oxygen levels helped shape opportunities for more complex organisms.

Eukaryotes appeared, and multicellularity got its start. Organisms also evolved ways to respond to low oxygen levels.

Later increases in oxygen helped expand the habitats available to large, active organisms.

Major increases in atmospheric oxygen came before widespread oxygenation of the deep ocean. In the long interval between them, life evolved amid uneven and changing oxygen supplies.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.

#6325. Why Do Helmets Still Fail to Stop Concussions? Scientists May Have Been Fighting the Wrong Force All Along.

A WWII physicist said twisting hits were the real danger. Sensors in 203 athletes’ mouths say otherwise.

An estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur in the U.S. each year. They’re so common that you might assume they’re not as serious as other injuries—but in fact, these mild traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) can often be more dangerous. While tendons, muscle, and bone heal good as new, repeated and sustained concussions—a typical occurrence in many athletic endeavors—can lead to dementia and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), an aggressive degenerative brain disease.

Although helmets have grown safer over the years in certain sports, concussions are still commonplace. That’s especially true in football, even after the high-profile introduction of the Guardian Cap for NFL preseason practices in 2022 and then in regular-season games in 2024. This suggests that there’s something about concussions, specifically the relationship of linear and rotational acceleration and the brain, that scientists still don’t understand.

During World War II, Scottish physicist A.H.S. Holbourn argued that rotational acceleration (think of an uppercut to the jaw) was more dangerous than linear acceleration (a straight-on, direct hit whose force goes through the center of the head). His theory was that rotation was worse because it stretches and strains brain tissue by moving different parts at different speeds. Scientists have focused on protecting against rotation ever since.

However, a new Stanford Medicine-led study suggests that linear acceleration, not rotation, may be the better predictor of concussion. The research comes from the lab of bioengineer David Camarillo, who’s spent more than a decade studying concussions and helmet safety. By analyzing unprecedentedly accurate impact data from motion-sensing mouthguards worn by 203 athletes across seven different sports, Camarillo and his team discovered that Holbourn’s initial assumptions weren’t correct. The results of their study were published in the journal Annals of Biomedical Engineering.

“Holbourn’s reasoning was based just on mechanics; it wasn’t biology,” David Camarillo, senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “The question we started out with many years ago was, ‘What are the forces required to cause concussion?’ If we understand the nature of those forces and the limits of the human brain, then it might be possible to prevent concussions.”

Previous studies relied on helmet-mounted sensors, but the authors note that those sensors are often inaccurate because helmets tend to move around a lot. Across the mouthguard-enabled data set, the researchers analyzed 3,851 impacts, of which 47 were verified as concussions. In their mathematical models comparing the data, peak linear acceleration was the single most predictive factor in whether a hit eventually produced a concussion. Camarillo and his team haven’t pinned down a mechanism for this result, but they suspect one of two culprits: the brain striking the inside of the skull, or cavitation, in which sudden pressure changes form tiny bubbles that then collapse.

If these results hold up in future studies, they could have profound implications for helmet safety and design. The mouthguard data showed that a hit producing 100 g of linear acceleration (100 times the acceleration of gravity) carries a 50 percent risk of concussion. That’s far lower than the often-cited 192 g threshold from earlier helmet-sensor studies. At 150 g, a hit that older data would have considered below the danger line, concussion risk tops 99 percent.

“Why are there so many concussions even when people are wearing helmets?” Camarillo asked. “Part of the answer could be in this paper, which is that the linear accelerations that we previously thought were safe, we now see are much more dangerous.”

In a way, the new results offer a bit of hope that helmets do have room for improvement, and with a greater focus on addressing linear acceleration, concussions could significantly drop in the coming years and decades. One Stanford-developed technology is a helmet with liquid-filled pads that reduces peak linear acceleration and knocks nearly 20 percentage points off the chances of concussion on high-impact hits versus standard football helmets.

“If linear acceleration is its own distinct mechanism of concussion and it’s very common, then we’ve been missing a lot,” Camarillo said. “We haven’t tried as hard to optimize for this variable. It gives me some hope that there’s a new opportunity for preventing concussions.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6324. Nov. 14, 2012: NASA announces an extended mission for Kepler

The Kepler Space Telescope, launched March 6, 2009, was designed to search the Milky Way for exoplanets. Using the transit method, Kepler ultimately observed over 500,00 stars and contributed to the discovery of almost 2,700 exoplanets.

Though Kepler was originally intended for a 3.5-year mission, NASA announced on Nov. 14, 2012, that the space telescope had successfully completed its primary mission and would be embarking on an extended mission. When a second gyroscope (also referred to as a reaction wheel) failed in May 2013 – the first having failed in July 2012 – that mission was in question, however, as it left the spacecraft with limited control for pointing. But engineers were able to craft a workaround using the momentum of the Sun’s light pressure to keep Kepler evenly and steadily directed, and the extended mission using this methodology, dubbed K2, was formally approved in May 2014. Kepler continued to function for a further four years, and was retired in October 2018 when it ran out of fuel. TESS (the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) has since inherited its planet-hunting mantle.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6323. Light and sound could change how we measure blood pressure

A wrist sensor read blood pressure beat by beat from laser-made sound in an artery, matching a cuff within a few mmHg in two volunteers.

In a clinic, a blood pressure check usually means a cuff squeezing an arm to produce a reading for that moment.

A sensor pressed to the wrist has now read blood pressure beat by beat, with no cuff at all.

The sensor flashes pulses of light into the skin and picks up the faint sound an artery gives off in response. That sound tells it how wide the artery is with every heartbeat.

In two volunteers tested over three months, its readings differed from a clinical finger-cuff monitor by only a few points on average.

Two people make a proof of concept rather than a finished product, and the researchers wrote that a full clinical trial is still to come.

Amir Rosenthal and Daniel Lange of the Technion in Haifa, Israel, led the work with doctoral student Gil Gelbert.

Rosenthal runs a lab for biomedical imaging and sensing at the university’s Viterbi Faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering.

Blood pressure is one of the most important indicators of heart health. Yet it is still usually measured with an inflatable cuff, which gives a reading at a single point in time.

The alternatives have been a catheter inside an artery or repeated cuff readings, and neither suits daily life.

Wrist sensors have tried to fill the gap with stand-in signals, such as the pulse that light-based sensors read through the skin. Those signals shift when the device moves and need frequent recalibration.

A more direct route is the artery itself. Each heartbeat widens an artery slightly, and the amount it widens tracks the pressure inside.

Ultrasound patches can follow that widening, but they need rows of transmitting elements and careful alignment over the artery.

The wrist’s radial artery is only about 0.08 inches (2 millimeters) across and sits about 0.16 inches (4 millimeters) deep, which makes that alignment hard to hold in a wearable.

The Technion team turned to an effect in which light makes sound. Near-infrared laser light pulses through the skin 100 times a second.

Blood absorbs that light far more than the tissue around it, so the artery warms and expands by a tiny amount and sends out an ultrasound wave.

A detector on the skin records the wave. The gap between the sound from the artery’s near wall and its far wall gives the artery’s inner width, and that width changes with every beat.

What makes the device unusual is its detector. It is a channel for light etched into a silicon chip and coated in a soft silicone layer.

The channel is about a thousandth of a millimeter wide, far thinner than a human hair.

Pressure from the sound wave changes how light moves through the channel, and a readout system measures the change.

Because the detector is so small, it picks up sound from almost any direction, so it doesn’t have to be aimed at the artery. A single element does the job that patches need arrays for.

An established formula then converts the artery’s width into blood pressure, calibrated once per person.

The team first tested the sensor on artificial arteries built to mimic the wrist.

Shifting the sensor up to 0.4 inches (10 millimeters) off center, or rotating it up to 30 degrees, changed the measured width by only about a hundredth of a millimeter.

A conventional piezoelectric detector element, tested the same way, worked only within half that range and lost the artery’s edges when turned by just 5 degrees.

On a 29-year-old man’s wrist, finding the artery took less than 10 seconds. The team then slid the sensor across his arm while it recorded, and the readings held steady.

A standard pulse-echo ultrasound element, by contrast, produced an error of roughly a fifth of a millimeter when moved just 0.3 millimeters.

The blood pressure test used two volunteers. One was the 29-year-old man, whose pressure ran slightly high. The other was a 42-year-old woman, whose pressure ran slightly low.

Over three months they sat for 120 measurements of 10 seconds each, some at rest and some while tensing their core muscles, which raises blood pressure.

A finger-cuff system approved for clinical use recorded the reference pressure at the same time.

The sensor was calibrated once per person at the start. For every later session it was taken off and put back by hand, with no markers to guide its position, the way a watch goes back on a wrist.

Averaged across all 120 measurements, the sensor’s readings differed from the cuff system by 2.6 mmHg on the lower, diastolic number. On the upper, systolic number, the gap was 4.7 mmHg.

The authors wrote that this matches the accuracy reported for the leading wearable ultrasound patches in studies of similar size.

In one session, the sensor tracked the man’s pressure continuously for more than 30 minutes, several days after it had been calibrated.

Two people are enough to show the idea works, not to show it works for everyone. The authors wrote that a full validation study would need more than 85 participants.

Only a study that size, they wrote, could tell whether the sensor performs differently in men and women.

Every reading was also taken sitting still. The authors wrote that sliding the sensor didn’t disturb the signal, but blood pressure during walking or exercise has not been tested.

Both lasers, the one that fires the pulses and the one that reads the detector, still sit on a lab bench.

The team wrote that compact laser diodes could replace them, and that the readout electronics could eventually be built into the chip itself.

The sensor also records the full shape of each pressure pulse, beyond the high and low numbers. The authors wrote that this information was not used in the study.

The researchers believe the technology could eventually go into smartwatches and medical patches.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6322. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

#6321. Webb reveals a stellar nursery with secrets even infrared cannot reach

Why does Sagittarius B2 produce so many stars? Webb’s infrared observations offer a closer look at an unusually active region near the Milky Way’s center.

Today’s Image of the Day reveals a crowded stretch of the Milky Way where bright stars and orange clouds surround patches of almost complete darkness.

Those dark areas may look like gaps in the scene, but they contain some of its most intriguing material: dense clouds concealing the birth of stars.

The James Webb Space Telescope captured this view of Sagittarius B2 with its Near-Infrared Camera, or NIRCam.

Released on September 24, 2025, the image offers a detailed look at a vast stellar nursery near our galaxy’s center.

Its brilliant points of light are only part of the story. Understanding what remains hidden could help astronomers explain why this particular cloud produces stars so much more actively than its surroundings.

Sagittarius B2 lies a few hundred light-years from Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the Milky Way’s heart.

This central neighborhood contains crowded star fields, thick clouds and complicated magnetic fields.

Yet an abundance of gas does not automatically translate into abundant star formation.

According to NASA’s release, Sagittarius B2 contains about 10 percent of the gas in the galactic center but accounts for roughly half of its star formation.

That imbalance makes it a valuable place to investigate what allows some clouds to become especially productive stellar nurseries.

Astronomers Adam Ginsburg and Nazar Budaiev of the University of Florida led the observing program.

The team used Webb to examine how massive stars emerge within this unusually dense environment.

Stars begin inside cold molecular clouds, where gas gathers into denser pockets.

As a clump gains material, its gravity strengthens. Eventually, gravity can pull it inward, beginning a collapse that heats the material and produces a developing star called a protostar.

At first, the object draws much of its energy from that collapse. Later, if its core becomes sufficiently hot and compressed, hydrogen nuclei begin combining to form helium.

This process, nuclear fusion, supplies the energy that allows a star to shine through the longest stage of its life.

The cloud surrounding a developing star can make that transition difficult to observe. Astronomers must examine stellar birth through the very material that makes it possible.

A bright, mature star may announce itself across space, while a much younger object remains buried in its original supply of gas and dust.

Webb’s instruments reveal different parts of this environment.

In the NIRCam image, stars crowd the field, interrupted by luminous clouds and dark structures.

Near-infrared light can pass through some of the obscuring dust, bringing objects into view that would be harder to distinguish in visible light.

A companion image from Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument, or MIRI, changes the emphasis.

Warm dust becomes much more prominent, while far fewer stars remain visible. Only the brightest stars emit strongly enough at these longer wavelengths to stand out through the clouds.

Together, the views show why one image cannot provide a complete inventory of a stellar nursery.

Changing the wavelengths changes which objects and structures dominate the scene. The same cloud can appear rich in stars in one view and rich in glowing dust in another.

Even Webb’s sensitivity has limits in Sagittarius B2.

The team’s observations used 14 filters covering wavelengths from 1.5 to 25 micrometers.

They revealed a layered cloud containing both exposed massive stars and deeply obscured populations.

The researchers also identified candidate regions of gas energized by massive stars that earlier radio observations had missed.

Elsewhere, MIRI detected radiation escaping from the embedded cluster Sagittarius B2 North along cavities associated with outflows.

These openings provide routes for light to emerge from an otherwise heavily concealed environment.

But many young stellar objects previously detected with the ALMA radio telescope remained invisible to Webb.

Their absence from the infrared images illustrates how effectively the surrounding material can conceal ongoing star formation.

The result gives today’s image a second way to be read. Its bright stars reveal what has emerged into view.

Its dark clouds mark places where the next part of the story is still unfolding beyond Webb’s sight.

Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, A. Ginsburg, N. Budaiev and T. Yoo (University of Florida); image processing: A. Pagan (STScI)

#6320. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 15: Mars and Jupiter in conjunction

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

After nine days in space, the Artemis II crewmembers faced their final and riskiest challenge: splashdown. In this excerpt from the book "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space," astronaut Jeremy Hansen describes the moment from his chair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nine days in space, the four crewmembers of NASA's Artemis II mission looked out their capsule window on April 10, 2026, and saw the bright-blue Earth below them. The crew had traveled more than 250,000 miles (400,000 kilometers) from our planet — farther from Earth than any humans had ever gone — and now, home was just a few hundred miles straight down.

Only one milestone remained: splashdown, a fast and fiery plunge into the Pacific Ocean that would mark the end of humanity's first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years.Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian Space Agency astronaut on the crew, had every reason to be confident that the team's Orion crew capsule would hold up just fine. But this was Hansen's first time in space, and his first time dropping through the sky like a fireball at 24,600 mph (39,600 kmh).

It wasn't that he was afraid for himself, Hansen explains in "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, the Groundbreaking Human Mission into Deep Space" (Hanover Square Press, 2026), which he co-wrote with John Larsen). Rather, he knew that his wife Catherine and three children would be among the millions of Earthlings watching the most dangerous moment of his mission from below.

In this excerpt from the book, Hansen describes the thrilling intensity of splashdown and the euphoria of knowing that he and his crewmates were going to make it back safely — and make history.

CSA astronaut Jeremy Hansen smiles inside the Orion crew capsule during the Artemis II lunar flyby.

Immediately after jettisoning the European Service Module, and exactly half an hour before we were due to splashdown, Mission Control initiated the crew module raise burn. This nineteen-second burn was the first and only burn using the small thrusters built into our Orion capsule. It slightly shallowed our entry trajectory to put us right in the sweet spot while also providing some added distance from the service module, as we'd be hitting the atmosphere in near succession. It, too, went flawlessly. I tightened my straps; it was time for the fireworks.

A re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere is absolutely on the short list of the most incredible experiences of my life. We slammed into it at 7:53 p.m., thundering down at over 10 kilometres [6.2 miles] per second. Per second.

The thrusters fired almost constantly to stabilize the capsule: loud thuds, as if Thor himself were hammering on our spacecraft, as the G-forces quickly began to build, aggressively scrubbing off the velocity we had added to our rocket nine days earlier. Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us. It started red and transformed into a bright, bluish-green, pulsating light. It was breathtaking, the bright colors igniting our senses.

It was insane to think about what we were doing. We all knew how this worked; we all knew the science. But deep inside, I also recognized that astronauts must have a screw loose to do this. Nobody in their right mind would strap themselves inside a metal canister that itself was sitting inside a giant fireball. But there was no other way down, and I had accepted the realities of this journey long in advance.

Although I was at peace, I felt guilty for the stress I was putting on my family. I had talked to them openly about the mission's risks, and this was the highest-risk moment. I tried to send my love telepathically, telling them it was going great.

The Orion capsule drops toward the Pacific Ocean with all parachutes successfully deployed.

As we continued our freefall, it looked like a thousand camera flashes were exploding inside Integrity. I lowered the sun visor on my helmet. There were only centimeters of heatshield and aluminum separating me from the more than 2500°C heat outside. Almost instantly, the heat inside our cramped home also began to rise, an increase that engineers refer to as "thermally benign." All I know is that I couldn't feel it, blissfully wrapped in my thermally controlled garments.

As we continued to fall, the G-forces built up to nearly four times the pressure we feel on Earth. I wasn't too worried, having endured more than five minutes of the same G-force, or more, in the NASA centrifuge trainer. I had half-expected the freefall back to Earth to seem short, but it was a long six minutes before the flames finally ceased and we re-established communications with Mission Control.

It had already been a wild ride, but I also knew another crazy part — parachute deployment and the actual splashdown — lay ahead. My adrenalin kept pumping.

Within seconds, we saw plasma forming outside our windows, and the heat at the base of our capsule grew so intense that flames soon engulfed us.

"Integrity, Houston. Comms check, post-blackout," we heard from Mission Control. It was music to our ears. It was exactly 8:00 p.m.

"Houston, Integrity," Reid [Wiseman, mission commander], replied. "We have you loud and clear."

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried. For the folks at NASA, it was clear that all had gone well during the descent — a small fleet of NASA and Air Force planes had captured it on high-resolution cameras. But, for me, it wasn't over yet. I wouldn't truly feel safe until our three main parachutes successfully deployed. If they didn't, we'd be a chunk of metal slamming into the ocean at incredibly high speed, and the chances of surviving that would be somewhere between minimal and non-existent.

I've watched many of my close friends return from space, and I find the minutes after surviving the re-entry heat until the parachutes deploy to be the hardest part to watch. When I see a capsule plunge through the clouds with no chutes, I always worry they might not appear at all. That's completely terrifying.

Jeremy Hansen arrives on the deck of the USS John P. Murtha after being recovered from the Orion capsule. All four crewmembers were in perfect health after splashdown.

I thought of Catherine and the kids, sending them a "don't worry, gang" message in my mind. Catherine later told me that she had a very bad feeling about the heatshield, so when we emerged from blackout, she began crying and didn't even focus on the parachutes.

Three minutes later, at an altitude of 7,100 metres, timed explosions released small chutes that pulled off the cover for two larger chutes, called drogues because they are intended to slow our acceleration to a speed that would allow our main parachutes to open without ripping. They did their job perfectly, but it was wild inside the capsule, jerking us back and forth like a ride at the fair.

This is when people the world over clapped, hugged, and, in some cases, cried.

One minute later, at only 1,500 metres above the ocean, the drogue chutes cut loose, and, for a few moments, we felt like we were falling backward. Then, in succession, the three main parachutes began deploying, blossoming slowly so they wouldn't tear apart. The rate of our fall slowed as the red-and-white nylon canopies, each 35 metres in diameter, filled with air. The thrusters kept firing, aiming the capsule's base directly toward the point of impact.

"Integrity, we see three good-looking parachutes," we heard from our CAPCOM. Within seconds, our splashdown speed had reduced to 27 kilometres per hour.

That's it, I said to myself. I'm pretty sure we can survive whatever else could be thrown at us now.

Christina [Koch, mission specialist] seemed to agree. We grabbed one another's hands in a moment of celebration.

Excerpted from "Earthrise: Inside Artemis II, The Groundbreaking Human Mission Into Deep Space" by John Larsen with Jeremy Hansen. © 2026 by John Larsen, used with permission by HarperCollins/Hanover Square Press.
