#6318. Archaeologists Found a Castaway Camp on an Island at the End of the World. Did a Legendary Sailor Build It?

The island behind a Jules Verne classic was hiding a shipwreck mystery.

While hunting penguins for oil (yes, people really do that) in 1873, famed Argentine sailor Luis Piedra Buena wrecked his schooner brig Espora off the southern tip of South America. He and his crew regrouped on a deserted beach, spent about two months building a new cutter, the Luisito, and sailed safely to Chile to tell their tale. Now, researchers believe they may have found pieces of a shipwreck and the remains of a “castaway camp” possibly tied to Piedra Buena on Isla de los Estados, an island “at the end of the world.”

In a new study published in the journal Antiquity, lead author Nicolás Ciarlo of Spain’s University of Cádiz and his colleagues describe how their research into the maritime history of the island, which lies across the Strait of Le Maire from the tip of Tierra del Fuego, led them to a castaway camp. They believe the camp may link the island’s Lacroix Inlet in Franklin Bay to the more than 150-year-old survival story.

Isla de los Estados is probably best known for a lighthouse that inspired Jules Verne’s novel The Lighthouse at the End of the World. The island forms the easternmost point of Argentina’s Tierra del Fuego Province, and from the 17th century onward it lay along a key sailing route.

By 1870, the Argentine government had granted the island to Piedra Buena. Although he never established a settlement there, he sailed past it countless times while pursuing his interests throughout Patagonia. Then disaster struck. “During a campaign for exploiting penguins for oil, he and his crew lost the schooner brig Espora,” according to the study.

The crew survived, built a cutter, and sailed to Punta Arenas, Chile. There, Piedra Buena described the time they had spent at Lacroix Inlet, although experts have long doubted that he identified the location correctly.

To test his account, the research team visited Lacroix Inlet in January 2026 with help from the Argentine Navy. There, they found the “remains of a shipwreck and a temporary camp” on a wind-battered stretch of coast at the base of a cliff, exposed to strong southwesterly storms. The “possible castaway camp” sat near a stream.

“Although there is still no common agreement, Piedra Buena’s account and other documentary evidence suggest that this bay is likely the place where the Espora sank,” the authors wrote. “The location and material culture of the temporary occupation at Lacroix Inlet point to a connection between this site and the nearby shipwreck remains and thus, possibly with the Espora and her crew.”

At the camp, which the team described as a “short-term occupation,” they found glass beads, buttons, and a bottle, along with nautical items such as a deck prism and a rudder hinge. Elsewhere in the inlet lay the remains of three wooden hulls, including timber that may have been used to build a structure. All the wood likely came from ships’ hulls, but it’s unclear whether it all came from the same vessel.

The team called the finds “novel data” on the history of seafaring around the island. Their preliminary assessment points to at least one shipwreck that led to a temporary settlement. “The identity of the vessel/s and the castaways’ trajectories are the subject of ongoing inquiry,” they wrote, adding that a thorough study of the timbers may provide definitive answers.

Some artifacts are especially telling. “The deck glass located on the surface is one of the most revealing artifacts,” Ciarlo told Discover Magazine. “To assess the identity of the Espora—as it happens with other shipwreck sites—is like putting together a puzzle. It does not rely on a unique proof, but on a critical analysis and merging of multiple lines of evidence.”

Still, questions remain. In the study, the authors acknowledged that they found no trace of the site where the Luisito was built, and it’s unclear whether the Espora was ever completely taken apart. They wrote that more work is needed at the camp and on the shipwrecks in the weather-beaten inlet.

“As archaeologists,” Ciarlo said, according to Phys.org, “being in this isolated and wild place allowed us to taste what a small group of castaways saw and felt about 150 years ago.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6317. Children’s brain responses to food may help predict later fat gain

Children who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger brain responses to food pictures, which were linked to greater body fat gain later.

Breakfast cereal, packaged bread and instant soup get blamed for childhood weight gain because of what’s in them.

A new study links children’s ultra-processed food intake to how their brains respond to pictures of food.

A year later, the children with stronger reactions had gained more body fat. Every child was a healthy weight when the study began, and this kind of study can show a link but not prove a cause.

Dr. Kathleen Page, a physician and professor of medicine and pediatrics at the Keck School of Medicine of USC, is the study’s senior author, and Jasmin Alves is the first author.

“Children’s brains are still developing, habits are still forming and food preferences are still being made. It’s an important period where the brain is very sensitive to food and the food environment,” Dr. Page said.

The 46 children were 7 to 10 years old and part of the BrainChild study.

That long-running project follows children whose mothers did or did not have diabetes during pregnancy, and it recruits them through Kaiser Permanente Southern California.

Each child had a BMI below the 85th percentile for their age and sex.

On two separate days, each child and a parent walked trained staff through everything the child had eaten in the previous 24 hours.

The researchers then sorted every food by how processed it was. On average, ultra-processed foods supplied about 68% of the children’s daily calories, close to the 67% a 2021 analysis found for American kids as a whole.

About a month later, each child lay in an MRI scanner after a 12-hour fast and then a glucose drink.

The scanner recorded how active two deep brain areas were during the food photos.

Both areas are part of a structure called the striatum, which handles motivation, learning and reward.

The ventral striatum is involved in anticipating and experiencing rewards. The dorsal striatum helps link cues with learned actions and habits.

Children who got more of their calories from ultra-processed foods had stronger dorsal striatum responses to the food photos.

The ventral striatum showed no clear pattern. The association with dorsal striatum responses remained after accounting for each child’s age, sex, body size and whether their mother had diabetes during pregnancy.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dr. Page emphasized that the association held even after the researchers accounted for total calorie intake, suggesting that how much children ate did not fully explain the pattern.

The children also consumed a standardized drink before their scans, “so the stronger response to food cues wasn’t simply due to hunger,” she said.

Rodent studies had already shown that a steady diet of sugar-rich food changes how the dorsal striatum works.

No earlier study had looked directly at how much ultra-processed food people habitually eat and how their striatum responds, the authors wrote.

The children came back for measurements roughly a year later, with an average gap of about 15 months.

Their BMI had risen by one point on average, their body fat by close to one percentage point, and their waists by about 1.5 inches (3.9 centimeters).

Children whose dorsal striatum had reacted more strongly to the food photos gained more in BMI and body fat. Eating more ultra-processed food was linked to a bigger waist a year later.

Ultra-processed food intake’s links to BMI and body fat were weak enough that chance could explain them.

The team then asked how much of the link between diet and fat gain involved the brain.

Once the dorsal striatum response was in the model, the association between ultra-processed food and body fat gain shrank by 44%, and the one with BMI by 31%.

Dr. Page said the result does more than repeat that these foods are tied to weight gain, because it points to a pathway in the brain.

“It actually gives us insight into the neurobiological underpinnings by which these foods may be linked to body composition over time.”

What stood out most to Dr. Page was that every child was a healthy weight when the study began.

“This suggests that the link between ultra-processed foods and the brain’s response to food cues may be detectable before obesity develops, rather than simply resulting from excess weight,” she told Earth.com.

Added sugar is in most ultra-processed foods, so the team checked whether sugar was driving the result.

Children who ate more added sugar tended to have stronger striatum responses too, but the pattern wasn’t clear enough to rule out chance.

When the team accounted for added sugar, the link between ultra-processed food and the dorsal striatum weakened and was no longer statistically clear.

Still, the authors wrote that sugar is unlikely to be the whole story.

Forty-six children is a small group, and the authors wrote that this limited their power to detect modest effects. Brain scans of this kind are also hard to reproduce in small groups.

Each child was scanned only once, so no one knows yet whether the stronger responses persist or fade as children get older.

An observational study like this one can’t say which came first. Children whose reward circuits already react more strongly to food may be the ones who reach for ultra-processed foods, rather than the other way around.

And because every child started at a healthy weight, the pattern may look different in children who already carry extra weight.

The research team said the burden shouldn’t fall only on families and children, because these foods are often the most accessible, affordable and convenient ones available.

“Changing the food environment to help people access healthier, more minimally processed foods is an important part of the solution,” Dr. Page noted.

For families in the meantime, Dr. Page said the practical goal is to shift the overall diet toward more minimally processed foods. “Parents should not feel that they have to eliminate every packaged food.”

Her examples were water instead of soda and fruit instead of fruit juice or fruit snacks. The aim is more vegetables, beans, nuts, eggs and other foods closer to their original form.

One way to test whether the diet is driving the brain response is to change the diet.

“A future intervention study could test whether replacing ultra-processed foods with mostly minimally processed foods changes how children’s brains respond to food cues and helps prevent excess body-fat gain,” Dr. Page said.

Meanwhile, the BrainChild team will keep following these children through puberty and into young adulthood.

Dr. Page said the next step is to see how their diets relate to changes in the developing brain. The team will also look at their risk for obesity over time.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

#6316. Nov. 15, 1988: The Buran orbiter launches

In 1976, the Soviet Union began development of the Buran orbiter. Concerned that the American space shuttle program might be used for military purposes, the Soviets responded with Buran and its Energia booster rocket, which were capable of carrying antisatellite and antimissile weapons and targeting locations on Earth’s surface. Though the nonmilitary objectives for Buran included ferrying crew and supplies to the Mir Space Station, Buran was also capable of flying unmanned and fully automated.

The Buran program marked several achievements – the development of 230 new technologies, a fully recoverable rocket capable of lifting 220,000 pounds (100,000 kilograms) to orbit, a shuttle that could carry up to 10 cosmonauts. However, it only made a single flight: On Nov. 15, 1988, Buran launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, performed two orbits, and returned to Earth. The 206-minute flight was seamless, and was performed fully under remote control, with no crew members aboard. Despite this success, the colossal expense of the program and the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union meant the end of Buran. In 2002, the roof of a hangar at Baikonur collapsed, killing eight people and destroying the orbiter and its rocket.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6315. Carbon sinking into Antarctica’s deep ocean holds a surprise

Dissolved organic matter changes little as water crosses Antarctica’s continental shelf, offering new insight into the ocean’s carbon cycle.

A recent study suggests that dissolved organic matter changes little as water crosses the Antarctic continental shelf and sinks toward the deep ocean.

Despite abundant marine life and shifting water masses, researchers found little change in its amount or chemical composition.

The study drew on water samples from two expeditions aboard the Polarstern, an icebreaker operated by the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research (AWI).

Ocean currents move water around the globe in a vast circulation system. The Antarctic continental shelf plays an essential part.

Deep water arrives from the north and rises onto the shelf. Extreme cold and sea ice formation make it denser.

This heavy water then sinks into the deep ocean. It helps form Antarctic bottom water, the coldest, densest, and one of the most voluminous water masses in the world’s oceans.

As the water crosses the shelf, it passes abundant marine life. Researchers wanted to know if these processes change the carbon before the water sinks.

The answer matters since rising temperatures and declining sea ice could change how the Southern Ocean stores and transports carbon.

The southern Weddell Sea shelf is a key place for Antarctic bottom water formation. It is remote and hard to reach. Studying it depends on specialized research vessels like the Polarstern.

Dissolved organic matter plays a crucial role in the global carbon cycle. It is released during the production and breakdown of marine life.

This matter holds tens of thousands of different compounds. Some are quickly eaten by microbes, while others persist for a long time.

It is the largest reservoir of organic carbon in the ocean. Understanding how it changes and moves is key to predicting the ocean’s response to climate change.

The team analyzed water samples from two Polarstern expeditions to the southern Weddell Sea (2016 and 2021). To find out whether the carbon changed, the team used several complementary methods.

The Institute for Chemistry and Biology of the Marine Environment (ICBM) at the University of Oldenburg has a distinctive collection of advanced analytical instruments. These allow detailed study of the molecular make-up and structure of complex organic matter mixtures.

State-of-the-art analytics at AWI’s MICADAS (Mini Carbon Dating System) facility helped the team determine the age of the carbon.

The shelf sees intense seasonal blooms of phytoplankton, so scientists expected freshly produced organic matter that microbes can readily break down to leave a clear molecular imprint on the sinking water.

Instead, they found almost no detectable change in the amount or composition of dissolved organic matter carried into the deep ocean.

The key to this paradox is time. Dense waters stay on the Weddell Sea continental shelf for an unusually long period, between six and twelve years.

During this time, the water also circulates beneath the large Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf.

The researchers suggest that this extended stay gives microbes time to break down newly produced organic matter, converting its carbon into dissolved inorganic carbon before the water leaves the shelf.

“Our study reveals that the molecular properties of dissolved organic matter are conserved during deep-water formation in the southern Weddell Sea,” said lead author Gonzalo Gomez-Saez from AWI.

“Our findings highlight dissolved organic matter as a stable component of the regional Southern Ocean carbon cycle.”

“Dissolved organic matter is a huge and complex store of carbon in the ocean. By examining its molecules in detail, we can investigate how it changes as water moves through the Antarctic continental shelf,” added senior author Thorsten Dittmar from ICBM.

The findings suggest that this large carbon store changes little during water movement and transformation on the southern Weddell Sea shelf.

“Global warming is now reaching the Antarctic shelf seas. If the large reservoir of dissolved organic matter is scarcely affected by processes on the shelf, this suggests that this carbon reservoir could remain largely unaffected by climate change in this region,” said study co-author Moritz Holtappels from AWI.

But not all ocean carbon behaves the same way.

Dissolved organic carbon remained largely stable in this study, while other forms of carbon may respond differently to environmental change.

That includes organic particles sinking to the seabed and dissolved inorganic carbon in seawater. These may react more to changes in temperature, sea ice cover, and marine life.

Researchers will keep studying how different forms of carbon respond to environmental change.

One effort is Antarctica InSync, an international initiative bringing scientists together to study the rapidly changing Antarctic environment.

Oceanographer and co-author Alexander Haumann will help lead a Polarstern expedition in 2028.

The team will investigate how carbon moves through the Southern Ocean during the Antarctic winter.

These observations will help scientists understand how climate change may affect the ocean’s ability to transport and store carbon.

Intense biological activity does not necessarily leave a lasting imprint on the dissolved organic matter carried into the deep ocean.

In the southern Weddell Sea, the water’s long journey across the shelf may help explain why.

Microbes get years, not weeks, to finish the job.

That stability is good news in one sense. This carbon reservoir may hold up as the region warms.

But it is not a blanket reassurance. Other carbon pools could shift.

The team’s next steps will probe those differences. For now, the southern Weddell Sea offers a rare case of carbon holding steady in a changing world.

The study is published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6314. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

#6313. This Bissell Carpet Cleaner Is Lightweight, Compact, and Easy to Store—All for Under $125

If you live in a smaller space or multilevel home, the TurboClean is worth a look.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Carpet cleaning is one of those chores that feels like a massive undertaking every time—not to mention, no one likes having to lug around a heavy carpet cleaner sloshing with water. The Bissell TurboClean Upright Carpet Cleaner is made for people like us, with a lightweight design and minimal learning curve.

This machine is great for small spaces, and for those who prefer streamlined and simplified household appliances. Although it does have a smaller water tank capacity and lacks handheld attachments, it provides a powerful clean paired with easy maneuverability and fast drying time.

The compact design makes it easy both to use and to store. It’ll be sitting alongside your favorite dry vacuum as a trusted staple of your cleaning routine in no time, as I found to be the case for myself.

I set aside a weekend morning to test the TurboClean upright across a frequently used area of my main living space, spanning the pathway from the door to the garage through to the kitchen. The area includes some carpet that I've vacuumed frequently, but not deep-cleaned in years, as well as a low-pile area rug. I didn’t pretreat the area with dry vacuuming, but I checked for any larger pieces of debris that might clog up the cleaner.

The cleaner was quick and easy to assemble, and filling the water tank was simple too. I followed the manufacturer’s instructions to add some of the included Bissell cleaning solution along with warm water. Afterward, I tackled my designated area of carpeting, followed by a section of the area rug.

Throughout the process, I monitored how well the cleaner performed in a few ways. I kept an eye on how long the water tank lasted before I had to empty the dirty water and refill the clean tank, as well as how many times I had to go over an area for a satisfactory clean. I also maneuvered the machine as close as possible to the baseboards and into corners to test movability and range. Finally, I checked how long it took for the carpet to dry afterward, as well as how easy it was to clean the machine when I wrapped it all up.

The first thing I noticed about the TurboClean Upright was its lightness. Weighing just under 13 pounds, it’s one of the lightest carpet cleaners I’ve tried. That light weight, combined with a compact base and smooth wheels, made it especially easy to move around, whether I was pulling it along straight pathways, turning corners, or navigating as close to the wall as I could get. Even with a full tank, I found it very manageable.

That lightness, though, didn’t mean flimsiness or poor performance. On the contrary: it pulled up considerably more dirt than I expected, providing a deep, visible clean on a high-traffic area of light-colored carpet.

While I didn’t have any serious stains for it to handle, it did do a great job on visible spots of dirt or water-drop stains that had become dried-in. It worked equally well on the area rug, refreshing it without damaging the fibers or dulling the colors.

As a compact machine, the TurboClean Upright does have one of the hallmark downsides to its class: the need for frequent refills. The water tank has a capacity of just over half a gallon. As I worked through my test area, I had to stop, empty the dirty water tank, and refill the cleaner with fresh water and cleaning solution.

If you’re trying to spot-clean a few small patches, you can probably get away without a refill, but if you’re actually doing a whole room or more, you’ll need to do the empty-and-refill routine—probably multiple times. It’s also worth noting that the machine does not heat the water from within. It recommends adding warm water (no warmer than 140°F) to the clean tank with the solution.

Fortunately, the process of refilling and, later, disassembling and cleaning, is very easy. The tank and handle feel a little light to the touch, but they’re sturdier than they seem, and it’s easy to get a grip and handle the empty/refill cycle without making a mess. Disassembling the main parts (the upper tank and the two-part handle) is as easy as the push of a button. There’s really very little in the way of maintenance, which I appreciated.

If you plan on cleaning an area with a lot of debris (like pet hair), I would suggest vacuuming first. Otherwise, you do run the risk of particles getting tangled up around the cleaning brush, which can take a while to get cleared.

For me, the biggest downside to this cleaner is its lack of any hand tools. Where most home carpet cleaners come with at least a handheld tool or a spot-cleaning tool of some kind, the basic model TurboClean Upright has none. While it’s still a light and small enough machine to maneuver around most spaces, the lack of extensions and tools does limit what it can do.

I was able to lower it enough to clean underneath a coffee table, and I could get fairly close to the wall, but not quite as deep into the corners. I wish there had been a stain tool, a pet tool, or even just a simple hand tool extension. Without those, the cleaner is unable to handle smaller crevices or upholstery.

I didn’t have any deep, dark stains that needed removing, but if I did have those, it would have been nice to be able to really focus the cleaning power on those areas. As currently designed, the best I could do was simply run the full cleaner over the same spot repeatedly.

All that being said, the TurboClean Upright does come in a deluxe “Pet” model as well. That model does include a 7-foot extendible hose, a self-cleaning “tough stains” brush, and a spraying crevice tool. Those additions offer more flexibility to tackle small spots and get into crevices, improving the cleaner’s performance and versatility. And, of course, anyone with pets will definitely want to look into this upgrade to gain the extra cleaning power for pet stains and hair.

The TurboClean Upright comes with two trial-size Bissell cleaning formulas: the Pro Max Clean + Protect and the Pet Pro Oxy Urine Eliminator. I used the Pro Max solution for deep cleaning, adding it to the clean tank up to the indicated “formula” line. The instructions also indicate that users can add a dose of the “Oxy Boost” formula for a stronger cleaning reaction, but since I didn’t have that on hand, I skipped that step.

After multiple passes across my testing area, I really appreciated the strong suction power. Although there’s not a specific “quick dry” mode, the manual does suggest running “dry passes” across the wet areas to suction up as much of the residual water as possible. It only took between one and two hours for the test section to feel pretty much dry to the touch.

The Bissell TurboClean Upright is ideal for smaller spaces and intuitive operation, bringing plenty of cleaning power but keeping the machine itself relatively compact and lightweight. I was able to easily clean carpeting and an area rug, and I could move around corners easily.

The smaller size does mean a smaller tank (requiring more frequent stops to refill), and I wish the standard model included some attachment tools for greater versatility. Still, if you’re looking for a reliable cleaner for a smaller area that does the job well (and doesn’t leave your carpet sopping wet), this could be a great pick for you.

#6312. Scientists have a bold new plan to slow down human aging by changing how our cells talk to each other

Scientists propose rebalancing the GPCR receptor family, which 40 percent of drugs already target, to delay several diseases of aging at the same time.

Heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and Alzheimer’s are often associated with aging. They get treated as three different problems, by three different specialists, with three different sets of pills.

To a group of pharmacologists, that is the wrong way of thinking.

The three diseases share a handful of aging processes, and those processes run through one family of receptors on the surface of cells. Nearly 40 percent of today’s drugs already act on that family.

The scientists propose treating the family as one network and nudging it back toward a younger balance, so that several diseases of aging are delayed at once.

It’s a proposal rather than an experiment. The paper reviews what is known about these receptors and lays out a plan. No drug or combination of drugs has been tested against aging in this way.

Stuart Maudsley of the Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, is the senior author, with nine co-authors in the United States, Britain, and Canada.

In an interview with Earth.com, he said the case rests on practicality rather than on proof. “Our argument is not that GPCRs have already been shown to outperform every other approach,” he said.

“It is that they offer an unusually practical set of entry points into this interconnected biology, because we already know how to target many of them with medicines.”

The receptors are called G protein-coupled receptors, or GPCRs. Each one sits in a cell’s outer membrane and passes a message from outside the cell to the machinery inside.

The message might come from a hormone, a nerve signal, or a nutrient. Humans have roughly 800 of them in five families, and about 720 belong to the largest family.

Many familiar medicines work on these receptors, each prescribed for one disease. Beta blockers for heart failure and blood pressure drugs that block angiotensin act on them.

So do the Parkinson’s drug istradefylline and the diabetes and weight-loss drugs semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Maudsley compared the body to a transport network. Repairing one road helps, he said, but it may not clear congestion caused by problems across the wider system.

In the same way, treating one disease pathway can be valuable without fixing the linked disturbances that leave a person open to several other conditions of aging.

The paper’s central observation is that the five families, which differ widely in structure, age in the same way. Cells carry fewer of the protective receptors on their surface.

The receptors end up in the wrong place inside the cell, their signaling weakens, and the subtypes that drive inflammation become more stable or more numerous.

The authors tie those changes to the standard list of aging’s hallmarks: chronic low-level inflammation, failing mitochondria, DNA damage, worn-out protein maintenance, and the exhaustion of stem cells.

The list also includes the buildup of senescent cells, which stop dividing but keep sending out inflammatory signals.

In the authors’ reading, the decline of this receptor family accounts for many of those hallmarks. The evidence behind that ranges from approved drugs to animal and cell studies.

That is the part Maudsley called most interesting. Very different receptor families, he said, connect to the same problems in aging, and that convergence is what makes a network therapy worth testing.

The plan is not to turn the receptors up. “Crucially, this is not about switching all GPCR activity up or down,” Maudsley said.

“Some signals may need strengthening, others restraining, and the right balance will depend on the tissue and the individual. Precision, rather than blanket stimulation, is the central idea.”

The authors describe several tools. One is a drug that triggers only part of a receptor’s response. Another binds a receptor at a second site to tune it rather than switch it.

A third is a single molecule that acts on several receptors at once. A computer model of an individual patient’s biology would help choose among them.

They also propose pairing receptor drugs with other anti-aging treatments, such as drugs that clear senescent cells or improve metabolism.

The authors wrote that this could be “the greatest leap in medicine since antibiotics.” They also wrote that biology may never offer a cure for everything.

Asked by Earth.com what the first test would be, Maudsley described a small one. Take an aged animal model. One group gets a treatment that supports metabolic resilience, another gets a treatment that limits persistent inflammation, and a third gets both.

Then measure physical function, metabolic control, and tissue health rather than a single lab marker.

The combination would have to beat either treatment alone, and the team would also need evidence that the benefit ran through the receptor network they meant to change.

If it did, he said, the next step would be a randomized trial in a defined patient group. That trial would test whether the network can be influenced safely in people, which is not the same as claiming to have slowed human aging.

Maudsley told Earth.com he expects the field to deliver on its goal of more healthy years within five to ten years, given the pace of computational biology. That is his forecast; the paper sets no date.

The paper names its own limits. Part of aging is the slow buildup of random copying errors in DNA, and the authors wrote that no treatment has been shown to reduce that error rate. Their strategy aims at what cells do in response to the damage, not at the damage itself.

Many GPCRs bind several different molecules and set off several signals, which makes a clean, selective drug hard to design.

For gene-based approaches, getting the treatment into most tissues is an unsolved problem. And stimulating stem cells to repair tissue could raise the risk of cancer.

Two of the authors have a commercial stake. Silke Dodel co-founded AstraNexa and founded Deep Science, two companies in Boca Raton, Florida, and Roza Bejanyan works for AstraNexa.

The other authors are at Moffitt, the Department of Pharmacology at the University of Cambridge, McGill University, and Florida Atlantic University.

Whether rebalancing a receptor network delays even two of these diseases of aging at the same time in an animal is the open question. The combination experiment Maudsley laid out is where an answer would start.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Science.

#6311. The Sky Today on Monday, November 16: Titan south, Rhea north

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 15: Mars and Jupiter in conjunction

It’s a great night to catch Saturn’s largest and brightest moon, Titan, as it skims south of the planet. Two hours after sunset, Saturn is roughly 40° high in the southeast, outshining all the other stars in this region of the sky. It lies to the lower left of the Circlet of Pisces and to the upper left of the bright star Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus.

Zoom in on Saturn with a telescope to first catch sight of its ring system, stretching 43” from end to end and tilted 8° to our line of sight. Currently we are seeing Saturn’s southern side, including the entirety of the planet’s southern hemisphere. The gas giant’s disk now measures 19” across.

Titan is difficult to miss, shining at mid-8th magnitude just south of the ringed planet. Don’t be fooled by a fainter 10th-magnitude field star, which lies just to Titan’s west. The three next-brightest moons, also 10th magnitude, are Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They lie closer to the planet. Tethys sits about 40” west of Saturn’s center shortly before 8 P.M. EST, while Dione is just west of the limb and Rhea just east of the planet. Dione and Rhea are moving westward, and Rhea will skim just north of Saturn’s pole along the way, standing due north of the planet around 10:40 P.M. EST. Tethys is moving east, and will disappear behind the planet’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 2:35 A.M. EST on the 16th (still late on the 15th along the Pacific Coast).

Ancient writers couldn't agree on how Egypt's last queen took her own life, and the famous snakebite story may owe more to her enemies than to the facts.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The death of Cleopatra is among the most famous in history. In 31 B.C., the Egyptian queen and her Roman ally and lover, Mark Antony, lost the Battle of Actium to Octavian, who would later become Rome's first emperor, Augustus. The following summer, Cleopatra was captured during a Roman ambush inside her royal tomb in Alexandria.

According to Octavian’s account, rather than facing the disgrace of defeat, the queen allowed a venomous asp snake to bite her and quickly succumbed to its poison. Some Roman writers, such as the historian Velleius Paterculus, repeated that story without question.

But others were far less certain of this account, calling it Roman propaganda to cement Octavian's rise to power. And most historians today doubt that a snake was involved at all. So how did Cleopatra die?

Live Science spoke with experts, who told us that the queen's death is still shrouded in mystery.

"We cannot know for sure exactly how Cleopatra died," Prudence Jones, a professor of classics at Montclair State University in New Jersey and author of "Cleopatra: A Sourcebook" (University of Oklahoma Press, 2006), told Live Science in an email.

What historians largely agree on is that Cleopatra VII, the last queen of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty, took her own life and that she chose a method that left her body composed and dignified.

Physical evidence of Cleopatra's death is elusive. Much of Alexandria's royal quarter now lies underwater, and underwater archaeologist Franck Goddio, who has been excavating it, hasn't found the queen's mausoleum, Jones said. Even if Cleopatra's remains surfaced, bones would be unlikely to show evidence of snake venom, she added, noting that forensics is outside her area of expertise.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Divers celebrate as a crane pulls an artifact from the waters at Abu Qir bay in Alexandria, Egypt on Aug. 21, 2025.

The best witness may have been Olympus, Cleopatra's personal physician. "Unfortunately, nothing survives of Olympus' account," Jones said.

What does remain is a story told largely by Cleopatra's enemies. The earliest surviving account is a poem by the Roman poet Horace, whose patron was a close friend of Octavian, said Jane Draycott, a historian at the University of Glasgow. His Ode 1.37, written around the time of her death, celebrates Octavian's victory and already pictures the queen handling serpents — yet it ends with grudging admiration for a woman who refused to be paraded as a trophy.

Following her capture, Cleopatra was held under military guard. By then, she had already tried to end her life twice. Cleopatra had tried to stab herself when Roman soldiers broke into the mausoleum where she had barricaded herself, and she later tried to starve herself, stopping only after Octavian threatened her children.

To Draycott, those attempts leave little doubt that Cleopatra would rather die than live as a captive. "She does not want to be a prisoner; she does not want to be led through the streets of Rome in triumph as a defeated foe," she told Live Science.

In the Greco-Roman world, suicide didn't carry the stigma it later acquired under Christianity, she added. "It was a way of wiping the slate clean, removing any shame, any disgrace from yourself." After the defeat of his remaining forces at Alexandria and hearing a false report of Cleopatra's death, Antony was the first of the two lovers to die by suicide.

According to the Greek biographer Plutarch, who based his account on that of Cleopatra's personal physician, Cleopatra visited Antony's tomb, bathed, ate and sent Octavian a sealed letter asking to be buried beside Antony, signaling that she meant to die. Octavian realized what was happening and sent messengers rushing to her, but they arrived too late. They found her dead in her royal regalia, with her attendants Iras and Charmion dying beside her.

A statue depicting Cleopatra's suicide by asp, the most famous of several ancient theories.

Jones has compiled what ancient historians, biographers, geographers and physicians wrote about Cleopatra's death. Every source mentions a snakebite, but several also suggest other possibilities, including a poisonous ointment, poison hidden in a hollow hairpin, and snake venom poured into a wound the queen made by biting herself. Only one of these writers, the geographer Strabo, was alive when Cleopatra died, and the only people in the room with her died, too.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio wrote that the sole clue was a pair of faint pricks on her arm. That doesn't settle much, however. "A cobra bite can appear as two small puncture wounds, but not all cobra bites appear this way and not all double puncture wounds result from snakebites," Jones said.

Jones traces the snake version of the story to Octavian, who was in Alexandria when Cleopatra died. Plutarch reported that an image of Cleopatra with an asp clinging to her was carried in Octavian's triumphal procession in Rome. "Octavian, however, was Cleopatra's enemy and for that reason we may not want to accept his account uncritically," Jones said.

Draycott suggested another possible source of confusion: Snake-shaped jewelry was fashionable in Alexandria at the time, so Romans viewing an effigy of the queen may have mistaken a snake bracelet for a real snake.

Draycott doesn't think one snake could have killed all three women. Jones is less certain. Snakes don't inject the same amount of venom with every bite, and some "dry bites" deliver none at all, Jones said. "On the other hand, I don't think it is impossible, as the body of a cobra contains enough venom to kill multiple people," she added.

The general view among historians, Draycott said, is that Cleopatra took some kind of poison — one that worked quickly and didn't cause seizures or vomiting. The absence of these symptoms is telling: An asp is believed to be what is now known as the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), whose venom causes a slow, agonizing death with respiratory failure.

A young Egyptian cobra (Naja haja) strikes a typical defensive pose in scrubland near Sidi Ifni, Morocco.

Cleopatra likely would have had other means, then. Alexandria was the Mediterranean's center of scientific study, and texts from the period, such as Nicander's "Theriaca," catalog venomous animals, Jones noted. Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII, even consulted the pharmacologist Zopyrus about antidotes. Plutarch claimed that Cleopatra personally oversaw experiments that observed the effects of deadly poisons on condemned prisoners.

Still, that claim and other poison stories should be read with caution, Draycott said, because they draw on Roman stereotypes about women. In the Roman view, "manly men will battle with swords," while women, seen as "deceitful and weak" at this time, were thought to kill in secret. "They'll sneak it into your food," Draycott said, summing up the stereotype.

Roman writers were equally suspicious. Poisoning allegations dogged the Hellenistic dynasties of ancient Egypt and the neighboring Seleucid kingdom, as well as Rome's own imperial family. Some were probably true, Draycott said, but others may have been foodborne illnesses or other health conditions people didn't understand.

The method may remain a mystery, but for most historians, the motive doesn't change: Cleopatra chose to die on her own terms.

#6309. The world grows more than enough food for everyone on Earth, yet hunger and food shortages increase each year

Economists argue that food shortages now come from war and climate shocks, not empty fields.

We do not have a problem growing food. In fact, global farms produce more calories per person every year, even as the human population grows.

The real problem is getting that food to the people who need it. Extreme hunger and local food shortages are currently expected to worsen in at least 13 countries.

Elizabeth Robinson, an environmental economist at the London School of Economics, argues that the planet isn’t short of food. Conflict is the main reason for those limited supplies, she wrote, and climate change is increasingly part of it.

Robinson directs the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at LSE. She made the case in an opinion article published in the BMJ‘s climate issue. She drew on U.N. hunger reports and climate assessments. with no new data of her own.

In an interview with Earth.com, she said the trouble starts with where the food is. “There is still plenty of food, but often it is in the wrong place, and takes too long to reach people in need,” Robinson said.

The U.N.’s Food and Agriculture Organization and World Food Program identify 13 hotspots where they expect acute food shortages to increase.

Armed conflict and violence affect twelve of them, Robinson wrote, and four face a risk of famine: Sudan, South Sudan, the Gaza Strip, and Somalia.

Beyond the hotspots, around 60 to 70 percent of the world’s most undernourished people live in areas affected by conflict. By one estimate she cited, 85 percent of those facing hunger live in conflict-affected countries.

Fighting cuts off food at every stage. Farmland is abandoned or becomes harder to farm, and people are driven from their homes. Access to markets is restricted, and prices climb past what families can pay.

Where conflict leads to food shortages, more children grow up stunted, Robinson wrote. The U.N. Security Council formally recognized the link between hunger and conflict in a 2018 resolution, and climate change is making that link harder to break.

Hotter years and more extreme weather, including heatwaves and swings in rainfall, cost farmers their crops as well as shifting the distribution of pests and plant diseases, Robinson wrote. Food prices also become less predictable.

An estimated 123.7 million more people experienced moderate or severe food shortages in 2023 because of extra heatwave days and drought months, compared with the 1981 to 2010 average. Robinson took that figure from the 2025 Lancet Countdown report on health and climate change.

Each force makes the other worse. Reports show that food shortages trigger violence and political unrest, and conflict, in turn, deepens hunger.

Researchers broadly agree that climate change is a threat multiplier, Robinson wrote, and studies show that climate shocks worsen hunger in places that are already at war.

Asked by Earth.com what has changed since she wrote the piece, Robinson said the timing is what worries her most.

“I am really concerned that just as a particularly strong El Niño is peaking, and the number of people facing severe hunger is increasing, funding for food assistance is falling,” Robinson said.

That El Niño is expected to strengthen, she said, which will be another climate shock for places where food security is already stressed.

The FAO and WFP have added northeast Nigeria and Somalia to the highest-concern group in their Hunger Hotspots outlook, she said. Haiti has now moved to the very high concern category.

In her view, conflict, climate shocks, El Niño and high input costs are all happening at the same time. The effects will build, she said, because planting and fertilizer supplies are being disrupted.

Robinson isn’t not convinced that the international community is taking the situation seriously enough.

Ukraine has historically supplied a significant share of the world’s wheat, corn, barley and sunflower oil, and Russia’s invasion disrupted each of those markets, Robinson wrote.

In addition, the U.S.-Iran war has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which is affecting energy and fertilizer prices. That matters for next season’s harvests in countries that depend on inputs from the region.

Supply is also concentrated. Just five breadbasket countries supply around four fifths of the corn traded internationally. Three crops, rice, wheat and corn, provide over 40 percent of the world’s food calories.

Governments can make shocks worse. After Russia invaded Ukraine, reports indicated that some countries hoarded grain while others imposed export restrictions, just as they had during the 2008 food crisis. Both moves amplify shocks, Robinson wrote.

Robinson’s prescription starts with emissions. Agriculture and the food system account for almost a third of global emissions, she wrote, and cutting them while feeding a growing population won’t be simple.

Shifting toward more plant-based diets in higher-income countries and cutting food loss and waste would lower emissions and leave more food available.

Countries that rely less on trade and more on storage and domestic production can dampen price spikes, she wrote. Cooperation on regional storage may be more achievable than global coordination.

Farmers need climate insurance, drought-resistant seeds and smart irrigation. The most vulnerable households need targeted safety nets, in cash or food, when prices rise.

In the short term, Robinson told Earth.com, keeping food moving through war zones may matter most. “So right now, protecting access routes could well do the most good, but this is very much a short term measure, and not easy,” she said.

“Climate change, conflict, and the resulting increase in hunger that is being experienced around the world, come from choices our governments are making,” she said.

That is her judgment after decades of work on food insecurity, and the BMJ article is a commissioned opinion piece, not a peer-reviewed study.

The open question is the size of the climate share. Researchers have not agreed on how much of conflict-linked hunger is driven by climate change. The 123.7 million figure counts heat and drought alone, not the wars they may feed.

In the short term, support that arrives before a crisis peaks, protecting local harvests or sending cash and food to affected households, can reduce hunger, Robinson wrote.

The lasting fix, however, is bigger: in the medium to long term, “systemic changes are needed across the full agri-food supply chain, from what we grow, and how, through to what we eat.”

“But we need to see far more commitment from governments,” she said. The food exists. Whether it reaches the people who need it before the next shock is up to the governments from whom she is asking for more.

The full article was published in the journal BMJ.

#6308. The 8 Best Salt Spreaders for Getting Out Ahead of Winter Storms

They’re more reliable and durable than a basic fertilizer spreader.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter doesn’t have to be severe for ice to be a problem—even one small storm can leave a slippery layer of frozen water that causes a fall. But putting down a simple layer of snow melt can easily prevent any accidents. It can also reduce the amount of time you have to mess with shovels or snowblowers. But believe it or not, how you put it down matters, and the best salt spreaders are there to guide you.

Snow melt, typically rock salt or calcium chloride, melts existing ice and prevents new ice from forming. Using a salt spreader, which spins and sprays your snow melt all around, helps ensure you get a nice, even coat over any area you prep. Gardeners may recognize the salt spreader as a close cousin of the fertilizer spreader, but with a more robust construction to endure winter weather and the corrosive nature of salt.

Salt spreaders come in a wide array of sizes to suit different jobs, including small handheld spreaders for front stoops and short walkways, walk-behind models for a long driveway, and large tow-behind spreaders for prepping parking lots. Whether you need to de-ice a front walk or an entire parking lot, we can help you find the best salt spreader for your snow removal situation.

Tony Carrick tapped his experience covering landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security to find the salt spreaders worth the money. Reviews Editor David Dritsas—who covers landscaping, tools, and DIY, including outdoor tools like snow blowers and snow shovels—then updated these recommendations ahead of winter. They picked the best salt spreaders based on their experiences using various models to treat driveways and sidewalks around the home. They also researched industry standards, detailed specifications, and user recommendations from customer reviews.

This salt spreader’s size, ability to control salt flow, and reasonable price tag make it a great all-around choice for salt spreading. With its 80-pound capacity, it can cover the average driveway, as well as sidewalks and walkways in a single load. It also comes well equipped to handle winter weather with large, pneumatic 12-inch wheels and a sturdy steel frame.

The spreader features a plastic spiked auger (though we prefer a metal spiked auger) that cuts through clumps of most deicing salts, preventing clogs. You should, however, avoid using rock salt, as it is larger and could get caught in the plastic construction.

We appreciate its three adjustable baffles, which allow you to reduce or expand its coverage area to prevent overspread onto the lawn and landscaping. This is a great mid-size salt spreader and a perfect fit for most homes.

If you’re looking to get the most bang for your buck out of a spreader, then go with this model from Scotts. Not only can you spread salt with it, but you can also use it to seed and fertilize your lawn. Unlike most fertilizer spreaders, this model can spread ice melt. Additionally, it features rubber tires, unlike the plastic wheels found on other Scotts spreaders, allowing it to handle icy conditions.

There’s a dial that gives you precise control over how much salt, seed, or fertilizer you’re releasing with each step—this is common on fertilizer spreaders but not so much with salt spreaders. And since it has Scott’s EdgeGuard technology, you can treat walks and driveways without showering your grass and landscaping with salt.

This combination of features makes it a great jack-of-all-trades spreader for those who want one machine for all seasons.

This top-of-the-line spreader from EarthWay can handle large jobs, holding up to 100 pounds, with holes and an auger large enough to pass rock salt up to 3 inches in size, plus a very large, 15-foot spread width.

It’s a little bit heavier than other models on our list—30 pounds alone before you even add the salt—but it rolls on two large, knobby 13-inch pneumatic tires, which help you avoid slipping and sliding over icy terrain.

These features make this walk-behind model a good option for professionals or homeowners with large paved areas to prep.

There’s no sense investing in an expensive walk-behind salt spreader if you only have to clear a walkway or front stoop. This handheld model gets the job done and doesn’t cost much. Plus, you can use it in the warmer months to seed and fertilize small patches of lawn and landscaping beds.

There are separate spreader settings for seed, fertilizer, and ice melt, and it holds up to 2 pounds of product. It even has an ergonomic arm support that makes it relatively comfortable to hold while you’re spreading product. Sure, it would be easier to use if it were automatic, but we’ll take the low-cost manual option any day of the week.

If you only need a small spreader but don’t want to deal with a hand crank, this rechargeable electric model may work better for you. It runs on a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, and in addition to working with salt and de-icer, you can also use it for seeds and fertilizer.

It has eight flow rate settings, allowing you to release as little or as much as you like, though levels 7 and 8 are intended for use with heavy salts. The speed is variable, and you can adjust the spread up to 127 degrees with a lever on the side. Narrowing the spread can help you be more precise and protect garden beds or lawns from getting salt burn.

The hopper is 2.7 liters, and the battery runs for up to two hours, making this motorized spreader more than up to the challenge of covering the driveways and sidewalks of most average homes. Since it's battery-powered and listed as not waterproof, it's recommended to clean it of any moisture when you're done using it.

Agri-Fab’s massive salt spreader offers one of the largest capacities of any non-professional-grade walk-behind model we’ve seen. Its massive hopper can hold a whopping 130 pounds of salt, which is enough to cover a long service road or an 80-car parking lot. It’s built to handle all that weight with a frame made from 1-inch-thick steel tubing. The large 12-inch pneumatic tires have heavy treads to prevent slipping on snow and ice.

The heavy-duty design wouldn’t be complete without a stainless steel impeller to break up clogs. It also features a waterproof cover to keep the ice melt dry if you have to go out on a rainy day. This commercial-grade salt spreader is built for big jobs.

If you’ve got an ATV or lawn tractor and a lot of ground to cover, spare your back and mount this towable spreader. With its 185-pound capacity, a single load can cover up to an acre of soon-to-be-snowy ground.

The universal hitch will work with all tractors, UTVs, and ATVs. The control rod extends far enough that you won’t have to get out of the driver’s seat to adjust the flow of salt. Its 15-inch pneumatic tires and thick-gauge steel frame keep it stable, even when pulled a little too fast. There’s also a hopper cover that keeps the salt from getting wet while working in rain or snow.

This is a great option if you have a long driveway or a large parking area to cover.

Due to its mountable design, this salt spreader gives you the capacity of a towable spreader, but won’t compromise the maneuverability of a four-wheeler. This semipro spreader can hold up to 15 gallons of ice melt, which means it’s really made for prepping long service roads, parking lots, and commercial spaces, rather than homes.

The ATVS15A spreader uses a plate and auger powered by a 23-volt motor to launch a 30-foot-wide swath of salt. The hopper has a lid that keeps your ice melt dry and prevents it from bouncing out of the top of the hopper.

Since you sit right in front of the spreader, accessing the on/off switch and gate controls is convenient from the driver’s seat. This is a solid commercial option for contractors who need to prep worksites, workers in small communities with service roads, and commercial areas that might be easier to reach on an ATV than a truck.

These are compact, watering can-sized basins with a handle and either a hand crank or a motorized trigger mechanism. Their compact size and light weight make spreading salt easy work, provided you only need to cover a small area. They can’t hold much salt and have a limited range, so they’re best reserved for small jobs like patio doorways, stoops, or a short front walkway.

This type of spreader sits on two wheels, with a large plastic basin and a spinning impeller at the base. As you push the spreader forward, the salt shoots out the front and both sides of the basin. These wheelbarrow-esque spreaders can hold a large amount of ice melt, so they’re the way to go for most homes with large patios, parking spaces, driveways, and sidewalks.

This is one of the largest options. If you’re responsible for clearing snow off a parking lot or a long driveway that’s more than a couple of hundred feet long, you may want to get a truly massive salt spreader that hitches to the back of an ATV or riding lawn mower.

Some spreaders offer even larger capacities that attach to the trailer hitch on a pickup truck or mount to the back of an ATV. Obviously, these spreaders can hold a much larger amount of salt than a walk-behind. It’s overkill for most homes, but small businesses or farms could use one to prep large parking lots, loading docks, and other large paved areas.

The more ice melt your salt spreader can hold, the more ground you can cover before you need to stop for a refill. As a rule of thumb, you’ll need to spread about 3 pounds of snow melt for every 1,000 square feet of area. Though there is some variation from model to model, picking the right type of spreader is the first and most important step.

Most handheld spreaders only hold enough salt to de-ice a short walk and a front stoop; walk-behind spreaders can hold about 65 to 130 pounds of ice; and towable spreaders often hold up to 185 pounds of salt.

Spread width measures how far your spreader will throw salt as you use it. Most spreaders have a range between 6 feet for walk-behind models and as far as 30 feet for larger towable spreaders.

While a wide spread can save you time, keep in mind that it may also lead you to spray salt onto your lawn and landscaping. Salt will dry out plants, so you want to avoid spraying green areas as much as possible. If you need to salt sidewalks and driveways that border grass and landscaped areas, look for adjustable spreaders with baffles so you can narrow your spread and avoid overspray.

You have a few options when it comes to ice melt. Calcium chloride is the best option. It melts ice even at extreme sub-zero temperatures, won’t harm your plants, and is less toxic than rock salt, but it’s also pricier.

Rock salt is the cheapest, but‌ it’s more toxic, won’t work in extreme cold, and can clog spreaders more easily. Magnesium chloride is the least toxic option and works at temperatures as low as 5 degrees Fahrenheit.

Whichever ice melt you choose, be sure to use it as directed, as all of the above can eat away at wood, steel, and concrete.

While they operate similarly, we don’t recommend putting rock salt in a fertilizer/seed spreader. Dedicated salt spreaders store corrosive salt and endure icy winter conditions. Using a fertilizer spreader to spread salt once or twice won’t break it, but it won’t work as well and may shorten its lifespan in the long term.

Salt spreaders typically have hoppers made from thick, durable plastic that sit on heavy-gauge steel frames and feature pneumatic rubber wheels with heavy tread that can grip slick paved surfaces. They also come equipped with metal moving parts that are capable of chopping up hard salt without wearing down.

If you want one spreader to do double duty, it would probably make more sense to use a salt spreader to spread seed or fertilizer. That said, fertilizer/seed spreaders often provide more precise control of the spread direction and quantity, which comes in handy when you have specific patches to cover and you want to be precise. Keep in mind that adding too much fertilizer to a lawn can cause it to burn out.

If you do put fertilizer in your salt spreader (or vice versa), make sure to clean out the salt thoroughly before placing any seed or fertilizer in the hopper. Any lingering salt in the mix will dry out the grass, damaging your lawn.

Bottom line: We would recommend buying two separate spreaders, despite their similarities.

Most residential-use salt spreaders can't handle rock salt, while many professional-level salt spreaders can. Check with the manufacturer to determine what types of de-icer are compatible with your salt spreader before loading it with rock salt, as it can damage the spreader’s impeller.

If rock salt isn’t compatible with your spreader, use a different type of ice melt, such as potassium chloride, magnesium chloride, or calcium chloride.

#6307. Sewage pollution may take a hidden ocean route into coastal air

Tijuana River sewage chemicals survive a 22-mile trip north underwater and then escape into San Diego's air, far from the river mouth.

When raw sewage pours into the ocean, closing the beach can help protect swimmers.

Chemicals from the Tijuana River sewage that reaches the Pacific at Imperial Beach can also enter the air.

The findings suggest that chemicals from the sewage travel north in ocean currents for about 22 miles (35 kilometers) before escaping into the air near La Jolla.

Wind alone could not explain their presence that far away.

Karolina Cysneiros de Carvalho, an atmospheric scientist, led the study at the University of California, Riverside and the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Colorado.

Her co-authors were UC Riverside’s William Porter and Kelley Barsanti and Kimberly Prather of UC San Diego.

The team sampled the air at four coastal sites in August and September 2024, when the river was carrying far more wastewater than it typically does during a dry summer.

“It was already known that compounds from this waste could enter the air, but we didn’t realize until now how far it could travel underwater before emerging,” Cysneiros de Carvalho said.

The Tijuana River drains land on both sides of the border, three quarters of it in Mexico. It carries untreated sewage, industrial waste and street runoff into the sea, a plume visible from orbit.

In most summers, its flow drops to almost nothing. In the summer of 2024, between 42 million and 55 million gallons (160 million to 207 million liters) a day kept coming, with no rain to explain it.

The team tracked one chemical first: dimethyl trisulfide, a sulfur compound given off by rotting organic matter and sewage.

They measured it at a hotspot on the river about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) inland, at the river’s estuary and at Imperial Beach.

The last site was the Scripps Institution of Oceanography pier in La Jolla, far up the coast.

The hotspot accounted for 83% of the combined signal across the four sites, and La Jolla for 2%. Small as that was, the compound was there, 22 miles from the river.

Dimethyl trisulfide breaks down fast in air.

By the team’s calculations, it falls to about a third of its starting level within 3.6 miles (5.8 kilometers), even when the night air is least reactive.

Carried by wind alone, at most 10% of the compound would survive the trip to La Jolla, and under some conditions almost none would remain.

“We found pollutants far from the source that couldn’t be explained by just the wind,” said William Porter, a UC Riverside atmospheric scientist and co-author.

On September 10, 2024, a pump station began diverting wastewater south, away from the river.

Levels of the compound at the La Jolla pier then fell by 86%.

The mid-morning signal was gone within 24 hours, but an early-morning peak lasted another two days before it dropped below detection.

The two-day tail mattered. The air mixed more after the diversion, which by itself would have diluted the compound about threefold.

It fell about twelvefold instead, so something besides mixing was removing it, and something had been holding a reserve of it long enough to leak out over two more days.

The evidence points to the ocean as that reserve. In water, the compound breaks down slowly.

It also escapes into the air slowly, largely because of resistance to its movement through the water toward the surface.

In the team’s models, 14% to 31% of the compound survives the 22-mile trip north in the top 6.6 feet (2 meters) of the sea. At a depth of 33 feet (10 meters), 61% to 76% survives.

Some compounds also stick loosely to organic particles in the water, which shelters them a little longer before they let go.

The water itself showed the route. Moorings off Del Mar, 5.6 miles (9 kilometers) past La Jolla, recorded a layer of unusually fresh water below the surface in August and September 2024.

It matched water measured off the river mouth to the south.

In earlier summers, when the river’s flow was negligible, the two sites looked distinct.

Ocean models show the coastal current turned northward in August 2024, right when the freshening appeared.

Dimethyl trisulfide wasn’t alone, either. Among hundreds of compounds the team measured, a group rose and fell with the river’s flow and with the tracer.

Their chemistry fell in a middle range: soluble enough to stay in seawater for the trip, volatile enough to leave it afterward.

The study did not measure whether the Tijuana River sewage chemicals reaching La Jolla’s air pose a health risk, and it covered one unusual season rather than a normal one.

The record at the pier runs less than a week past the diversion, so how the pattern changes over months is open.

Winter rains, shifting currents and changing river flows could all alter the pattern.

Porter said the result shows water and air pollution are not separate problems.

“You can’t just shut down the beach and call it good,” he said. “We need to clean up the water not just for swimming but for breathing.”

The next test is measuring the same chemicals in the water and the air at once, at several depths, through a full year.

That would show how often the ocean carries sewage chemicals this far, and how much escapes into the air.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.
