#6305. Five cows abandoned on a remote island in 1871 grew into a herd of about 2,000 despite extreme inbreeding

Five cattle introduced to Amsterdam Island in 1871 grew into a herd of 2,000 before being eradicated in 2010.

In 1871, a French farmer from La Réunion brought five cattle to Amsterdam Island, in the southern Indian Ocean, and left them there.

Their descendants peaked at about 2,000 animals. A 2024 genomic study found the herd highly inbred, with average inbreeding of 33 percent.

The animals showed no significant purging of their most harmful mutations, yet the population persisted until it was eradicated in 2010. Their genomes point to a brief founding bottleneck and an ancestry already suited to the island.

Amsterdam Island covers about 21 square miles (55 square kilometers) and lies some 2,760 miles (4,440 kilometers) southeast of Madagascar. It belongs to the French Southern and Antarctic Lands.

Once ashore, the cattle roamed and bred freely. They “thrived within a few generations in a seemingly inhospitable environment,” the researchers wrote.

The herd reached peaks of around 2,000 animals in 1952 and again in 1988. A sharp decline in 1953 followed an outbreak of infectious disease, probably paratuberculosis.

Concern that the cattle threatened endemic species led to control measures from 1988, aimed at restoring the island’s terrestrial ecosystem. Culls took place in 1988 and 1993, and the herd was eradicated in 2010 following a decision by the authorities.

The herd was controlled by shooting and fencing to protect the Amsterdam albatross, a seabird found only on the island. The fences came down once they were no longer needed, according to the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP).

Mathieu Gautier of the Centre for Biology and Management of Populations in Montpellier, France, led the research, published online in June 2024.

Laurence Flori, also in Montpellier, and Tom Druet of the University of Liège in Belgium were joint senior authors. The team genotyped 18 animals, 12 collected in 1992 and six in 2006, and sequenced the whole genomes of eight females from the 1992 group.

The herd’s ancestry mixed two cattle groups. About 73.1 percent came from European taurine cattle and about 26.9 percent from Indian Ocean zebu, with uncertainty ranges of roughly 71 to 77 percent and 23 to 29 percent.

All eight sequenced animals carried the same maternal lineage, mitochondrial haplogroup T1b1. That lineage is found in most African cattle, including African zebus.

The two ancestries mixed almost at the same time as the herd was founded. Assuming a six-year generation time, the estimate puts that mixing around 1860, give or take 15 years.

Genome-based models point to an intense but brief bottleneck in the late 19th century. Using a method called GONE, they estimate that about 20 generations ago, the effective population size fell to about 4.8.

Effective population size measures how many animals actually pass on their genes, not how many are alive. The same models put the herd’s later effective size at about 1,500, and they showed no sign of a decline tied to the 1950s disease outbreak.

Most of the inbreeding arose a few generations after the bottleneck, in ancestors living about 15 generations back. Because the population expanded quickly, little new inbreeding built up later.

The herd’s autozygosity, the stretches of DNA carried in two identical copies from a shared ancestor, was mainly related to the founder event.

Average inbreeding barely changed between the two sampling years, from 32.6 percent in 1992 to 32.9 percent in 2006. Genetic diversity fell only moderately despite the high inbreeding.

Inbreeding can expose harmful recessive mutations, which show their effects only when an animal inherits two copies. Natural selection can then weed them out, a process called purging.

Genetic drift is the random change in gene variant frequencies from one generation to the next, and it is strongest in small populations.

On Amsterdam Island, the genomes showed high drift and slightly weaker selection against mildly harmful variants.

Unlike some populations that have stayed small for a long time, the herd showed no significant purging of highly harmful variants.

The bottleneck also left a flatter spread of gene variant frequencies across the genome, a signature of strong genetic drift.

The authors attribute the herd’s success in a harsh environment to preadaptation inherited from its European taurine ancestors.

That suggests the island posed no strong climatic challenge. It also contradicts earlier claims, based on crude physical data, that the cattle had shrunk through island dwarfism.

A scan of the genomes for signs of selection pointed mostly to genes related to nervous system function. The researchers link those genes to rapid feralization, as domestic animals returned to a free-roaming life.

That shift was driven by changes in behavior and complex social restructuring, according to the study.

The herd offers insight into how populations can establish themselves quickly and adapt in challenging environments. Feral populations like this one also carry unique genetic legacies that raise ethical questions for conservation efforts.

The study was published in the journal Molecular Biology and Evolution.

#6304. Most transgender youth satisfied after choosing hormone therapy

Taking gender-affirming hormone therapy was the right decision for 97 percent surveyed

Demonstrators rally at the U.S. Supreme Court in 2025 in support of gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. The vast majority of transgender and gender diverse young people are satisfied with their decision to take hormone therapy, according the largest survey on the topic.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, said they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”

Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

The new research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

#6302. Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical?

Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical shapes, such as ovals or pears, depending on composition?

Bodies large enough to be considered planets have enough mass that gravity molds them into a roughly spherical shape.

The key word here is roughly — other factors also come into play, such as a planet’s composition (rocky or gassy) and its rate of spin. The faster a planet spins, the more its rotation causes it to bulge outward at the equator. That’s because as a planet rotates, there’s a tug-of-war between the way material wants to fly off the planet due to rotation and the way gravity wants to pull all that planet’s material inward. The battle between these forces is most intense at the equator.

In our solar system, Mercury and Venus are slowly spinning rocky planets; therefore, they are the most spherical of the Sun’s worlds.

Earth and Mars spin a little faster, so they are about 0.3% and 0.6% thicker at the equator than the poles, respectively. This shape is called an oblate spheroid. However, because these planets have a solid surface that is higher in some places than others, they are not perfect oblate spheroids — they are minutely lumpy and bumpy, as data from orbiting satellites have detailed. In fact, the surface area of Earth’s Southern Hemisphere is very slightly larger than its Northern Hemisphere, making Earth marginally pear-shaped. It’s important to note, however, that despite these deviations, Earth is still almost spherical — if you used a basketball to represent the shape of our planet, its deviation from a perfect sphere would be only about 0.03 inch (0.08 centimeter) at the middle.

The gas giants Jupiter and Saturn bulge outward the most — Jupiter is nearly 7% thicker at its equator than its poles, and Saturn is 10.7% thicker around the middle. Ice giants Uranus and Neptune have smaller central bulges, only 2.3% and 1.7% thicker at the equator, respectively.

What about exoplanets, though? Some planetary systems we’ve found experience much more extreme conditions, with large, gassy planets orbiting very close to their stars (called hot Jupiters). One of these hot Jupiters is WASP-121 b, which orbits a blazingly hot star. In fact, this planet orbits so closely to its star that gravitational forces have stretched it out into a football shape. Astronomers believe that if the planet were much closer to its star, it would be ripped apart entirely.

In addition to its stretched-out shape, WASP-121 b and other planets, including WASP-69 b and KELT-9 b, appear to have puffed-up atmospheres and cometlike tails. These tails form as their host stars blast the planets with high-energy radiation, knocking gas particles into space.

As for pear-shaped exoplanets, astronomers haven’t found anything to suggest they exist to the extent you’re likely picturing. Other terrestrial planets likely have deformations similar to Earth’s — or perhaps slightly more extreme — but even “extreme” in this case probably translates to a planet appearing essentially spherical from a great distance.

This question and answer were originally published online October 24, 2020.

#6301. Scientists find a way to spot planets hidden in Webb’s images

New software helps Webb spot faint planets by modeling stellar glare, revealing a planetary signal missed in earlier image processing.

Photographing faint planets around other stars requires exceptionally stable telescope optics. Even the James Webb Space Telescope’s optical components can shift by a few nanometers during observations.

A shift that small changes the glare around a star enough to swamp a planet’s light.

A team led from Northwestern University has now reduced the effects of those shifts with software instead of hardware.

Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a doctoral student at Northwestern University and its astrophysics center, CIERA, led the work with his adviser, Jason Wang.

The team’s program builds a working model of Webb’s own optics and tunes it until the model’s starlight matches the real glare, wobbles included.

Run on Webb images taken two years ago, it picked out the giant planet 51 Eridani b at a wavelength where standard processing had found nothing.

Across four sets of observations, it made Webb two to 15 times more sensitive to faint planets.

“That is a very tricky problem because even the tiniest changes in the telescope can affect how that glare appears,” Ferrer-Chavez said.

“Slight shifts or tilts – even on the scale of just a few nanometers – can change the pattern of light.”

Young giant planets shine at about one hundred-thousandth the brightness of their stars in infrared light.

A mask inside the camera, called a coronagraph, blocks most of the starlight. A halo of leftover glare remains, and a planet has to be found inside it.

For about 20 years, astronomers have handled that halo by photographing a second, planet-free star and subtracting its glare from the first image.

The method works best when the telescope’s optics remain unchanged between observations.

The optics do not remain perfectly stable.

Pointing errors and heat drifts change the optics between one picture and the next, so the two halos don’t match.

That mismatch sets the limit on how faint a planet can be.

Wang said engineers try to make telescopes extremely stable and haven’t fully succeeded. “Small thermal changes could cause a mirror to expand or contract by a picometer,” he said.

“Telescopes like JWST have cryocoolers to keep the instrument super cold. Those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate.”

The team’s program, called FLIP, starts from the standard computer model of Webb’s optics maintained by the Space Telescope Science Institute.

It adds about a million adjustable settings for the mirrors, the position of the star behind the mask and the response of every pixel.

Then it nudges those settings until the simulated glare matches a real image.

The nudging uses the mathematical machinery that trains artificial intelligence, which can adjust millions of settings at once.

“We used the same computational tools that researchers use to train AI models, but we did not actually use AI,” Wang said. “Because we already know the physics, we don’t need AI to understand what’s happening.”

FLIP first tunes itself on a reference star, then fine-tunes on the image that might hold a planet.

To keep it from erasing a real planet along with the glare, the team plants fake planets in the image and stops the fitting when their signals stop improving.

A full run takes about 35 minutes on a single graphics card.

The team reprocessed published Webb images of three stars and compared FLIP with the standard method on each.

Around HIP 65426, the known planet’s signal was about 1.6 times stronger. Around 51 Eridani, the planet’s signal doubled at one wavelength.

At 4.3 micrometers, where the original analysis had found nothing, FLIP produced a detection.

The 4.3-micrometer band matters because carbon dioxide in the planet’s atmosphere absorbs light there, which is part of why the planet was so faint.

Earth’s own atmosphere blocks that light, so no telescope on the ground can make the measurement.

The third star, TYC 5899, has no known planets, and its reference images were taken four months before the science image, the kind of gap that defeats the standard method.

FLIP still recovered a fake planet planted in the data that the standard method missed. Close to the star, it was about 15 times more sensitive.

“We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn’t see,” Wang said. “This is real data in a real scenario.”

In all four observations, residual glare still limited FLIP’s sensitivity, leaving room for further improvement.

The authors also wrote that their model can correct for the telescope’s small shifts but hasn’t yet been calibrated to measure them.

The detector model and the computing cost both need work, they wrote.

The team’s next step is to measure the planet’s brightness at 4.3 micrometers and test earlier hints that its atmosphere holds about five times the heavy elements of its star.

More than 100 Webb observations have been taken in surveys like the one that produced the TYC 5899 image. The team wrote that the discovery potential of reprocessing them is large.

The biggest test the authors named is NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, designed to photograph Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars.

Current plans call for it to hold steady to about a picometer, 100 to 1,000 times steadier than Webb.

Whether software can ease that requirement hasn’t been tested, and the authors pointed to the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope as the place to find out.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

As NASA's Voyager 1 probe reaches one light-day from Earth, we look back at its legendary photos of Jupiter that changed our view of the solar system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a new milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

One of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

Voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which launched half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

Just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation showed that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

Taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons showed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency announced its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#6299. Earth’s magnetic poles flipped repeatedly before an ancient mass extinction

Ancient rocks in southern China reveal that Earth’s magnetic field reversed roughly every 90,000 years before a Permian mass extinction.

Earth’s magnetic field may seem like a permanent fixture, but its north and south poles have repeatedly switched places.

About 261 million years ago it was swapping them roughly 11 times every million years, one of the fastest rates ever recorded.

The burst of flipping ran right up to one of the planet’s major mass extinctions. The geologists who measured it think the two may be connected, though they can’t yet prove it.

Min Zhang led the work with Yongxin Pan, both at the Institute of Geology and Geophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Shu-zhong Shen of Nanjing University.

Colleagues at Utrecht University and BOKU University in Vienna took part.

Earth’s field comes from liquid iron churning in the outer core. Heat leaving the core drives that churning, so when the pattern of heat loss changes, the field changes too.

One of the ways the magnetic field changes is by flipping, north becoming south.

For about 50 million years, from roughly 318 to 265 million years ago, the field didn’t flip at all. Geologists call that stretch the Kiaman Superchron, and it is the longest run of stable polarity known.

Then the stable stretch ended, and what came next had been only patchily measured.

Few places kept laying down sediment while sea levels fell worldwide, so the rock layers that would record the field are missing in most places.

The Fengshan section, a limestone outcrop near Liuzhou in southern China, is one of the few places where those years survive without a gap.

The limestone formed on a shallow seafloor close to the equator. Its fossils are rich enough that geologists use it as a reference point for one of the Permian’s boundaries.

As the limestone formed, grains of the iron mineral hematite inside it lined up with the magnetic field of the day and then locked in place.

Zhang’s team collected 876 oriented samples from two parts of the outcrop and heated each one in steps up to 1,274°F (690°C). Heating removes the magnetic signals the rock picked up later and leaves the original one.

Only 309 of the 876 samples, about a third, gave a clean reading. The other 567 were too scrambled to use.

A flip counted only when at least three clean samples in a row showed the same new polarity.

Stacked together, the two parts of the outcrop record 29 stretches of one polarity or the other across 3.75 million years, from about 262.5 to 258.75 million years ago.

The flips were not spread evenly. In the first 750,000 years the field reversed fewer than five times per million years.

The researchers identified a period of unusually frequent reversals before the end-Guadalupian extinction, with an estimated rate of about 11 per million years.

Eleven reversals per million years is a flip roughly every 90,000 years, on a planet that had just gone 50 million years without one.

After the extinction the field flipped less often, with only three more polarity stretches in the rest of the record.

The extinction itself, about 261 million years ago, is the smaller of the Permian’s two great mass extinctions, but reef ecosystems collapsed and marine life was decimated.

The usual explanation is a huge outpouring of lava known as the Emeishan large igneous province, plus falling seas and lost habitat as Pangea finished assembling.

Why would the field go from 50 million years of stability to flipping every 90,000 years?

As the continents came together to form Pangea, slabs of old ocean floor were pushed down into the mantle.

Such slabs can take several tens of millions of years to sink to the base of the mantle.

By the late middle Permian, the authors suggested, slabs from Pangea’s assembly may have arrived there.

A cold slab reaching the bottom of the mantle would draw extra heat out of the core beneath it. The core would then lose heat faster in some places than in others.

Computer simulations of the core show that uneven heat loss like that makes the field flip more often.

The authors were careful about those simulations. All of them run under conditions far from the real Earth’s, they wrote, and their results depend heavily on the settings chosen.

The field matters to life because it deflects most of the charged particles streaming in from the Sun and deep space. A field that flips often may also be weaker.

Earlier studies did estimate the field’s strength through the Permian, and those estimates fall from the middle of the period to its end.

The researchers noted that they vary a lot in quality, though.

With a weaker field, more of those particles would reach the upper atmosphere.

The authors laid out a series of possible effects from there: ozone destroyed, oxygen lost to space, and more ultraviolet light reaching the ground.

Malformed pollen and plants with extra UV-protective compounds have been found at the end-Permian extinction, about nine million years later.

For the end-Guadalupian event, the team wrote, direct evidence of that kind is still limited.

Volcanic eruptions are a competing explanation for any ozone loss, because the lava outpourings may have released halogens that destroy ozone.

A weaker field would allow more charged particles to reach the upper atmosphere, but frequent reversals alone do not establish how weak it became.

One gap is the field’s strength. A weak field, not a flipping one, is what would let radiation through, and the authors wrote that better strength records across this same interval are needed.

Tighter dates and computer models that connect the core to the atmosphere are the other two items on their list.

For now, the Fengshan limestone records unusually frequent magnetic reversals before a major mass extinction, while leaving their possible connection unresolved.

The full study was published in the journal National Science Review.

#6298. Nov. 16, 1974: Arecibo sends a message

On Nov. 16, 1974, a group gathered at Arecibo Observatory in the rainforest interior of Puerto Rico, there for a reopening celebration after upgrades to the facility. After the requisite speeches, scientists used the radio telescope to send what would be known as the Arecibo message: 1,679 bits of data in 73 lines, each 23 characters long. To the assembled crowd, the dispatch sounded like nearly three minutes of two tones. But encoded in those tones was message crafted by a team of scientists led by Frank Drake and including Carl Sagan: a rough illustration of a human, the structure of a DNA double helix, and a map of the Earth’s position in the solar system.

The communication was aimed at M13, a globular cluster about 25,000 light-years away in Hercules. Since it would take thousands of years for the signal to arrive there – not to mention time for a signal to be sent back by any extraterrestrial civilization that intercepted it – the Arecibo message wasn’t so much an actual attempt at communication as it was a demonstration of how we might do so.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6296. We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI worms could spread like octopuses or slime molds, exploiting smart devices

Common forms of cyberattack include viruses and worms. Researchers recently added new styles of attack to the twisted menagerie: worms that act more like octopuses or slime molds.

VICTOR HABBICK VISIONS/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

AI is already powering new, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams showed how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a new worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, says AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”

Here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

Historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, says Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments showed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

And there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.)

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan says. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

“The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler says. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

The Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan says.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

The octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a new device, the head would use AI to plan how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler says. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover new places to copy itself (third image).

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026

The head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan says.)

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan says they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers showed another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work shows that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

Anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that showed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan says. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler says.

Guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan says. “We are working on the problem day and night.”

#6295. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.
